Chapter 30 · Intermediate

Chapter 30 — SSH: encrypted remote access, identity keys and host trust

Bits to Banking · System Administration: From Zero · Umicom Foundation

Audience: first-time users and returning learners; practical examples appropriate for supervised younger learners.

Estimated study time: 50–80 minutes.

Prerequisites: Chapters 15–18 and 34 (read 34 later for extended security).

Why this matters

A contributor wants to inspect a Linux test machine from a Windows laptop. SSH can provide encrypted access, but the learner must understand two different kinds of trust: proving that the server is the intended server and proving to the server who the user is. Mixing those questions is a common source of security mistakes.

What you will be able to do

By the end of this chapter you should be able to explain the new terms in ordinary language, select a safe read-only command for the right operating system, recognise a normal result and identify an unverified result. You should also be able to describe what permission would be needed before making a real system change.

The mental model

An SSH client contacts an SSH server over a network connection, commonly TCP port 22. The server presents a host key so the client can recognise the same server in future sessions. The client can authenticate with a password or user key pair, subject to server policy. A private key is secret and remains on your computer; a public key can be registered with authorised servers. The known_hosts file remembers server host keys. A changed host-key warning is a trust event requiring verification, not an inconvenience to suppress with StrictHostKeyChecking=no.

What a trustworthy first SSH connection looks like

Before connecting, the learner must know the hostname or address from a trusted administrator, their authorised username and the expected server host-key fingerprint. The host key may be new because the machine has never been contacted, but that does not make an unverified first connection automatically trustworthy. Once the administrator confirms the fingerprint independently, the client can establish a recorded identity for future connections.

An SSH public key file ending in .pub is intended to be distributed for authentication. The matching private key is not. Do not paste either into commands from a stranger who says it is required to repair GitHub authentication. You may see SSH used for Git transport (git@github.com:...) without ever opening an interactive server terminal; the same cryptographic trust concepts apply, but the permitted operations differ.

Words you should know

Term Meaning
SSH Secure Shell, a protocol for authenticated and encrypted remote sessions.
Host key A server identity key checked by the client.
Private key Secret half of an authentication key pair.
Public key The shareable half used to verify signatures.
Known hosts A client-side record of recognised server identities.

Windows: PowerShell 7, one command at a time

Use a normal non-elevated PowerShell window. Do not type the PS C:\...> prompt. If a command is unavailable or returns Access Denied, record that result; do not attempt to defeat the restriction.

The lines in a code block may contain more than one interactive command. Run them in order, checking each result before continuing. No .ps1 file is created or required.

Windows step 1 — Check whether the SSH client exists

Get-Command ssh -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Expected result: An application path appears if OpenSSH client is installed.

What this does: PowerShell runs the command in your current session and displays information or, where clearly indicated, changes only your own practice files. If output differs, record the actual result before going further.

Windows step 2 — Read the OpenSSH version

ssh -V

Expected result: A version line often appears on the error stream; no network connection is made.

What this does: PowerShell runs the command in your current session and displays information or, where clearly indicated, changes only your own practice files. If output differs, record the actual result before going further.

Windows step 3 — Check for an existing training key without opening it

Test-Path "$HOME\.ssh\umicom_training_ed25519"

Expected result: True means a private training key file with this name exists. Do not overwrite it.

What this does: PowerShell runs the command in your current session and displays information or, where clearly indicated, changes only your own practice files. If output differs, record the actual result before going further.

Windows step 4 — Inspect only the public key fingerprint if a public key exists

ssh-keygen -lf "$HOME\.ssh\umicom_training_ed25519.pub"

Expected result: Displays a public-key fingerprint. If the file does not exist, skip this step.

What this does: PowerShell runs the command in your current session and displays information or, where clearly indicated, changes only your own practice files. If output differs, record the actual result before going further.

Linux: terminal and distribution differences

Run the following only in an authorised Linux computer or VM. If you use Windows only, read this section for comparison. A program being absent does not mean the whole operating system is faulty.

Linux step 1 — Confirm the SSH client is available

ssh -V

Expected result: Outputs the installed OpenSSH client version.

Linux step 2 — Inspect your own SSH folder metadata, if present

ls -ld "$HOME/.ssh"

Expected result: Permissions and owner; if the folder is absent, that is not an error for first-time users.

Linux step 3 — Inspect public keys only, when present

ls -l "$HOME/.ssh"/*.pub

Expected result: Lists public key files; if none exist, shell glob behaviour differs by shell.

Worked support scenario

During a scheduled lesson, a previously used SSH host suddenly reports that its host key changed. Do not remove the known-host entry automatically. Ask the administrator to verify the machine fingerprint by a trusted independent channel, such as the console or approved inventory. Only after that verification should the client record the new identity. Never email or publish private key contents, password prompts or sensitive host details.

Common mistakes and safe responses

Mistake Better response
“A public SSH key is the password.” The public key is not secret; the private key must remain protected.
“Delete known_hosts whenever there is a warning.” Host-key warnings can indicate a legitimate rebuild or an attack; verify independently.
“The port being open means login is safe.” Connectivity alone does not prove server identity or permission to connect.

Exercises

  1. Explain the difference between a server host key and a user authentication key.

  2. Check ssh -V without contacting a remote machine.

  3. Write a safe response to an unexpected host-key warning.

Review questions and suggested answers

Show the suggested answers after attempting the exercises

  1. Host key identifies the server; a user key pair can authenticate the client.

  2. The command is local and read-only.

  3. Stop, preserve the warning, verify the expected fingerprint through an authorised channel, then proceed only after confirmation.

Chapter 31 · Intermediate

Chapter 31 — Diagnose DNS, TCP ports and firewall boundaries

Bits to Banking · System Administration: From Zero · Umicom Foundation

Audience: first-time users and returning learners; practical examples appropriate for supervised younger learners.

Estimated study time: 55–85 minutes.

Prerequisites: Chapters 15–16.

Why this matters

A browser says a learning website cannot be reached. The problem might be its name, the network route, the server process, its listening port or a security policy. A single failed test cannot reliably distinguish these possibilities. System administrators isolate one layer at a time.

What you will be able to do

By the end of this chapter you should be able to explain the new terms in ordinary language, select a safe read-only command for the right operating system, recognise a normal result and identify an unverified result. You should also be able to describe what permission would be needed before making a real system change.

The mental model

A hostname such as example.com is a human-friendly identifier. DNS translates names into addresses; the application then attempts a connection to a server address and port. A successful DNS lookup does not prove TCP reachability. A successful TCP connection does not prove that the HTTP service returns a correct application response. A ping refusal also does not prove that a web service is down because ICMP can be blocked. A firewall applies policy to traffic; it should never be disabled wholesale merely to “see if that fixes it”.

Make each network check answer only one question

Name resolution asks “which address should this name refer to?”. A TCP connection asks “did I reach an accepting endpoint on this port?”. An HTTPS request asks “did the web server negotiate transport security and return an application-level response?”. The three checks build on one another but cannot be substituted for each other. A successful TCP probe on 443 does not prove that the certificate is trusted, the application is authenticated or the requested page exists.

Be precise about localhost. 127.0.0.1 always refers to the same host network namespace that issued the request; it does not refer to your colleague’s machine. In containers or virtual machines, the localhost of one environment is often different from the host's localhost. An educational server bound to loopback should not be exposed externally just to make a remote demo work. Use approved routing and listen policies instead.

Words you should know

Term Meaning
DNS System that maps domain names to resource records such as IP addresses.
TCP Connection-oriented transport protocol used by many services.
Port Number identifying a service endpoint at a host.
Firewall Policy enforcement point controlling network traffic.
Loopback Local network interface, normally 127.0.0.1 or ::1.

Windows: PowerShell 7, one command at a time

Use a normal non-elevated PowerShell window. Do not type the PS C:\...> prompt. If a command is unavailable or returns Access Denied, record that result; do not attempt to defeat the restriction.

The lines in a code block may contain more than one interactive command. Run them in order, checking each result before continuing. No .ps1 file is created or required.

Windows step 1 — Inspect an ordinary public DNS name

Resolve-DnsName example.com

Expected result: A or AAAA address records can appear. If DNS is not configured, record the failure.

What this does: PowerShell runs the command in your current session and displays information or, where clearly indicated, changes only your own practice files. If output differs, record the actual result before going further.

Windows step 2 — Test a documented HTTPS endpoint

Test-NetConnection -ComputerName example.com -Port 443

Expected result: TcpTestSucceeded indicates whether a TCP connection succeeded during this attempt; it is not an HTTP application test.

What this does: PowerShell runs the command in your current session and displays information or, where clearly indicated, changes only your own practice files. If output differs, record the actual result before going further.

Windows step 3 — View local TCP listeners

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | Select-Object -First 12 LocalAddress, LocalPort, OwningProcess

Expected result: Shows bound sockets when the cmdlet is available; no firewall rule changes.

What this does: PowerShell runs the command in your current session and displays information or, where clearly indicated, changes only your own practice files. If output differs, record the actual result before going further.

Windows step 4 — Fetch only response headers

curl.exe --head https://example.com/

Expected result: Shows an HTTP result if the host/network permits access. curl.exe avoids the older Windows PowerShell alias ambiguity.

What this does: PowerShell runs the command in your current session and displays information or, where clearly indicated, changes only your own practice files. If output differs, record the actual result before going further.

Linux: terminal and distribution differences

Run the following only in an authorised Linux computer or VM. If you use Windows only, read this section for comparison. A program being absent does not mean the whole operating system is faulty.

Linux step 1 — Resolve the same name

getent ahosts example.com

Expected result: Address records as provided by the host name service configuration.

Linux step 2 — List locally listening TCP endpoints

ss -ltn

Expected result: Listening sockets; process owners may be hidden without permissions.

Linux step 3 — Ask for HTTPS headers only

curl -I https://example.com/

Expected result: The response is subject to network policies; no login should be necessary.

Worked support scenario

A local C23 HTTP server is expected at 127.0.0.1:8765. First verify the server actually started and recorded its bind address. Then try curl.exe -i http://127.0.0.1:8765/ on Windows or curl -i http://127.0.0.1:8765/ on Linux. A connection refusal means no acceptor is reachable at that endpoint; it is not an instruction to turn off the firewall or expose the service publicly. The test remains loopback-only.

Common mistakes and safe responses

Mistake Better response
“The hostname resolves, so the site must be healthy.” DNS covers name resolution, not application response.
“Ping fails, therefore the computer is offline.” ICMP may be blocked while TCP services are reachable.
“Fix the problem by disabling the firewall.” Preserve security controls and investigate the exact path, port and allowed policy.

Exercises

  1. Explain the difference between a DNS failure and a TCP connection refusal.

  2. Run one read-only network probe against an approved public or loopback endpoint.

  3. Draw the path from browser to hostname, address, port and application response.

Review questions and suggested answers

Show the suggested answers after attempting the exercises

  1. DNS failure means no usable name resolution; refusal occurs after addressing when no accepting endpoint is reached.

  2. Record endpoint, time, command and result.

  3. Browser → DNS → IP routing → TCP endpoint → HTTP application is a useful outline.

Chapter 32 · Intermediate

Chapter 32 — Understand disk space, filesystems and safe capacity checks

Bits to Banking · System Administration: From Zero · Umicom Foundation

Audience: first-time users and returning learners; practical examples appropriate for supervised younger learners.

Estimated study time: 45–70 minutes.

Prerequisites: Chapters 13–14.

Why this matters

A training application fails to save a file. Before touching configuration, check whether the destination exists, whether the user can write there and whether sufficient storage is available. Disk capacity is a finite resource, and different storage layers can fail for different reasons.

What you will be able to do

By the end of this chapter you should be able to explain the new terms in ordinary language, select a safe read-only command for the right operating system, recognise a normal result and identify an unverified result. You should also be able to describe what permission would be needed before making a real system change.

The mental model

A physical disk stores data, while a partition or volume describes a managed region. A filesystem organises files and directories within a volume. Windows frequently uses NTFS and drive letters; Linux often mounts filesystems at directories such as /home and /var. Free space is different from free inodes on some filesystems: a Linux volume can have available bytes but run out of metadata entries. A disk can have free space and still produce I/O errors. Reading filesystem information is a safe first step; formatting, repartitioning or repairing a device is not part of this beginner course.

Why administrators treat available space as evidence, not a repair instruction

A file save can fail because the filesystem is full, but the same symptom may come from permissions, a stale path, locked files or quota rules. When a compiler prints “no space left”, identify the exact output path and mount point before clearing anything. Build directories contain reproducible artefacts, yet they can also contain logs and diagnostic evidence important to an investigation. Removing a build folder without review may make the original failure impossible to reproduce.

Storage reports can also differ across tools. Free disk blocks, available blocks for ordinary users, filesystem quota and cloud-drive availability are not necessarily the same quantity. A percent utilisation indicator is an overview, not an exact promise that a particular file can be written. System administrators keep the measurements alongside the workload and timestamp.

Words you should know

Term Meaning
Volume A managed filesystem storage unit or logical drive.
Filesystem Rules that map filenames and metadata to stored content.
Mount point Directory through which a Linux filesystem is accessed.
Free space Capacity available for new data.
Inode Unix-like filesystem metadata object identifying a file.

Windows: PowerShell 7, one command at a time

Use a normal non-elevated PowerShell window. Do not type the PS C:\...> prompt. If a command is unavailable or returns Access Denied, record that result; do not attempt to defeat the restriction.

The lines in a code block may contain more than one interactive command. Run them in order, checking each result before continuing. No .ps1 file is created or required.

Windows step 1 — List mounted file-system drives

Get-PSDrive -PSProvider FileSystem

Expected result: Drives with free and used space appear when the provider supports those properties.

What this does: PowerShell runs the command in your current session and displays information or, where clearly indicated, changes only your own practice files. If output differs, record the actual result before going further.

Windows step 2 — Inspect volume details where available

Get-Volume | Select-Object DriveLetter, FileSystem, SizeRemaining, Size

Expected result: Volumes are listed. A machine may restrict some fields or omit removable volumes.

What this does: PowerShell runs the command in your current session and displays information or, where clearly indicated, changes only your own practice files. If output differs, record the actual result before going further.

Windows step 3 — Check the size of your sample learning file

Get-Item "$HOME\UmicomLearning\Notes\README.md" | Select-Object Name, Length

Expected result: Shows file size in bytes if the practice file exists.

What this does: PowerShell runs the command in your current session and displays information or, where clearly indicated, changes only your own practice files. If output differs, record the actual result before going further.

Windows step 4 — Identify the exact practice directory

Resolve-Path "$HOME\UmicomLearning"

Expected result: Shows the resolved location; never assume a sample directory sits on the intended drive.

What this does: PowerShell runs the command in your current session and displays information or, where clearly indicated, changes only your own practice files. If output differs, record the actual result before going further.

Linux: terminal and distribution differences

Run the following only in an authorised Linux computer or VM. If you use Windows only, read this section for comparison. A program being absent does not mean the whole operating system is faulty.

Linux step 1 — Check mounted filesystem usage

df -h "$HOME"

Expected result: Disk capacity of the filesystem containing your home directory.

Linux step 2 — Check inode usage when relevant

df -i "$HOME"

Expected result: Displays metadata-entry utilisation on supported filesystems.

Linux step 3 — Read-only summary of block devices

lsblk -f

Expected result: Device and filesystem metadata; may be limited inside containers.

Worked support scenario

An Umicom student cannot build the C23 laboratory because linking reports No space left on device. Save the first error, inspect the filesystem containing the build output, and record its available space. Do not delete source files or run git clean automatically. The safest next step may be requesting additional space or reviewing generated build artefacts under a clearly identified temporary build directory with its owner.

Common mistakes and safe responses

Mistake Better response
“The C: drive has space, so every path has space.” Output may be redirected to another volume or network share.
“A full disk means files must be deleted immediately.” Confirm the owning workspace and approved retention/backup policy first.
“A percentage tells the complete storage health story.” I/O errors, failing hardware and quotas also matter.

Exercises

  1. Explain how a partition differs from a filesystem.

  2. Check free space on your own practice workspace without changing files.

  3. Identify two reasons a save could fail despite available disk space.

Review questions and suggested answers

Show the suggested answers after attempting the exercises

  1. Partition divides a device; filesystem organises and names stored data.

  2. Use Get-PSDrive or df -h.

  3. Permissions, quotas, file locks, filesystem errors or invalid paths may block writes.

Chapter 33 · Intermediate

Chapter 33 — Backups, restore drills and proving that recovery works

Bits to Banking · System Administration: From Zero · Umicom Foundation

Audience: first-time users and returning learners; practical examples appropriate for supervised younger learners.

Estimated study time: 60–90 minutes.

Prerequisites: Chapter 14 and Chapter 7.

Why this matters

A backup file exists, but does it contain the latest version? Can it actually be opened? A backup strategy is useful only when a restore can be demonstrated. In this practical exercise we will make a copy of your own harmless training README and restore that copy to a separate test location.

What you will be able to do

By the end of this chapter you should be able to explain the new terms in ordinary language, select a safe read-only command for the right operating system, recognise a normal result and identify an unverified result. You should also be able to describe what permission would be needed before making a real system change.

The mental model

The common 3-2-1 planning heuristic describes three copies of important data, on two types of storage, with at least one copy elsewhere. It is not a substitute for considering encryption, retention, access controls, immutable copies or ransomware. A backup is a recoverable copy; a restore drill proves whether it can be used; a hash helps compare exact bytes. A matching SHA-256 digest of two files is strong evidence that their contents match, but it does not prove the backup job had permission to capture every required file or that a complete application can be restored.

The difference between a safe sample restore and disaster recovery

In this lesson the restored file is a Markdown README. That is deliberate. A banking ledger, medical record system or live treasury service may store interconnected files, transaction logs and databases. Copying only one database file while the server is changing it can create an inconsistent backup. Production recovery needs application-aware snapshots, tested dependencies, security controls and a documented sequence to return the complete service safely.

The training drill also protects the previous copy. We first check whether the destination exists, then copy the practice file, then hash both copies, then restore to a third location. These stages are observable and reversible. A good restore runbook names the original source, backup location, restore destination and result of a meaningful application-level check. The very first lesson for a beginner is that verifying a backup means testing what can be recovered—not merely counting backup files.

Words you should know

Term Meaning
Restore drill A controlled trial that recovers data from a backup.
Retention How long copies must be preserved.
RPO Recovery Point Objective: acceptable data loss measured in time.
RTO Recovery Time Objective: acceptable time to restore a service.
Checksum/hash A compact calculated value used to compare content identity.

Windows: PowerShell 7, one command at a time

Use a normal non-elevated PowerShell window. Do not type the PS C:\...> prompt. If a command is unavailable or returns Access Denied, record that result; do not attempt to defeat the restriction.

Windows step 1 — Check the training source and stop if missing

Test-Path "$HOME\UmicomLearning\Notes\README.md"

Expected result: Proceed only if True. Do not substitute an actual private work document.

What this does: PowerShell runs the command in your current session and displays information or, where clearly indicated, changes only your own practice files. If output differs, record the actual result before going further.

Windows step 2 — Create a dedicated backup practice folder

What this does: PowerShell runs the command in your current session and displays information or, where clearly indicated, changes only your own practice files. If output differs, record the actual result before going further.

What this does: PowerShell runs the command in your current session and displays information or, where clearly indicated, changes only your own practice files. If output differs, record the actual result before going further.

What this does: PowerShell runs the command in your current session and displays information or, where clearly indicated, changes only your own practice files. If output differs, record the actual result before going further.

Windows step 5 — Prove the copy matches the source

Get-FileHash "$HOME\UmicomLearning\Notes\README.md" -Algorithm SHA256
Get-FileHash "$HOME\UmicomLearning\BackupDrill\README-backup.md" -Algorithm SHA256

Expected result: The two hash values should match. These are two interactive commands, not a stored script.

What this does: PowerShell runs the command in your current session and displays information or, where clearly indicated, changes only your own practice files. If output differs, record the actual result before going further.

Windows step 6 — Restore into a different place and read it

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path "$HOME\UmicomLearning\RestoreDrill" -Force
Copy-Item -LiteralPath "$HOME\UmicomLearning\BackupDrill\README-backup.md" -Destination "$HOME\UmicomLearning\RestoreDrill\README.md"

Expected result: Only run when the restore destination is absent. The restored heading should be readable.

What this does: PowerShell runs the command in your current session and displays information or, where clearly indicated, changes only your own practice files. If output differs, record the actual result before going further.

Linux: terminal and distribution differences

Run the following only in an authorised Linux computer or VM. If you use Windows only, read this section for comparison. A program being absent does not mean the whole operating system is faulty.

Linux step 1 — Create two harmless practice folders

mkdir -p "$HOME/UmicomLearning/BackupDrill" "$HOME/UmicomLearning/RestoreDrill"

Expected result: Creates user-owned practice directories only.

Linux step 2 — Copy the example without replacing an existing backup

cp -n "$HOME/UmicomLearning/Notes/README.md" "$HOME/UmicomLearning/BackupDrill/README-backup.md"

Expected result: GNU cp -n refuses overwrite; inspect existence first to be certain the intended copy was made.

Expected result: Matching digests indicate the two read files have matching content.

Linux step 4 — Restore to a separate test folder

cp -n "$HOME/UmicomLearning/BackupDrill/README-backup.md" "$HOME/UmicomLearning/RestoreDrill/README.md"

Expected result: Do not run if a prior restored copy exists.

Worked support scenario

A course coordinator wants a backup of a volunteer-run support tracker before a software update. Describe how you would agree a restore target, define an RPO/RTO, prevent private information from leaking into public cloud storage, verify that the backup completed, and practise restoration to a separate safe environment. The classroom exercise uses only the README; no personal or financial information should be copied.

Common mistakes and safe responses

Mistake Better response
“Backup completed” means it can restore an application. A job log cannot prove a complete restore; test the actual recovery path.
“Never mind overwriting yesterday’s copy.” Overwriting the only previous snapshot removes a recovery point; use a retention policy.
“Publish a checksum and filenames publicly.” Paths and backup inventories can be sensitive. Keep evidence appropriately restricted.

Exercises

  1. Explain RPO and RTO using a training Notes service.

  2. Verify a separate, harmless restored file without opening private directories.

  3. State which additional steps a real production database would require beyond copying one README.

Review questions and suggested answers

Show the suggested answers after attempting the exercises

  1. RPO describes the age of acceptable restored state; RTO describes the time allowed to recover.

  2. Compare hashes and open the restored test file.

  3. Consistent snapshots, application-aware backup, database transaction recovery, permissions and operational acceptance.

Chapter 34 · Intermediate

Chapter 34 — Protect credentials, use MFA and practise least privilege

Bits to Banking · System Administration: From Zero · Umicom Foundation

Audience: first-time users and returning learners; practical examples appropriate for supervised younger learners.

Estimated study time: 45–70 minutes.

Prerequisites: Chapters 9, 19–20 and 25.

Why this matters

The most expensive mistake in an introductory Git lesson is not a syntax error: it is accidentally sharing a password or token in a repository, screenshot or support log. Good administration treats credentials as secrets from the beginning.

What you will be able to do

By the end of this chapter you should be able to explain the new terms in ordinary language, select a safe read-only command for the right operating system, recognise a normal result and identify an unverified result. You should also be able to describe what permission would be needed before making a real system change.

The mental model

A password is one authentication factor; a hardware authenticator or app-based challenge can provide an additional factor. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) reduces the risk of a stolen password being enough to sign in. A personal access token, SSH private key and API secret are all credentials even when they do not look like a password. Least privilege applies to humans and background services. Permission to administer a computer is separate from permission to access customer, patient or colleague data. Rotating a token after exposure is necessary, but repository history may still contain the leaked value and must be remediated according to project policy.

Where secrets accidentally leak during ordinary development

A shell command can reveal sensitive information in its arguments, console history, screenshots, diagnostic logs or copied support transcripts. A repository can preserve deleted lines inside Git history even after the working file looks clean. This is why we do not store secrets.env, personal access tokens, credentials or recovery codes in tracked source files. Template files may describe required variable names, but should never contain production values.

A properly delegated task should also limit what the account can do. A classroom contributor needs permission to edit a documentation fork, not to administer a production Linux server or view beneficiaries’ personal records. An Umicom application that needs to read published lessons should not automatically receive write access to security configuration. Security works best when permissions and ownership are designed before an incident forces emergency changes.

Words you should know

Term Meaning
MFA Authentication using at least two independent factors.
Token Credential issued for a defined application or operation.
Secret store Protected location or service for sensitive credentials.
UAC Windows prompt that controls privilege elevation.
Security incident Event where confidentiality, integrity or availability may be at risk.

Use a normal non-elevated PowerShell window. Do not type the PS C:\...> prompt. If a command is unavailable or returns Access Denied, record that result; do not attempt to defeat the restriction.

Worked support scenario

Someone accidentally commits secrets.env containing a service token. Do not just remove the line and push another commit: the secret may remain in history and in clones. Stop publication if possible, revoke/rotate the exposed credential, alert the authorised security contact, assess access and retention, and follow the repository’s approved history-remediation procedure. Avoid including the actual secret in a public incident ticket.

Common mistakes and safe responses

Mistake Better response
“Private GitHub repository means secrets are safe to commit.” Repo access can expand, history persists, and accounts can be compromised.
“Run every installer as Administrator.” Use standard privileges unless a legitimate installation step explicitly requires elevation.
“MFA is the same as a stronger password.” MFA adds a distinct authentication factor; it is not only password length.

  2. Explain why gh auth status is safer than displaying token files.

  3. Write the first four actions after discovering a leaked access token.

  1. SSH private key, OAuth or personal access token, API secret, recovery codes.

  2. It reports status without printing stored credentials.

  3. Stop exposure, revoke token, report appropriately, inspect impact and preserve evidence.

Chapter 35 · Intermediate

Chapter 35 — Read system metrics, logs and an incident timeline

Bits to Banking · System Administration: From Zero · Umicom Foundation

Audience: first-time users and returning learners; practical examples appropriate for supervised younger learners.

Estimated study time: 50–80 minutes.

Prerequisites: Chapters 12, 23 and 27.

Why this matters

At 09:00 a build starts. At 09:02 disk space drops. At 09:03 the linker fails. At 09:04 a service reports an error. Which event caused the failure? An experienced administrator gathers evidence in order rather than assuming the latest visible warning is the root cause.

What you will be able to do

By the end of this chapter you should be able to explain the new terms in ordinary language, select a safe read-only command for the right operating system, recognise a normal result and identify an unverified result. You should also be able to describe what permission would be needed before making a real system change.

The mental model

Observability means understanding a system from useful signals. Metrics are measurements such as available memory or request rate. Logs are event records containing timestamps and context. Traces describe the path of one operation across components. These signals are complementary: high CPU is not itself an error, and a log entry that says ERROR may describe an issue unrelated to the incident. Always record the time zone, host, process and source revision, because an event from yesterday’s version cannot prove today’s build behaviour.

How to avoid reading the wrong evidence

Metrics answer questions about quantities; logs record discrete events; traces connect work across components. A high number of log entries may be completely normal during build progress, while one concise linker error can block the entire application. The responsible investigator narrows the time window, searches for the first failing stage, and keeps a reference to the original raw output when permitted. Compiler warnings and test outcomes should be attributed to the exact CMake preset and source revision that produced them.

If two machines use different time zones, their “09:00” events may not be simultaneous. Prefer timestamps with offsets and note clock synchronisation. Also protect privacy when sharing diagnostic artefacts. A useful report can say “the service failed to read an expected config file at 14:03 UTC” without publishing the contents of the private configuration or the username in its path.

Words you should know

Term Meaning
Metric A numeric measurement over time.
Log A recorded event with context and timestamp.
Trace A connected view of events belonging to one operation.
Correlation ID Identifier used to link related operations or records.
Root cause The underlying factor whose correction prevents recurrence.

Windows: PowerShell 7, one command at a time

Use a normal non-elevated PowerShell window. Do not type the PS C:\...> prompt. If a command is unavailable or returns Access Denied, record that result; do not attempt to defeat the restriction.

The lines in a code block may contain more than one interactive command. Run them in order, checking each result before continuing. No .ps1 file is created or required.

Windows step 1 — Identify the five processes with highest accumulated CPU time

Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 5 ProcessName, CPU, Id

Expected result: CPU is usually accumulated process time, not live percentage utilisation.

What this does: PowerShell runs the command in your current session and displays information or, where clearly indicated, changes only your own practice files. If output differs, record the actual result before going further.

Windows step 2 — Inspect recent Application events

Get-WinEvent -LogName Application -MaxEvents 10 | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, ProviderName, LevelDisplayName

Expected result: Recent messages appear when access permits; save only redacted evidence for sharing.

What this does: PowerShell runs the command in your current session and displays information or, where clearly indicated, changes only your own practice files. If output differs, record the actual result before going further.

Windows step 3 — Read free space in the same session

Get-PSDrive -PSProvider FileSystem | Select-Object Name, Free, Used

Expected result: Helps judge whether storage pressure is plausible.

What this does: PowerShell runs the command in your current session and displays information or, where clearly indicated, changes only your own practice files. If output differs, record the actual result before going further.

Windows step 4 — Observe local time zone

Get-Date -Format o

Expected result: An ISO-formatted timestamp includes local offset; useful for cross-machine comparisons.

What this does: PowerShell runs the command in your current session and displays information or, where clearly indicated, changes only your own practice files. If output differs, record the actual result before going further.

Linux: terminal and distribution differences

Run the following only in an authorised Linux computer or VM. If you use Windows only, read this section for comparison. A program being absent does not mean the whole operating system is faulty.

Linux step 1 — Check load averages and system uptime

uptime

Expected result: Load averages relate to demand for runnable or uninterruptible tasks, not an absolute CPU percentage.

Linux step 2 — Read memory availability

free -h

Expected result: Shows available and used memory on Linux.

Linux step 3 — Inspect recent permitted journal entries

journalctl -n 10 --no-pager

Expected result: No output or permission errors must be recorded honestly.

Linux step 4 — Record an offset-aware timestamp

date --iso-8601=seconds

Expected result: A timestamp suitable for an incident timeline on GNU/Linux.

Worked support scenario

An Umicom Studio test reports Not Run after a CMake reconfiguration. The first question is not “which source file should be deleted?” Check that the test executable exists, that the build completed, and that the same build directory and source revision were used. Distinguish a test which ran and failed from a test which never executed. Attach the smallest relevant log excerpt with paths and credentials redacted.

Common mistakes and safe responses

Mistake Better response
“An ERROR event is automatically the incident root cause.” Check relevance, ordering and reproduction before concluding.
“Top CPU time means current CPU saturation.” Process CPU fields may be cumulative, not instant utilisation.
“No output from journalctl proves no failure happened.” Retention, time filters and access rights influence visibility.

Exercises

  1. Construct a five-event timeline for a fictional build failure.

  2. Explain why timestamps should include time zone.

  3. Define which observations would distinguish a missing test executable from a failing assertion.

Review questions and suggested answers

Show the suggested answers after attempting the exercises

  1. Record source revision, configure, build, test registration and observed failure times.

  2. Hosts may have different local offsets, so naïve ordering can be wrong.

  3. Build output, expected executable path, CTest registration and process exit/test log.

Chapter 36 · Intermediate

Chapter 36 — Capstone: investigate and hand over a support incident

Bits to Banking · System Administration: From Zero · Umicom Foundation

Audience: first-time users and returning learners; practical examples appropriate for supervised younger learners.

Estimated study time: 70–110 minutes.

Prerequisites: Chapters 25–35.

Why this matters

This capstone asks you to support an imaginary training computer used for Umicom Notes and Bits2Banking. The student reports that a practice file cannot be found, a build recently failed, and their GitHub push was rejected. The challenge is to determine which facts can be verified without risking production code or another person’s data.

What you will be able to do

By the end of this chapter you should be able to explain the new terms in ordinary language, select a safe read-only command for the right operating system, recognise a normal result and identify an unverified result. You should also be able to describe what permission would be needed before making a real system change.

The mental model

A professional support runbook begins with scope and authority. It separates observation, controlled change, verification and handover. You will collect identity, current directory, file existence, disk space, Git state and test results in that order. Then you will assess missing evidence with a native C23 teaching model. You will not run an OS repair command, override a Git push, change user permissions, restart services or invent a passing test. Many support incidents remain partially unresolved at handover; a clear list of unknowns is part of a successful investigation.

A complete support investigation has boundaries

Imagine two people use the same Umicom Framework remote repository through independent parent repositories. A clean umicomOS parent does not prove the Framework submodule worktree is clean or on main. A user may also have untracked source files inside the submodule that are not yet published. Before a git pull, report the repository root, branch/detached state, untracked-file status and any unpublished commits. If a checkout would overwrite local work, stop and preserve it for review. Never select --force or reset --hard to make a training screenshot look successful.

After the investigation, a second engineer should be able to reproduce your observations. Your handover states: “I tested X using command Y against revision Z at time T; it returned R. I did not run A because permission or prerequisites were missing.” That is a more valuable result than an unsupported statement that everything was repaired. The lesson ends where professional systems administration begins: clear evidence, explicit authority and controlled change.

Words you should know

Term Meaning
Scope Which machine, service, repository and time window are relevant.
Handover Structured notes that allow another authorised person to continue.
Blast radius Systems or people that might be affected by a change.
Evidence gap A fact that has not been collected or verified.
Change approval Explicit permission to apply a potentially disruptive action.

Windows: PowerShell 7, one command at a time

Use a normal non-elevated PowerShell window. Do not type the PS C:\...> prompt. If a command is unavailable or returns Access Denied, record that result; do not attempt to defeat the restriction.

Worked support scenario

Prepare a one-page handover headed “Training workstation — 14 October 2026”. Include system type, reporter, agreed scope, evidence timestamps, commands, exact observed results, steps deliberately not run, possible causes ranked by evidence, the next permitted action and the person who must approve it. Your final outcome may be “Unable to confirm the original save failure; learning workspace verified; Git push issue needs repository-specific investigation.” That is a valid honest conclusion.

Common mistakes and safe responses

Mistake Better response
“I must fix something to pass the course.” A safe diagnosis with accurate unknowns can be a complete professional outcome.
“The latest git status includes all submodule changes.” Submodules and parent gitlinks are separate histories; inspect both explicitly when authorised.
“Any green teaching model means the production OS is healthy.” The C23 model evaluates supplied fictional observations and cannot certify a real OS.

Exercises

  2. Explain why an error from a missing directory does not justify resetting Git.

  3. List three changes requiring explicit approval before you would proceed.

Review questions and suggested answers

Show the suggested answers after attempting the exercises

  1. Use actual results or mark NOT RUN, and include time and scope.

  2. Filesystem navigation errors and Git history repair are unrelated until evidenced otherwise.

  3. Broad permission changes, force pushes, service restarts or deletion of build/source directories.

Stage 3 · Practical infrastructure · Chapter 37

Chapter 37 — Plan a safe home administration laboratory

Bits to Banking · System Administration: From Zero · Umicom Foundation
Audience: beginners of any age; younger learners should use a supervised computer.
Suggested study time: 55–75 minutes.
Before this chapter: Chapters 1–9 and 24: terminals, folders, safe observation.

The question this chapter answers

How can I understand and check this part of a computer without accidentally changing something important?

Why this matters

System administrators learn by changing machines, yet experimentation on a family computer or production server can be expensive. Before changing a setting, decide where the experiment will take place and how to return to a known condition. A learning laboratory can be nothing more than an ordinary folder and read-only commands; a virtual machine is useful later, but is not a prerequisite.

A beginner should be able to explain which machine is being used, which account is signed in, which files belong to the lesson and whether any command needs elevated permission. On a school computer, managed laptop or shared household device, ask for permission before installing software or changing configuration.

A useful mental model

Imagine a school science experiment. You label the specimen, record the initial condition and keep the experiment separate from things people depend on. Your operating system is the laboratory bench; your practice folder is the safe work area. The host is the physical computer. A guest is an operating system running inside a virtual machine (VM). A snapshot is a VM feature that may restore its virtual disk and settings; it is not a substitute for backups of important files.

Figure 37 — The concept and its safe evidence boundary.

Key terms, explained before using them

Term Meaning
Host The physical computer that provides CPU, memory and storage.
Guest An operating system running within a virtual machine.
Privilege Permission to perform an operation, such as changing system settings.
Snapshot A VM checkpoint whose availability and scope depend on the VM product.
Rollback Returning to a verified previous state after a change.
Lab boundary An explicit rule saying what the student may and may not change.

Read this before typing commands

Authorisation and safety: Use your own computer or an explicitly authorised learning environment. Start with an ordinary user account. Commands that install software, change access, restart services or modify networks are outside this exercise unless the text clearly identifies a harmless practice-file operation. You never need to disable a firewall or change system permissions to complete this chapter.

Reading code blocks: Open PowerShell 7 on Windows (pwsh) or a terminal on Linux. Type the line inside the block, not the example prompt. Run one command at a time. Some examples contain multiple interactive commands separated by semicolons; verify their results individually. These are interactive commands, not scripts added to Umicom.

Windows — PowerShell 7 practice

Do these steps on Windows. If you use Linux, read them for comparison and continue below. A missing command means that a tool or module may be unavailable; it is not a reason to bypass computer policy.

Step 1 — Open a normal PowerShell session

pwsh

Expected result: A prompt appears, usually beginning with PS and a folder path.

Why this command matters: Start PowerShell 7 if installed. The command opens a shell; it does not grant administrator rights.

Safety and troubleshooting: If pwsh is not installed, the older Windows PowerShell can be used to install it with the approved package-manager instructions in Chapter 8.

Step 2 — Identify the working directory

Get-Location

Expected result: A folder path such as C:\Users\Student appears.

Why this command matters: This path matters because relative file names are resolved against it. A successful Get-Location never creates or deletes files.

Safety and troubleshooting: Do not include PS C:...> when typing a command shown in a lesson.

Step 3 — Check that a private practice folder is available

Test-Path -LiteralPath "$HOME\UmicomLearning"

Expected result: True if the folder exists; False if it does not.

Why this command matters: Testing for existence before creating directories avoids confusing an existing personal workspace with a new one.

Safety and troubleshooting: Use your own home directory rather than a shared system folder.

Step 4 — Create only your own practice directory

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\UmicomLearning\SysadminLab"

Expected result: Directory details appear; no system service is changed.

Why this command matters: The operation is limited to the learner's profile. -Force allows already-existing folders; it is not an instruction to overwrite work inside them.

Safety and troubleshooting: If you are on a managed machine and cannot create folders, stop and ask the device owner.

Step 5 — Inspect available storage before choosing a VM

Get-PSDrive -PSProvider FileSystem

Expected result: Drive names, used space and free space are displayed where supported.

Why this command matters: A VM consumes storage and RAM even though it appears to run in a window. Beginners should confirm spare capacity before downloading images.

Safety and troubleshooting: Do not erase files merely to meet a VM's advertised free-space requirement.

Linux — terminal practice

Run these in a Linux terminal on an authorised computer or VM. Some distributions do not install the same commands. An unavailable check should be reported as unavailable; do not assume an unobserved result is successful. No command below requires sudo.

Step 1 — Locate your home directory

pwd

Expected result: Your current directory appears; after login it is often under /home/username.

Why this command matters: A shell prompt can look different across distributions; only the command should be typed.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 2 — Check free space on the current filesystem

df -h .

Expected result: A mounted filesystem and available capacity appear.

Why this command matters: The dot means current directory. The command reads the filesystem's capacity without repartitioning it.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 3 — Create a user-owned learning directory

mkdir -p "$HOME/UmicomLearning/SysadminLab"

Expected result: The folder exists; the command may produce no output.

Why this command matters: Do not use sudo or root for your own practice files.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Worked Umicom support scenario

A family shares one Windows laptop. One person wants to learn how background services work. They create a private practice folder and run observation-only commands first. Before trying a VM they write down memory and free-space requirements and agree that the family laptop's security settings, disk partitions and accounts are out of scope. The first successful lab is a correctly labelled baseline, not a machine with more software installed.

A disciplined investigation sequence

  1. Describe the symptom precisely. Identify what failed and the expected result.
  2. Identify the environment. Record current account, machine class, working directory and observation time; redact private identifiers.
  3. Run the smallest relevant read-only check. Choose evidence that distinguishes two possible causes.
  4. Compare results with the requirement. Missing, blocked or outdated checks are not successful checks.
  5. Separate fact and interpretation. Label hypotheses explicitly.
  6. Propose, do not silently apply, a change. State approval, effect, rollback and validation criteria.

Common mistakes and how to respond

Incorrect assumption Better engineering response
I have administrator rights, so I should use them. An elevated shell increases the consequences of mistakes. Begin with a normal shell.
A VM snapshot protects the host computer. Snapshots normally describe VM state, not the host's files or account permissions.
A successful command means the experiment was safe. Safety also depends on authorisation, scope, reversibility and evidence of the original state.

Practical exercises — try these before opening the answers

  1. Define a safe lab boundary.
  2. Distinguish host and guest.
  3. Propose one rollback method.
Suggested answers and reasoning — open after attempting the exercises
  1. Define a safe lab boundary. Write three allowed activities and three prohibited activities. Allow reading system information and working in your own practice directory; prohibit modifying another user's files and restarting production services.
  2. Distinguish host and guest. Describe which computer would still run if the virtual machine were shut down.
  3. Propose one rollback method. For an ordinary practice document, a verified backup is suitable. For a VM, a tested snapshot may be useful but not sufficient for important data.

Engineering connection: Umicom Framework

Umicom Studio, the Framework and OS project can all be studied without changing their remote repositories. The learner should begin by reading documentation and running safe status commands. Kernel and OS experiments belong in an isolated, explicitly configured VM or emulator, not on the host boot disk.

Stage 3 · Practical infrastructure · Chapter 38

Chapter 38 — Capture an operating-system baseline and recognise drift

Bits to Banking · System Administration: From Zero · Umicom Foundation
Audience: beginners of any age; younger learners should use a supervised computer.
Suggested study time: 50–70 minutes.
Before this chapter: Chapter 37: lab boundaries and working directory.

The question this chapter answers

How can I understand and check this part of a computer without accidentally changing something important?

Why this matters

When a computer becomes slow after a software change, people often say it was 'fine yesterday'. That observation is useful, but too vague to diagnose. A baseline is a dated description of the machine before a change: OS edition and build, CPU architecture, available storage, installed tools and the task that is expected to work. Drift means the current state no longer matches that reference.

You do not need to capture everything. Hardware serial numbers, user names, network identifiers and private application paths can be sensitive. Record only the data necessary for the exercise and leave confidential details on the authorised machine.

A useful mental model

Think of a doctor recording temperature, pulse and symptoms before treatment. The system administrator also separates a measurement from an interpretation. 'PowerShell 7 reports 7.x' is an observation; 'this version caused the build failure' is a hypothesis requiring a reproducible test. A useful baseline is small enough to compare later and precise enough to identify which machine and time it describes.

Figure 38 — The concept and its safe evidence boundary.

Key terms, explained before using them

Term Meaning
Baseline An approved or documented starting condition.
Drift A difference between the recorded starting condition and the later system.
Edition Product packaging, such as Windows Pro or a Linux distribution variant.
Architecture Processor and operating-system execution family such as x64 or ARM64.
Timestamp A date and time attached to an observation; include timezone context.
Build ID A specific OS or software revision rather than an informal product name.

Read this before typing commands

Authorisation and safety: Use your own computer or an explicitly authorised learning environment. Start with an ordinary user account. Commands that install software, change access, restart services or modify networks are outside this exercise unless the text clearly identifies a harmless practice-file operation. You never need to disable a firewall or change system permissions to complete this chapter.

Reading code blocks: Open PowerShell 7 on Windows (pwsh) or a terminal on Linux. Type the line inside the block, not the example prompt. Run one command at a time. Some examples contain multiple interactive commands separated by semicolons; verify their results individually. These are interactive commands, not scripts added to Umicom.

Windows — PowerShell 7 practice

Do these steps on Windows. If you use Linux, read them for comparison and continue below. A missing command means that a tool or module may be unavailable; it is not a reason to bypass computer policy.

Step 1 — Check the PowerShell version

$PSVersionTable.PSVersion

Expected result: A version object displays major, minor and patch information.

Why this command matters: This tells you which shell is running, not necessarily which Windows release is installed.

Safety and troubleshooting: Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7 can coexist; running one does not automatically replace the other.

Step 2 — Inspect Windows edition, version and architecture

Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object WindowsProductName, OsVersion, OsArchitecture

Expected result: Three named fields appear; some values vary by Windows build.

Why this command matters: Select-Object limits information to relevant fields instead of exporting the entire machine inventory.

Safety and troubleshooting: Some Windows tools require elevated access or modules; a missing field should be recorded as unavailable rather than guessed.

Step 3 — Read CPU model and logical processors

Get-CimInstance Win32_Processor | Select-Object Name, NumberOfCores, NumberOfLogicalProcessors

Expected result: Processor name, physical cores and logical processor count appear.

Why this command matters: A core is a physical execution resource; logical processors may include simultaneous multithreading. The two counts need not be equal.

Safety and troubleshooting: Do not infer laptop performance solely from logical processor count.

Step 4 — Record a timezone-aware timestamp

Get-Date -Format o

Expected result: An ISO-style timestamp with fractional seconds and local offset appears.

Why this command matters: A time zone offset helps compare records from different machines. It is essential when investigating build or service events.

Safety and troubleshooting: The timestamp is the observation time, not necessarily the time the problem began.

Step 5 — Record selected native tool versions

git --version; cmake --version

Expected result: Git and CMake versions print when installed.

Why this command matters: These semicolon-separated interactive commands do not write scripts. Capture output for your own notebook, and compare the result after tool upgrades.

Safety and troubleshooting: If the command is not recognised, write 'not installed or not on PATH', not 'version zero'.

Linux — terminal practice

Run these in a Linux terminal on an authorised computer or VM. Some distributions do not install the same commands. An unavailable check should be reported as unavailable; do not assume an unobserved result is successful. No command below requires sudo.

Step 1 — Read distribution identity

cat /etc/os-release

Expected result: Fields such as NAME and VERSION_ID appear.

Why this command matters: A Linux distribution's release is different from the Linux kernel version.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 2 — Read the kernel revision

uname -r

Expected result: A kernel release string appears.

Why this command matters: Kernel and userland may be upgraded on different schedules; preserve both observations.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 3 — Check the hardware architecture

uname -m

Expected result: A string such as x86_64 or aarch64 appears.

Why this command matters: The value affects whether a compiled native binary can execute on the system.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 4 — Attach a dated observation

date -Is

Expected result: A timezone-aware date appears.

Why this command matters: If dates differ unexpectedly between hosts, check time configuration before correlating logs.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Worked Umicom support scenario

A C23 build worked on Computer A but fails on Computer B. The team records GCC and CMake versions, Windows OS version, target architecture, PATH resolution and the exact configure command. They find that B uses a different compiler selected from PATH. This is evidence of an environment difference; they still need to rerun the build with the intended toolchain before declaring it the root cause.

A disciplined investigation sequence

  1. Describe the symptom precisely. Identify what failed and the expected result.
  2. Identify the environment. Record current account, machine class, working directory and observation time; redact private identifiers.
  3. Run the smallest relevant read-only check. Choose evidence that distinguishes two possible causes.
  4. Compare results with the requirement. Missing, blocked or outdated checks are not successful checks.
  5. Separate fact and interpretation. Label hypotheses explicitly.
  6. Propose, do not silently apply, a change. State approval, effect, rollback and validation criteria.

Common mistakes and how to respond

Incorrect assumption Better engineering response
The CPU model identifies the operating-system architecture. A machine's CPU capability and installed OS architecture are related but distinct.
Yesterday's baseline is proof that nothing changed. Only the items actually measured are covered; unobserved services or configurations may also change.
I should publish the complete Get-ComputerInfo output. Prefer a short selected-field report and redact personal or organisation-specific values.

Practical exercises — try these before opening the answers

  1. Make a five-line baseline.
  2. Explain two possible causes of build drift.
  3. Verify one assumption.
Suggested answers and reasoning — open after attempting the exercises
  1. Make a five-line baseline. Include observation time, OS name/version, architecture, shell version and Git version or 'not installed'.
  2. Explain two possible causes of build drift. Compiler changes, environment PATH order, dependency updates or CMake preset differences.
  3. Verify one assumption. Run the same version command twice and compare. If it differs, investigate whether you used different shells or executables.

Engineering connection: Umicom Framework

Framework and Studio should record exact source commit, selected build preset, compiler identity and test result, not just an application version label. Do not mistake a clean Git status for proof that a build passed; those are separate observations.

Stage 3 · Practical infrastructure · Chapter 39

Chapter 39 — Understand accounts, groups and scheduled work

Bits to Banking · System Administration: From Zero · Umicom Foundation
Audience: beginners of any age; younger learners should use a supervised computer.
Suggested study time: 60–80 minutes.
Before this chapter: Chapters 9, 25 and 26: identities and permissions.

The question this chapter answers

How can I understand and check this part of a computer without accidentally changing something important?

Why this matters

An administrator must know who is allowed to run a task and when it will run. A user account represents an identity; a group groups permissions; a scheduled task executes at a chosen trigger such as logon or a time. A task may run under a different identity from the person who configured it. This difference explains why a task that succeeds in an interactive terminal sometimes fails unattended.

The safe beginner exercise is read-only. We will inspect our identity and the existence of scheduled work. Creating scheduled jobs that alter system settings or run privileged commands requires separate approval and is not part of this batch.

A useful mental model

Picture a library. The cardholder is the identity, membership in the staff group allows certain actions, and an appointment book says when work happens. A scheduled task has all three concerns: a trigger, an execution identity and an action. A human typing a command has an interactive session and usually a different environment from a background task.

Key terms, explained before using them

Term Meaning
Security principal An identity that can receive permissions.
Group A named set of identities used to simplify authorisation.
Scheduled task An OS-managed declaration of what should run and when.
Trigger An event or time that makes a task eligible to run.
Service account An identity intended to run software rather than represent a human user.
Environment Settings and paths available to a process when it starts.

Read this before typing commands

Authorisation and safety: Use your own computer or an explicitly authorised learning environment. Start with an ordinary user account. Commands that install software, change access, restart services or modify networks are outside this exercise unless the text clearly identifies a harmless practice-file operation. You never need to disable a firewall or change system permissions to complete this chapter.

Reading code blocks: Open PowerShell 7 on Windows (pwsh) or a terminal on Linux. Type the line inside the block, not the example prompt. Run one command at a time. Some examples contain multiple interactive commands separated by semicolons; verify their results individually. These are interactive commands, not scripts added to Umicom.

Windows — PowerShell 7 practice

Do these steps on Windows. If you use Linux, read them for comparison and continue below. A missing command means that a tool or module may be unavailable; it is not a reason to bypass computer policy.

Step 1 — Identify your signed-in Windows account

whoami

Expected result: The current account appears in domain-or-machine\username form.

Why this command matters: This reads the identity of the current process. It does not list passwords or prove which permissions a remote service has.

Safety and troubleshooting: Avoid posting your full account identifier publicly if privacy matters.

Step 2 — Inspect group memberships

whoami /groups

Expected result: Group names and security attributes appear.

Why this command matters: Membership can explain why a command is authorised or refused, but some tokens have disabled or filtered groups.

Safety and troubleshooting: Do not assume the presence of Administrators in the output means the current command prompt is elevated.

Step 3 — Inspect a sample of scheduled tasks

Get-ScheduledTask | Select-Object -First 8 TaskName, State, TaskPath

Expected result: A small table of task names and states appears where the module is available.

Why this command matters: This is an inventory operation. Task State such as Ready does not prove a task succeeded on its last run.

Safety and troubleshooting: Managed environments may restrict task visibility. Record the limitation rather than changing permissions.

Step 4 — Read details of one existing task without changing it

Get-ScheduledTask | Select-Object -First 1 | Select-Object TaskName, State, TaskPath

Expected result: The selected task's visible properties are displayed.

Why this command matters: Use Get-ScheduledTaskInfo separately when authorised to inspect execution results and timings.

Safety and troubleshooting: Avoid running, disabling or editing tasks that belong to the operating system.

Linux — terminal practice

Run these in a Linux terminal on an authorised computer or VM. Some distributions do not install the same commands. An unavailable check should be reported as unavailable; do not assume an unobserved result is successful. No command below requires sudo.

Step 1 — Inspect your effective identity and groups

id

Expected result: UID, primary GID and supplementary groups appear.

Why this command matters: Linux permission checks use numeric identifiers as well as names; they are not the same as Windows security identifiers.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 2 — List current user timer units on systemd systems

systemctl --user list-timers --all --no-pager

Expected result: Timers appear, or the list may be empty.

Why this command matters: A timer can trigger a service unit. Some systems do not use systemd; absence of the command does not mean Linux lacks scheduling.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 3 — Inspect your user account entry

getent passwd "$USER"

Expected result: A passwd database record may appear.

Why this command matters: Account listings are configuration metadata and never contain recoverable modern login passwords.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Worked Umicom support scenario

An overnight report did not run. The report works when started manually. Before changing anything, the administrator checks the task's configured account, trigger, last result, working directory and required network resources. A scheduled task can fail because its environment differs or its credential has expired; simply running it as Administrator can conceal the real cause and weaken controls.

A disciplined investigation sequence

  1. Describe the symptom precisely. Identify what failed and the expected result.
  2. Identify the environment. Record current account, machine class, working directory and observation time; redact private identifiers.
  3. Run the smallest relevant read-only check. Choose evidence that distinguishes two possible causes.
  4. Compare results with the requirement. Missing, blocked or outdated checks are not successful checks.
  5. Separate fact and interpretation. Label hypotheses explicitly.
  6. Propose, do not silently apply, a change. State approval, effect, rollback and validation criteria.

Common mistakes and how to respond

Incorrect assumption Better engineering response
The task exists, therefore it ran. Configuration and execution evidence are separate. Look for last run time, result and application output.
An account name tells me every permission. Effective permissions combine account, groups, ACLs, policy and current execution token.
A scheduled task should be fixed by granting broad admin rights. First identify the specific resource and permission required; least privilege is the default.

Practical exercises — try these before opening the answers

  1. Draw the three parts of scheduled work.
  2. Explain an environment-dependent failure.
  3. Invent a safe diagnostic question.
Suggested answers and reasoning — open after attempting the exercises
  1. Draw the three parts of scheduled work. Identify trigger, execution account and program/action.
  2. Explain an environment-dependent failure. A scheduled task may lack an interactive PATH, mapped drive or working directory expected by manual execution.
  3. Invent a safe diagnostic question. Ask whether the task was triggered and what process/result was recorded before suggesting a configuration change.

Engineering connection: Umicom Framework

Recurring builds, data imports and reconciliation jobs must use Framework-owned task services and explicit service identities. A future Umicom administration panel may display schedules, but it must not silently create privileged Windows Task Scheduler or systemd jobs from untrusted user input.
