Chapter 40 — Understand disks, volumes, filesystems and free space

Bits to Banking · System Administration: From Zero · Umicom Foundation
Audience: beginners of any age; younger learners should use a supervised computer.
Suggested study time: 55–80 minutes.
Before this chapter: Chapters 5–7 and 32: paths, drives and file systems.

The question this chapter answers

How can I understand and check this part of a computer without accidentally changing something important?

Why this matters

A disk is a storage device. A partition is a defined region on a disk. A volume is a logical storage unit that often has a drive letter or mount point. A filesystem organises files within the volume. Beginners often use the word 'drive' for all four, which can lead to wrong conclusions when a backup is full or an application cannot write.

Our exercises only inspect storage. Formatting, repartitioning, resizing and clearing disks can destroy information, so they are excluded. The goal is to answer: where does the learning project live, how much space is available, and which device actually holds it?

A useful mental model

Imagine a large filing cabinet (disk). You divide it into drawers (partitions). A drawer might be labelled C: (volume or mount point). Inside it, an index and folders describe where papers belong (filesystem). Modern systems complicate the analogy with virtual disks, network shares, encryption and storage pools; that is why we inspect actual mappings rather than guessing.

Key terms, explained before using them

Term Meaning
Block device Storage exposed as addressable units or sectors.
Partition A defined range on a physical or virtual disk.
Volume A logical container for a filesystem.
Filesystem Rules and metadata that organise directories and file content.
Mount point A directory or letter through which a filesystem is accessed.
Free space Capacity available for new data, subject to quotas and permissions.

Read this before typing commands

Authorisation and safety: Use your own computer or an explicitly authorised learning environment. Start with an ordinary user account. Commands that install software, change access, restart services or modify networks are outside this exercise unless the text clearly identifies a harmless practice-file operation. You never need to disable a firewall or change system permissions to complete this chapter.

Reading code blocks: Open PowerShell 7 on Windows (pwsh) or a terminal on Linux. Type the line inside the block, not the example prompt. Run one command at a time. Some examples contain multiple interactive commands separated by semicolons; verify their results individually. These are interactive commands, not scripts added to Umicom.

Windows — PowerShell 7 practice

Do these steps on Windows. If you use Linux, read them for comparison and continue below. A missing command means that a tool or module may be unavailable; it is not a reason to bypass computer policy.

Step 1 — Show filesystem drives

Get-PSDrive -PSProvider FileSystem

Expected result: Drive names, roots and free/used figures appear where supported.

Why this command matters: Some drives are network shares rather than physical disks. A mapped drive can disappear when a new session starts.

Safety and troubleshooting: Do not infer a disk's health from free space alone.

Step 2 — Inspect volumes without changing partitions

Get-Volume | Select-Object DriveLetter, FileSystem, HealthStatus, SizeRemaining, Size

Expected result: Volumes and their reported attributes appear.

Why this command matters: This shows Windows logical volumes, not necessarily one row per physical disk. Some entries have no drive letter.

Safety and troubleshooting: Some systems restrict this command; do not switch to an elevated shell merely to finish the exercise.

Step 3 — Read the current workspace location

Get-Location

Expected result: The working directory appears.

Why this command matters: Compare its drive letter to the volume inventory to identify likely storage. Symlinks, junctions and network shares can alter the true location.

Safety and troubleshooting: If you use Z: or another mapped share for Umicom sources, confirm it is connected before building.

Step 4 — Inspect your own home-directory folders

Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $HOME -Directory | Select-Object -First 10 Name

Expected result: Only the first ten folder names in your own profile appear.

Why this command matters: This bounds output and avoids scanning another person's directories. A folder name does not reveal its exact size.

Safety and troubleshooting: Never run a cleaning command based solely on a folder's name.

Linux — terminal practice

Run these in a Linux terminal on an authorised computer or VM. Some distributions do not install the same commands. An unavailable check should be reported as unavailable; do not assume an unobserved result is successful. No command below requires sudo.

Step 1 — Read disk, filesystem and mount columns

lsblk -o NAME,SIZE,FSTYPE,MOUNTPOINTS

Expected result: A tree of storage devices and mount points appears.

Why this command matters: Modern Linux may use encrypted layers, LVM or loop devices; the parent-child structure is significant.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 2 — Check space where the current directory lives

df -h .

Expected result: The filesystem containing the current directory is displayed with free capacity.

Why this command matters: A mount inside another directory may live on a different disk. Do not assume /home and / share capacity.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 3 — Identify the current directory

pwd

Expected result: Your working path appears.

Why this command matters: Use it to explain where a later file copy would go.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Worked Umicom support scenario

A beginner has 100 GB free on C: but the Umicom build fails when writing to Z:. The person checked the wrong filesystem. They inspect the repository path and both volume inventories. A write failure can also result from permissions or disconnection, so the diagnosis remains provisional until those checks are performed.

A disciplined investigation sequence

  1. Describe the symptom precisely. Identify what failed and the expected result.
  2. Identify the environment. Record current account, machine class, working directory and observation time; redact private identifiers.
  3. Run the smallest relevant read-only check. Choose evidence that distinguishes two possible causes.
  4. Compare results with the requirement. Missing, blocked or outdated checks are not successful checks.
  5. Separate fact and interpretation. Label hypotheses explicitly.
  6. Propose, do not silently apply, a change. State approval, effect, rollback and validation criteria.

Common mistakes and how to respond

Incorrect assumption Better engineering response
Free space means the disk is healthy. Health depends on hardware, filesystem integrity, performance and error logs, not just capacity.
Deleting the build directory is always safe. Some repositories have generated evidence or user-created files in the build tree. Inspect and back up before removing anything.
All visible drives are physical disks. Drive letters and mount points may refer to virtual, removable or network storage.

Practical exercises — try these before opening the answers

  1. Create a storage map on paper.
  2. Explain a network drive failure.
  3. Propose safe space investigation.
Suggested answers and reasoning — open after attempting the exercises
  1. Create a storage map on paper. Record one project path, its drive or mount point, its filesystem and available space.
  2. Explain a network drive failure. A mapped share may be unavailable in an unattended process even when a user can open it interactively.
  3. Propose safe space investigation. Check the intended volume, identify large owned test artefacts and obtain approval; do not start with deletion.

Engineering connection: Umicom Framework

Umicom builds should be independent of a user's current working directory and must not assume build artefacts are on the same volume as source. Native packaging and installers should report target space requirements and errors accurately.

Chapter 41 — Make and verify a recoverable practice backup

Bits to Banking · System Administration: From Zero · Umicom Foundation
Audience: beginners of any age; younger learners should use a supervised computer.
Suggested study time: 65–90 minutes.
Before this chapter: Chapters 7, 14 and 33: practice files, backups and hashes.

The question this chapter answers

How can I understand and check this part of a computer without accidentally changing something important?

Why this matters

Copying a file is easy. Recovering the correct version after a mistake is harder. A backup exercise must answer four questions: what did we protect, where is the copy, how did we verify it, and can we restore without overwriting the original? A synchronised folder is not automatically an independent backup; accidental deletions can synchronise too.

The lesson uses a harmless Notes document inside your own home directory. We create it explicitly, copy it to another practice folder, compute SHA-256 hashes and restore to a different destination. No production project, bank data or system directory is involved.

A useful mental model

Treat the original document as a library book, the backup as an independently stored copy, and the hash as a fingerprint of its bytes. Equal SHA-256 hashes provide strong evidence that the two files have identical content; they do not prove that the content was meaningful, authorised or free of malicious instructions. A restore drill proves the copy is usable for the chosen operation.

Figure 41 — The concept and its safe evidence boundary.

Key terms, explained before using them

Term Meaning
Source The original file or dataset being protected.
Backup A retained copy designed to support recovery.
Restore The act of recovering data from backup into a usable state.
SHA-256 A cryptographic hash algorithm that produces a fixed-length digest.
Retention How long backup versions are kept.
RPO/RTO Maximum tolerable data loss / target time to restore service.

Read this before typing commands

Authorisation and safety: Use your own computer or an explicitly authorised learning environment. Start with an ordinary user account. Commands that install software, change access, restart services or modify networks are outside this exercise unless the text clearly identifies a harmless practice-file operation. You never need to disable a firewall or change system permissions to complete this chapter.

Reading code blocks: Open PowerShell 7 on Windows (pwsh) or a terminal on Linux. Type the line inside the block, not the example prompt. Run one command at a time. Some examples contain multiple interactive commands separated by semicolons; verify their results individually. These are interactive commands, not scripts added to Umicom.

Windows — PowerShell 7 practice

Do these steps on Windows. If you use Linux, read them for comparison and continue below. A missing command means that a tool or module may be unavailable; it is not a reason to bypass computer policy.

Step 1 — Create a separate training source folder

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\UmicomLearning\BackupLab\source"

Expected result: The folder exists inside the account's home profile.

Why this command matters: The destination is deliberately outside any Umicom repository. We do not modify source-controlled project files.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this folder already contains important files, stop and choose a different practice name.

Step 2 — Create a small harmless note

Set-Content -LiteralPath "$HOME\UmicomLearning\BackupLab\source\notes.txt" -Value "Fictional Umicom Notes practice data"

Expected result: notes.txt contains one practice line.

Why this command matters: This is an interactive command that creates a learning document; it is not a PowerShell application script.

Safety and troubleshooting: Set-Content replaces file contents. Only use this exact command in a new practice folder after checking that the name is free.

Step 3 — Create a backup destination

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\UmicomLearning\BackupLab\backup"

Expected result: A backup folder exists.

Why this command matters: In production, a robust backup would normally be stored on an independent medium or approved storage system. This local exercise teaches the mechanics only.

Safety and troubleshooting: A second folder on the same disk does not protect against total disk failure.

Step 4 — Copy the practice document

Copy-Item -LiteralPath "$HOME\UmicomLearning\BackupLab\source\notes.txt" -Destination "$HOME\UmicomLearning\BackupLab\backup\notes.txt"

Expected result: A second notes.txt appears in backup.

Why this command matters: Copy-Item transfers bytes. The operation does not prove that a later restore works; we still check content and hash.

Safety and troubleshooting: Check that the destination file does not already contain an important version before copying.

Step 5 — Compare cryptographic hashes

Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 -LiteralPath "$HOME\UmicomLearning\BackupLab\source\notes.txt", "$HOME\UmicomLearning\BackupLab\backup\notes.txt"

Expected result: Two rows with the same hash should appear.

Why this command matters: An equal hash indicates that these two practice files contain identical bytes. Record both paths and the observation time.

Safety and troubleshooting: If hashes differ, stop: do not silently overwrite the backup to make the report look successful.

Step 6 — Restore into a separate review directory

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\UmicomLearning\BackupLab\restored"; Copy-Item -LiteralPath "$HOME\UmicomLearning\BackupLab\backup\notes.txt" -Destination "$HOME\UmicomLearning\BackupLab\restored\notes.txt"

Expected result: Restored notes.txt exists without replacing the source file.

Why this command matters: The same hash check can now compare backup and restored copies. This tests a recovery path independently from the original.

Safety and troubleshooting: Stop and investigate any access denied or file-not-found response rather than elevating privileges.

Linux — terminal practice

Run these in a Linux terminal on an authorised computer or VM. Some distributions do not install the same commands. An unavailable check should be reported as unavailable; do not assume an unobserved result is successful. No command below requires sudo.

Step 1 — Create the practice directories

mkdir -p "$HOME/UmicomLearning/BackupLab/source" "$HOME/UmicomLearning/BackupLab/backup" "$HOME/UmicomLearning/BackupLab/restored"

Expected result: Three directories exist in your own home directory.

Why this command matters: These directories are test destinations, not production backup storage.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 2 — Create the sample note

printf '%s\n' 'Fictional Umicom Notes practice data' > "$HOME/UmicomLearning/BackupLab/source/notes.txt"

Expected result: A small text file is created.

Why this command matters: The redirection operator overwrites the named file; run only in a fresh practice folder.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 3 — Copy and compare

cp -n "$HOME/UmicomLearning/BackupLab/source/notes.txt" "$HOME/UmicomLearning/BackupLab/backup/notes.txt"; sha256sum "$HOME/UmicomLearning/BackupLab/"{source,backup}/notes.txt

Expected result: Two matching SHA-256 hashes should appear after a successful copy.

Why this command matters: cp -n does not overwrite an existing destination. Confirm what happened before interpreting the hash output.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 4 — Restore to a new location

cp -n "$HOME/UmicomLearning/BackupLab/backup/notes.txt" "$HOME/UmicomLearning/BackupLab/restored/notes.txt"

Expected result: The restored file can be compared against the backup.

Why this command matters: Leave the source untouched so you can distinguish backup verification from restoration.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Worked Umicom support scenario

An editor accidentally saves the wrong contents into a fictional Notes document. The student does not use a broad restore over the live folder. They identify the approved backup generation, verify its hash and copy it into a separate review directory. After opening the restored document they compare it with the intended version and only then plan any authorised replacement.

A disciplined investigation sequence

  1. Describe the symptom precisely. Identify what failed and the expected result.
  2. Identify the environment. Record current account, machine class, working directory and observation time; redact private identifiers.
  3. Run the smallest relevant read-only check. Choose evidence that distinguishes two possible causes.
  4. Compare results with the requirement. Missing, blocked or outdated checks are not successful checks.
  5. Separate fact and interpretation. Label hypotheses explicitly.
  6. Propose, do not silently apply, a change. State approval, effect, rollback and validation criteria.

Common mistakes and how to respond

Incorrect assumption Better engineering response
A copy on the same disk is a disaster-recovery backup. It cannot protect against failure of that disk or loss of the whole computer.
Matching hashes prove a good recovery plan. They show matching bytes, but you must test whether the restored application or document works.
I should overwrite the original immediately during a drill. Restore separately first to avoid destroying the remaining good evidence.

Practical exercises — try these before opening the answers

  1. Explain the difference between copy, backup and restore.
  2. Record a three-line verification report.
  3. Describe two failures the local drill does not cover.
Suggested answers and reasoning — open after attempting the exercises
  1. Explain the difference between copy, backup and restore. A copy is duplication; a backup includes recoverability, retention and independent protection; restoration proves usability.
  2. Record a three-line verification report. Include original path, backup path, SHA-256 comparison and whether restore succeeded.
  3. Describe two failures the local drill does not cover. Physical disk loss and loss or theft of the computer; use approved independent storage for real resilience.

Engineering connection: Umicom Framework

Real Umicom document, Data Server and configuration backups belong to approved owners and services. A learner's Copy-Item practice is not a replacement for Framework persistence, audit or deployment recovery. Git is revision control, not a complete backup policy.

Chapter 42 — Read access-control rules without changing them

Bits to Banking · System Administration: From Zero · Umicom Foundation
Audience: beginners of any age; younger learners should use a supervised computer.
Suggested study time: 55–75 minutes.
Before this chapter: Chapters 9 and 26: least privilege and filesystem permissions.

The question this chapter answers

How can I understand and check this part of a computer without accidentally changing something important?

Why this matters

'Access denied' is a useful diagnostic result: it tells us that the attempted operation crossed a permission boundary. Beginners sometimes respond by running everything as administrator, but doing so hides the actual requirement and increases risk. The safer sequence is to identify the file owner, the current user, relevant groups and the permissions on the specific resource.

This lesson reads access-control information only. It does not edit registry permissions, run icacls grant commands, change ownership or modify system ACLs. Practice on a directory owned by the learner and never inspect other people's private documents without permission.

A useful mental model

A secure door may check both identity and an access list. In Windows, an ACL contains access-control entries for users and groups, potentially including deny rules and inherited permissions. In Linux, basic mode bits describe owner, group and other access, while POSIX ACLs can add entries. Neither format is interchangeable with the other; each must be interpreted in its platform context.

Key terms, explained before using them

Term Meaning
ACL Access control list: rules attached to an object.
ACE A single rule or entry inside an ACL.
Owner Identity associated with an object, with specific administrative rights.
Inheritance Permissions flowing from a containing folder under defined rules.
Least privilege Granting only the capabilities needed for the authorised task.
Permission denial A refused access attempt, not proof of a system malfunction.

Read this before typing commands

Authorisation and safety: Use your own computer or an explicitly authorised learning environment. Start with an ordinary user account. Commands that install software, change access, restart services or modify networks are outside this exercise unless the text clearly identifies a harmless practice-file operation. You never need to disable a firewall or change system permissions to complete this chapter.

Reading code blocks: Open PowerShell 7 on Windows (pwsh) or a terminal on Linux. Type the line inside the block, not the example prompt. Run one command at a time. Some examples contain multiple interactive commands separated by semicolons; verify their results individually. These are interactive commands, not scripts added to Umicom.

Windows — PowerShell 7 practice

Do these steps on Windows. If you use Linux, read them for comparison and continue below. A missing command means that a tool or module may be unavailable; it is not a reason to bypass computer policy.

Step 1 — Identify the current identity

whoami

Expected result: Your signed-in Windows identity appears.

Why this command matters: Record this before comparing ACL entries. The account used by a scheduled service may be different.

Safety and troubleshooting: Never assume you are elevated just because the account belongs to an Administrators group.

Step 2 — Create a practice directory if needed

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\UmicomLearning\AclLab"

Expected result: A folder exists under your profile.

Why this command matters: The folder is for observations and optional fictional files. It is not a substitute for a dedicated security test environment.

Safety and troubleshooting: If a folder of that name already has important contents, pick another name rather than resetting its permissions.

Step 3 — Read the folder's access control list

Get-Acl -LiteralPath "$HOME\UmicomLearning\AclLab" | Format-List Owner, AccessToString

Expected result: An owner and access entries appear where allowed.

Why this command matters: ACL output may be long. Read each identity and right, and note whether the rules were inherited.

Safety and troubleshooting: Do not paste full ACL listings publicly if they expose organisation user names or domain names.

Step 4 — Compare groups with actual rights

whoami /groups

Expected result: Group memberships are printed.

Why this command matters: Group membership alone does not settle the effective permission; object-specific ACLs and denial rules also matter.

Safety and troubleshooting: A failed file read should be diagnosed, not fixed with blanket Full Control grants.

Linux — terminal practice

Run these in a Linux terminal on an authorised computer or VM. Some distributions do not install the same commands. An unavailable check should be reported as unavailable; do not assume an unobserved result is successful. No command below requires sudo.

Step 1 — Read identity and group IDs

id

Expected result: Numeric and human-readable account and group data appear.

Why this command matters: The kernel checks numeric IDs and effective credentials, not just friendly names.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 2 — Inspect your home directory's mode

ls -ld "$HOME"

Expected result: Permission characters, owner and group appear.

Why this command matters: The first character describes file type; the following nine represent owner/group/other access for basic mode bits.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 3 — Read formatted mode metadata

stat -c '%A %U:%G %n' "$HOME"

Expected result: Human-readable mode, owner and path appear.

Why this command matters: Some filesystems expose additional ACLs or mount restrictions not visible in mode bits alone.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Worked Umicom support scenario

A student cannot write a build artefact to a shared folder. They verify they can write to their own home folder and inspect the shared location's policy with an authorised supervisor. This isolates a permission issue from a compiler error. The correct remedy may be using an approved build directory rather than changing the shared folder's permissions.

A disciplined investigation sequence

  1. Describe the symptom precisely. Identify what failed and the expected result.
  2. Identify the environment. Record current account, machine class, working directory and observation time; redact private identifiers.
  3. Run the smallest relevant read-only check. Choose evidence that distinguishes two possible causes.
  4. Compare results with the requirement. Missing, blocked or outdated checks are not successful checks.
  5. Separate fact and interpretation. Label hypotheses explicitly.
  6. Propose, do not silently apply, a change. State approval, effect, rollback and validation criteria.

Common mistakes and how to respond

Incorrect assumption Better engineering response
Running as Administrator is a harmless test. It changes the security context and can create files owned by the wrong account.
File ownership means unrestricted access. Owner rights differ across systems and may be constrained by ACLs, encryption and policy.
Everyone should receive Full Control to make a project build. Find the minimum required access for the chosen build directory instead.

Practical exercises — try these before opening the answers

  1. Identify three factors in an access decision.
  2. Explain why a build succeeds only as administrator.
  3. Describe a safe alternative.
Suggested answers and reasoning — open after attempting the exercises
  1. Identify three factors in an access decision. Principal, object-specific permissions and execution context.
  2. Explain why a build succeeds only as administrator. It may target a protected folder, require an inappropriate installation path or rely on privileged environment settings.
  3. Describe a safe alternative. Build in a user-owned workspace and request focused access through approved administration processes if needed.

Engineering connection: Umicom Framework

Umicom Framework process, filesystem and security services should report permission errors with context, not silently retry with elevated privileges. Studio should not require Administrator rights merely to compile a user's own C23 learning project.

Stage 3 · Practical infrastructure · Chapter 43

Chapter 43 — Follow one network request from a name to a port

Bits to Banking · System Administration: From Zero · Umicom Foundation
Audience: beginners of any age; younger learners should use a supervised computer.
Suggested study time: 65–85 minutes.
Before this chapter: Chapters 15, 16 and 31: IP addresses, DNS and TCP.

The question this chapter answers

How can I understand and check this part of a computer without accidentally changing something important?

Why this matters

When an application says 'cannot connect', the problem might be the name, IP route, port, firewall, listening service or application response. These are different layers. A beginner gains confidence by testing them in order instead of changing settings at random. We will use a publicly documented example domain for an optional internet test, and a fictional local Umicom Notes service for explanations.

The lesson does not create a listening server, contact a bank or require any credentials. Internet-dependent tests may be unavailable in a classroom, and their failure is not proof that the learner's computer is broken.

A useful mental model

A DNS name is like a contact name in a phone's address book; DNS resolution finds one or more network addresses. An IP route decides where to send a packet. A TCP port identifies a service endpoint on that address. A successful TCP connection proves that a transport session could be established; it does not prove the application returned the correct data or authenticated the user.

Figure 43 — The concept and its safe evidence boundary.

Key terms, explained before using them

Term Meaning
DNS A naming system that maps domains to resource records such as IP addresses.
IP address A logical network address assigned to an interface or host.
Gateway A router used to reach other networks when necessary.
TCP port A numeric service endpoint within a transport connection.
Listener A service waiting for incoming connections.
Connection refused A failed connection attempt indicating no accepting endpoint or an active refusal, subject to network context.

Read this before typing commands

Authorisation and safety: Use your own computer or an explicitly authorised learning environment. Start with an ordinary user account. Commands that install software, change access, restart services or modify networks are outside this exercise unless the text clearly identifies a harmless practice-file operation. You never need to disable a firewall or change system permissions to complete this chapter.

Reading code blocks: Open PowerShell 7 on Windows (pwsh) or a terminal on Linux. Type the line inside the block, not the example prompt. Run one command at a time. Some examples contain multiple interactive commands separated by semicolons; verify their results individually. These are interactive commands, not scripts added to Umicom.

Windows — PowerShell 7 practice

Do these steps on Windows. If you use Linux, read them for comparison and continue below. A missing command means that a tool or module may be unavailable; it is not a reason to bypass computer policy.

Step 1 — Inspect interface configuration

Get-NetIPConfiguration | Select-Object InterfaceAlias, IPv4Address, IPv4DefaultGateway

Expected result: Active interface names, addresses and gateways are shown when the module is available.

Why this command matters: A machine can have several interfaces, including VPNs and virtual adapters. The displayed IP may be private and does not need to be posted publicly.

Safety and troubleshooting: A missing gateway can be normal for an isolated network or a host-only virtual machine.

Step 2 — Resolve an example domain

Resolve-DnsName example.org

Expected result: One or more DNS records appear when name resolution is available.

Why this command matters: DNS answers may change over time and can differ between networks. Do not copy a sample IP address as a permanent configuration value.

Safety and troubleshooting: If the command is not recognised, confirm you are on Windows PowerShell with the DNS client module available.

Step 3 — Test an HTTPS TCP endpoint

Test-NetConnection -ComputerName example.org -Port 443

Expected result: The result contains a TCP success/failure indicator and connection details.

Why this command matters: Port 443 is commonly used by HTTPS. This checks TCP reachability, not certificate validity or application correctness.

Safety and troubleshooting: A classroom firewall may block the test intentionally. Do not disable security controls to make it pass.

Step 4 — Inspect local listening ports without editing them

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object -First 10 LocalAddress, LocalPort, OwningProcess

Expected result: Up to ten listening socket records appear.

Why this command matters: A socket bound to 127.0.0.1 accepts only loopback traffic. One bound to 0.0.0.0 may accept traffic on multiple IPv4 interfaces subject to firewall rules.

Safety and troubleshooting: The list is observational; do not terminate unknown processes from a port number alone.

Linux — terminal practice

Run these in a Linux terminal on an authorised computer or VM. Some distributions do not install the same commands. An unavailable check should be reported as unavailable; do not assume an unobserved result is successful. No command below requires sudo.

Step 1 — Read network addresses

ip -brief address

Expected result: Interface names and assigned addresses appear when iproute2 is installed.

Why this command matters: Addresses may come from VPNs or container interfaces, so identify the relevant interface first.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 2 — Inspect routes

ip route

Expected result: Routing rules and a default route may be shown.

Why this command matters: An isolated VM may deliberately have no route to the internet; that can be the correct security design.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 3 — Resolve a domain

getent ahosts example.org

Expected result: Address records appear when resolution succeeds.

Why this command matters: A missing answer can reflect network policy, DNS failure or lack of configured resolver; investigate without assuming one cause.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 4 — Test application-level HTTPS headers, if curl is installed

curl -I https://example.org

Expected result: HTTP headers or a clear connection/TLS error appear.

Why this command matters: Unlike a raw TCP test, this also exercises TLS and HTTP. It does not prove unrelated services work.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Worked Umicom support scenario

A local native Umicom training server should listen on 127.0.0.1:8765. DNS is irrelevant because the destination is numeric loopback. The learner checks whether the server was started, whether the port is listening, then whether an HTTP request succeeds. If the listener is absent, changing the home router's DNS cannot solve the immediate problem. If it listens on a different port, the client configuration needs review.

A disciplined investigation sequence

  1. Describe the symptom precisely. Identify what failed and the expected result.
  2. Identify the environment. Record current account, machine class, working directory and observation time; redact private identifiers.
  3. Run the smallest relevant read-only check. Choose evidence that distinguishes two possible causes.
  4. Compare results with the requirement. Missing, blocked or outdated checks are not successful checks.
  5. Separate fact and interpretation. Label hypotheses explicitly.
  6. Propose, do not silently apply, a change. State approval, effect, rollback and validation criteria.

Common mistakes and how to respond

Incorrect assumption Better engineering response
DNS succeeded, so the application works. Resolution proves only part of the path; TCP, TLS and application-level checks remain.
Ping fails, so the host is down. ICMP may be restricted even when the intended TCP service is healthy.
A port is listening, so it is safe to expose. Network exposure requires authentication, authorisation, TLS policy and firewall review.

Practical exercises — try these before opening the answers

  1. Draw a five-step network path.
  2. Distinguish two failure messages.
  3. State one privacy precaution.
Suggested answers and reasoning — open after attempting the exercises
  1. Draw a five-step network path. Client name → DNS → IP route → TCP endpoint → application response.
  2. Distinguish two failure messages. Name resolution failure occurs before a destination IP is selected; TCP refusal occurs during transport connection.
  3. State one privacy precaution. Do not publish internal IP ranges, machine names, VPN adapters or private connection diagnostics unnecessarily.

Engineering connection: Umicom Framework

The Umicom Framework web adapter owns listening sockets and network policy. A learner should not add custom sockets to Studio or OS for a simple test when the existing Framework service can report endpoint and health information. Test loopback endpoints first and keep training services off public interfaces.

Stage 3 · Practical infrastructure · Chapter 44

Chapter 44 — Understand firewalls and listening services without changing rules

Bits to Banking · System Administration: From Zero · Umicom Foundation
Audience: beginners of any age; younger learners should use a supervised computer.
Suggested study time: 60–80 minutes.
Before this chapter: Chapter 43: network layers, ports and listeners.

The question this chapter answers

How can I understand and check this part of a computer without accidentally changing something important?

Why this matters

A firewall decides which network traffic should be allowed or blocked according to policy. New administrators sometimes disable a firewall to test a problem. That approach changes the system's protection and often obscures whether the real issue is incorrect binding, a missing listener or a specific rule. The correct beginner exercise is to inspect state and identify the intended network boundary.

We will not create, delete, disable or relax firewall rules. A lab using a machine you own still deserves a change plan before configuration: which direction, interface, application, port, users and expected rollback apply?

A useful mental model

A firewall resembles a controlled building entrance. The door may be open for one approved visitor and closed for others. A local program listening on a TCP port is like a desk that accepts requests inside the building. The desk can exist even when an external visitor cannot enter; equally, an open entrance does not help if no desk is staffed.

Figure 44 — The concept and its safe evidence boundary.

Key terms, explained before using them

Term Meaning
Inbound rule Policy controlling traffic arriving at a machine or network.
Outbound rule Policy controlling traffic leaving a machine or network.
Profile A set of firewall behaviour for network contexts such as private or public.
Loopback Communication with the same machine, often 127.0.0.1 for IPv4.
Bind address Address on which a service accepts connections.
Listening socket A kernel-managed endpoint waiting for connection attempts.

Read this before typing commands

Authorisation and safety: Use your own computer or an explicitly authorised learning environment. Start with an ordinary user account. Commands that install software, change access, restart services or modify networks are outside this exercise unless the text clearly identifies a harmless practice-file operation. You never need to disable a firewall or change system permissions to complete this chapter.

Reading code blocks: Open PowerShell 7 on Windows (pwsh) or a terminal on Linux. Type the line inside the block, not the example prompt. Run one command at a time. Some examples contain multiple interactive commands separated by semicolons; verify their results individually. These are interactive commands, not scripts added to Umicom.

Windows — PowerShell 7 practice

Do these steps on Windows. If you use Linux, read them for comparison and continue below. A missing command means that a tool or module may be unavailable; it is not a reason to bypass computer policy.

Step 1 — Inspect Windows Defender Firewall profiles

Get-NetFirewallProfile | Select-Object Name, Enabled, DefaultInboundAction, DefaultOutboundAction

Expected result: Profiles and enabled/policy values appear where the NetSecurity module is available.

Why this command matters: Different profiles may be active under different network classifications. Enabled is a policy observation, not proof every desired connection is allowed.

Safety and troubleshooting: Do not execute Set-NetFirewallProfile or disable rules during this educational exercise.

Step 2 — Show a bounded set of listening TCP endpoints

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object -First 12 LocalAddress, LocalPort, OwningProcess

Expected result: Up to twelve records appear.

Why this command matters: LocalAddress helps distinguish loopback-only from broader binds. OwningProcess is a PID, not a permanent service name.

Safety and troubleshooting: Do not publish sensitive internal endpoint inventories in public chats.

Step 3 — Inspect one process only if an actual PID was observed

Get-Process | Select-Object -First 8 Name, Id, Path

Expected result: A small process list appears. Some Path properties may be unavailable.

Why this command matters: Processes can start/stop and PIDs can be reused. Correlate a port and process at nearly the same time.

Safety and troubleshooting: Avoid killing the process; identify its purpose first.

Step 4 — Check a named local HTTP endpoint only when you started it

Test-NetConnection -ComputerName 127.0.0.1 -Port 8765

Expected result: TCP connectivity reports true if a service is listening and accepting connections there.

Why this command matters: A failure is expected when the Umicom training server is not running. It does not prove the firewall is incorrectly configured.

Safety and troubleshooting: Do not start an unknown downloaded server merely to get a green result.

Linux — terminal practice

Run these in a Linux terminal on an authorised computer or VM. Some distributions do not install the same commands. An unavailable check should be reported as unavailable; do not assume an unobserved result is successful. No command below requires sudo.

Step 1 — List local listening TCP ports

ss -lnt

Expected result: A table of listening endpoints appears if iproute2 utilities are installed.

Why this command matters: A bind to 127.0.0.1 differs from a bind to all interfaces. Without elevated access, process owner information may be restricted.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 2 — Inspect local firewall tooling without modifying it

command -v ufw; command -v firewall-cmd; command -v nft

Expected result: Available commands print their locations; absent tools cause no output for that entry.

Why this command matters: Linux distributions use different firewall managers. Not finding ufw does not imply the host has no firewall.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 3 — Observe the configured service rather than modifying traffic policy

ss -lnt | head -n 12

Expected result: The first twelve lines of listener information appear.

Why this command matters: This is enough to discuss TCP listeners without generating a full system inventory.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Worked Umicom support scenario

A fictional Umicom Notes server starts successfully but is reachable only from the same computer. The learner sees it bound to 127.0.0.1. That design is intentional for the course: the server is not a network service for other computers. Changing firewall rules would not turn a loopback-only socket into a correctly secured external service and would create unnecessary exposure.

A disciplined investigation sequence

  1. Describe the symptom precisely. Identify what failed and the expected result.
  2. Identify the environment. Record current account, machine class, working directory and observation time; redact private identifiers.
  3. Run the smallest relevant read-only check. Choose evidence that distinguishes two possible causes.
  4. Compare results with the requirement. Missing, blocked or outdated checks are not successful checks.
  5. Separate fact and interpretation. Label hypotheses explicitly.
  6. Propose, do not silently apply, a change. State approval, effect, rollback and validation criteria.

Common mistakes and how to respond

Incorrect assumption Better engineering response
Turning off the firewall is the quickest diagnostic. It changes the security boundary and makes results harder to attribute. Inspect policy and endpoint first.
Every listener is an internet-facing service. The bind address, host route, NAT and firewall determine actual reachability.
One blocked test means security is broken. Some traffic is meant to be blocked. Compare the requirement to the rule and observation.

Practical exercises — try these before opening the answers

  1. Explain loopback in one sentence.
  2. Distinguish port 8765 and IP 127.0.0.1.
  3. Define a proposed change review.
Suggested answers and reasoning — open after attempting the exercises
  1. Explain loopback in one sentence. Loopback is traffic addressed to the same host, often using 127.0.0.1.
  2. Distinguish port 8765 and IP 127.0.0.1. The IP selects a network address; the TCP port selects the service endpoint.
  3. Define a proposed change review. Identify requester, approved purpose, minimum port/direction, scope, test and rollback before touching firewall policy.

Engineering connection: Umicom Framework

Umicom Framework should own network listeners and exposure policy. Product applications should request an approved service endpoint rather than creating their own unrestricted sockets or firewall rules. Operational checks must distinguish 'intentionally blocked' from 'failure'.

Stage 3 · Practical infrastructure · Chapter 45

Chapter 45 — Recognise service health versus process state

Bits to Banking · System Administration: From Zero · Umicom Foundation
Audience: beginners of any age; younger learners should use a supervised computer.
Suggested study time: 65–85 minutes.
Before this chapter: Chapters 11, 27 and 28: Windows services, systemd units and logs.

The question this chapter answers

How can I understand and check this part of a computer without accidentally changing something important?

Why this matters

A process is a running program instance. A service is a managed background workload. 'Running' tells us something about process state, but not whether the service can complete its assigned task. A banking reconciliation engine might still be running while its input queue is blocked. A note-taking service may respond to a health check but fail to save documents because its storage is full.

Professional operators define success in business terms. For a fictional Umicom Notes service, we may require its storage location to be writable, its service to start, and a save-and-read test to succeed. Merely finding a PID is not enough.

A useful mental model

Imagine a restaurant that has its lights on and employees inside. That is analogous to a running process. A healthy service actually accepts and completes orders. A readiness check asks whether it is suitable to receive work now; a liveness check asks whether it is responsive enough to remain running. These signals should not be conflated or used to create automatic restart loops without clear policies.

Figure 45 — The concept and its safe evidence boundary.

Key terms, explained before using them

Term Meaning
Process An OS-managed execution instance with resources and an identity.
Service A managed, generally long-lived workload exposed through defined operations.
Liveness A narrow indication that a workload remains responsive or operating.
Readiness Evidence that a service can safely accept its intended work.
Dependency A component that must function before another operation can succeed.
Degraded Partially functioning state with documented limitations.

Read this before typing commands

Authorisation and safety: Use your own computer or an explicitly authorised learning environment. Start with an ordinary user account. Commands that install software, change access, restart services or modify networks are outside this exercise unless the text clearly identifies a harmless practice-file operation. You never need to disable a firewall or change system permissions to complete this chapter.

Reading code blocks: Open PowerShell 7 on Windows (pwsh) or a terminal on Linux. Type the line inside the block, not the example prompt. Run one command at a time. Some examples contain multiple interactive commands separated by semicolons; verify their results individually. These are interactive commands, not scripts added to Umicom.

Windows — PowerShell 7 practice

Do these steps on Windows. If you use Linux, read them for comparison and continue below. A missing command means that a tool or module may be unavailable; it is not a reason to bypass computer policy.

Step 1 — List a small sample of Windows services

Get-Service | Select-Object -First 10 Name, Status, DisplayName

Expected result: Service names and statuses appear.

Why this command matters: Stopped may be intentional for services that start on demand. Do not treat every stopped service as an incident.

Safety and troubleshooting: Do not run Start-Service or Stop-Service in the shared learning environment.

Step 2 — Inspect service configuration from the CIM provider

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -Filter "Name='Spooler'" | Select-Object Name, State, StartMode, PathName

Expected result: When present, a Print Spooler configuration record appears.

Why this command matters: The configuration reports a binary path and start mode. It does not establish that printing a document works.

Safety and troubleshooting: Spooler can be absent or disabled on server images; that is not automatically a fault.

Step 3 — Read a bounded service-control event sample

Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System';ProviderName='Service Control Manager'} -MaxEvents 6 | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, Message

Expected result: Recent events appear if available and permitted.

Why this command matters: Timestamps and provider names help correlate events with user-visible symptoms. Event IDs are meaningful in the context of their provider.

Safety and troubleshooting: Messages can contain private paths or machine names; redact before sharing.

Step 4 — Record when you observed the status

Get-Date -Format o

Expected result: A timestamp with timezone offset appears.

Why this command matters: When a service changes state rapidly, two observations minutes apart may tell very different stories.

Safety and troubleshooting: Do not claim the same service state persists indefinitely.

Linux — terminal practice

Run these in a Linux terminal on an authorised computer or VM. Some distributions do not install the same commands. An unavailable check should be reported as unavailable; do not assume an unobserved result is successful. No command below requires sudo.

Step 1 — Inspect service unit status without modifying it

systemctl --user list-units --type=service --all --no-pager

Expected result: User-owned service units appear on hosts with user systemd.

Why this command matters: A Linux service may be managed by a system unit rather than a user unit; use authorised scope-specific commands.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 2 — Read recent user-journal entries

journalctl --user -n 10 --no-pager

Expected result: Up to ten entries appear when the user journal is available.

Why this command matters: A journal entry is evidence of a message, not necessarily proof that the originating process failed.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 3 — Check for a real listening port

ss -lnt

Expected result: Listening TCP endpoints appear.

Why this command matters: Combine process state with endpoint and application-level tests to evaluate readiness.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Worked Umicom support scenario

The Umicom Notes training application is marked Running. Students cannot open an existing note. Instead of repeatedly restarting the process, the operator examines the relevant directory permissions, available space, application error and actual read result. A failed dependency explains why a running application is not ready. The corrective action must address that dependency, not just its symptom.

A disciplined investigation sequence

  1. Describe the symptom precisely. Identify what failed and the expected result.
  2. Identify the environment. Record current account, machine class, working directory and observation time; redact private identifiers.
  3. Run the smallest relevant read-only check. Choose evidence that distinguishes two possible causes.
  4. Compare results with the requirement. Missing, blocked or outdated checks are not successful checks.
  5. Separate fact and interpretation. Label hypotheses explicitly.
  6. Propose, do not silently apply, a change. State approval, effect, rollback and validation criteria.

Common mistakes and how to respond

Incorrect assumption Better engineering response
The green Running label proves the system is operational. It describes lifecycle state; verify the intended operation separately.
All failures should trigger automatic restarts. Restarts can hide data loss or amplify load when storage or databases remain unhealthy.
A liveness probe should perform payments or write production data. Keep probes bounded and safe; separate liveness, readiness and business-transaction verification.

Practical exercises — try these before opening the answers

  1. List three readiness checks for Notes.
  2. Explain when a service can be degraded.
  3. Propose an incident response order.
Suggested answers and reasoning — open after attempting the exercises
  1. List three readiness checks for Notes. A configured service process, accessible document storage and a successful authorised read-only document request.
  2. Explain when a service can be degraded. A nonessential feature may fail while required work remains available, with the limitation clearly reported.
  3. Propose an incident response order. Observe process → check dependencies → test the real operation → record evidence → request approved change.

Engineering connection: Umicom Framework

Umicom Framework's existing supervisory, observability and build services should provide production health. The new Update 40 native C23 teaching laboratory combines fictional readiness observations and dependencies; it is not a background monitoring agent or a replacement for Framework.

Stage 3 · Practical infrastructure · Chapter 46

Chapter 46 — Plan software updates with approval, testing and rollback

Bits to Banking · System Administration: From Zero · Umicom Foundation
Audience: beginners of any age; younger learners should use a supervised computer.
Suggested study time: 60–85 minutes.
Before this chapter: Chapters 8, 29 and 35: software updates and incident evidence.

The question this chapter answers

How can I understand and check this part of a computer without accidentally changing something important?

Why this matters

Updates close security vulnerabilities and fix defects, but they can also change APIs, dependencies and behaviour. An administrator should know what is proposed to change, who approved it, when users will be affected, what must be tested afterwards and how to recover if the change fails. An update window is a planned time with defined owners and acceptance criteria.

Our exercises list available updates and installed versions only. They do not execute winget upgrade --all, apt upgrade, restart a system or modify protected packages. Applying updates to a shared or production computer is a separate, authorised operational task.

A useful mental model

Treat an update like replacing a bridge component while traffic depends on it. You first inspect the proposed replacement, plan a safe time and identify a bypass or rollback route. For software, record package identity, current version, target version, dependencies, known compatibility constraints and relevant test cases. A successful installer exit code is not the same as an application that still works correctly.

Key terms, explained before using them

Term Meaning
Patch A software change intended to correct defects or vulnerabilities.
Maintenance window An agreed time for controlled changes.
Dependency A library, service or package on which software relies.
Rollback A return to a verified acceptable state.
Acceptance test A measurable check proving a required behaviour still works.
Change record A documented request, owner, reason, test and outcome.

Read this before typing commands

Authorisation and safety: Use your own computer or an explicitly authorised learning environment. Start with an ordinary user account. Commands that install software, change access, restart services or modify networks are outside this exercise unless the text clearly identifies a harmless practice-file operation. You never need to disable a firewall or change system permissions to complete this chapter.

Reading code blocks: Open PowerShell 7 on Windows (pwsh) or a terminal on Linux. Type the line inside the block, not the example prompt. Run one command at a time. Some examples contain multiple interactive commands separated by semicolons; verify their results individually. These are interactive commands, not scripts added to Umicom.

Windows — PowerShell 7 practice

Do these steps on Windows. If you use Linux, read them for comparison and continue below. A missing command means that a tool or module may be unavailable; it is not a reason to bypass computer policy.

Step 1 — Check whether winget is installed

winget --version

Expected result: The Windows Package Manager version appears where installed.

Why this command matters: The version command does not change installed packages. On managed devices the package manager may be disabled by policy.

Safety and troubleshooting: If missing, use approved organisational software channels rather than downloading installers from unknown sites.

Step 2 — List candidate updates without installing them

winget upgrade

Expected result: Packages with available updates may appear; output format can change.

Why this command matters: This is a review step. Read publisher, source and proposed version before deciding whether anything should be upgraded.

Safety and troubleshooting: Do not run winget upgrade --all as part of an observation-only lesson.

Step 3 — Read a few installed Windows updates

Get-HotFix | Sort-Object InstalledOn -Descending | Select-Object -First 8 HotFixID, InstalledOn, Description

Expected result: Some recorded Windows updates appear.

Why this command matters: This cmdlet does not show every component or all update types. A missing entry is not conclusive proof a security fix is absent.

Safety and troubleshooting: Some computers restrict this view. State that a check was not available rather than guessing.

Step 4 — Read application version before planning change

git --version

Expected result: The installed Git version appears.

Why this command matters: For Umicom contributors, a Git update can change credential handling or command behaviour, so record the starting version before a planned upgrade.

Safety and troubleshooting: The command checks the executable resolved by PATH, not every installed copy of Git.

Linux — terminal practice

Run these in a Linux terminal on an authorised computer or VM. Some distributions do not install the same commands. An unavailable check should be reported as unavailable; do not assume an unobserved result is successful. No command below requires sudo.

Step 1 — Identify the package manager available

command -v apt; command -v dnf; command -v pacman

Expected result: Available commands print their paths; missing ones may cause a nonzero result.

Why this command matters: Debian/Ubuntu commonly use apt, Fedora/RHEL use dnf, and Arch uses pacman. Use the correct family for the machine.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 2 — List Debian/Ubuntu candidate updates only if apt exists

apt list --upgradable

Expected result: Candidate packages appear from existing metadata.

Why this command matters: This does not refresh metadata or install updates. Package information may be stale if the last refresh was long ago.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 3 — Read distribution details before planning

cat /etc/os-release

Expected result: Distribution and version details appear.

Why this command matters: Never copy upgrade instructions blindly from a different distribution or release.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Worked Umicom support scenario

A team wants to upgrade the MSYS2 GCC toolchain while Umicom Framework has a successful baseline. The maintenance record identifies the exact compiler version, the CMake preset and the selected regression tests. After the update they rerun the same builds and inspect ABI and test changes. If integration fails they revert to a verified toolchain according to the approved package policy, not by deleting arbitrary source files.

A disciplined investigation sequence

  1. Describe the symptom precisely. Identify what failed and the expected result.
  2. Identify the environment. Record current account, machine class, working directory and observation time; redact private identifiers.
  3. Run the smallest relevant read-only check. Choose evidence that distinguishes two possible causes.
  4. Compare results with the requirement. Missing, blocked or outdated checks are not successful checks.
  5. Separate fact and interpretation. Label hypotheses explicitly.
  6. Propose, do not silently apply, a change. State approval, effect, rollback and validation criteria.

Common mistakes and how to respond

Incorrect assumption Better engineering response
Any available update should be installed immediately on every computer. Security urgency matters, but operational deployment still requires approved controls, staged rollout and recovery.
A package manager's success means the application's tests passed. Installation and application qualification are separate phases.
Rolling back a binary always rolls back data safely. Database schemas or written data may not be backward compatible; recovery needs its own plan.

Practical exercises — try these before opening the answers

  1. Design a small change record.
  2. List four acceptance checks after a toolchain update.
  3. Explain why an update list is not an action list.
Suggested answers and reasoning — open after attempting the exercises
  1. Design a small change record. Include request, scope, old/new version, owner, time window, tests, rollback and final outcome.
  2. List four acceptance checks after a toolchain update. Compiler version, CMake configuration, native build and focused tests (plus wider regression when required).
  3. Explain why an update list is not an action list. Available updates must be evaluated for scope, dependencies, priority and authorisation.

Engineering connection: Umicom Framework

Umicom Framework's native build and release services should own technical qualification. A PowerShell package listing is an administrator's interactive observation, not a replacement for the Framework release pipeline, build evidence or source-preservation policy.

Chapter 47 — Build an incident timeline from logs and metrics

Bits to Banking · System Administration: From Zero · Umicom Foundation
Audience: beginners of any age; younger learners should use a supervised computer.
Suggested study time: 70–95 minutes.
Before this chapter: Chapters 12, 27 and 35: event logs, service states and incident evidence.

The question this chapter answers

How can I understand and check this part of a computer without accidentally changing something important?

Why this matters

When a problem appears, people remember different details. A timeline replaces those impressions with ordered observations. Each entry should identify when something was seen, which machine or service it concerns, what command or system produced the evidence and whether the result is verified. A good report separates facts, assumptions and proposed next steps.

Logs may contain paths, names, request identifiers and occasionally secrets accidentally printed by applications. Only inspect authorised systems and share the smallest redacted extract needed for investigation. This chapter never asks you to upload real private logs or change logging retention.

A useful mental model

Think of a sports referee's match record. It records what happened at particular times without inventing reasons. An administrator might record a failed login at 14:02, a service stop event at 14:03 and an application error at 14:04. Those times suggest a sequence, but correlation alone does not prove that the login caused the stop. To establish causation you need a reproducible mechanism and matching evidence.

Figure 47 — The concept and its safe evidence boundary.

Key terms, explained before using them

Term Meaning
Log entry A timestamped message recorded by a service or operating system.
Metric A numeric measurement such as CPU load or queue depth.
Correlation ID An identifier used to connect records from the same operation.
Incident timeline Ordered evidence describing observations around a problem.
Redaction Removal or masking of sensitive values before sharing.
Hypothesis A possible explanation not yet established as fact.

Read this before typing commands

Authorisation and safety: Use your own computer or an explicitly authorised learning environment. Start with an ordinary user account. Commands that install software, change access, restart services or modify networks are outside this exercise unless the text clearly identifies a harmless practice-file operation. You never need to disable a firewall or change system permissions to complete this chapter.

Reading code blocks: Open PowerShell 7 on Windows (pwsh) or a terminal on Linux. Type the line inside the block, not the example prompt. Run one command at a time. Some examples contain multiple interactive commands separated by semicolons; verify their results individually. These are interactive commands, not scripts added to Umicom.

Windows — PowerShell 7 practice

Do these steps on Windows. If you use Linux, read them for comparison and continue below. A missing command means that a tool or module may be unavailable; it is not a reason to bypass computer policy.

Step 1 — Record your own observation timestamp

Get-Date -Format o

Expected result: A local timestamp with offset appears.

Why this command matters: Use it to label the moment you observed the service, not to claim when the problem started.

Safety and troubleshooting: Do not compare timestamps from machines with wrong clocks without first noting the uncertainty.

Step 2 — Inspect a small Application log sample

Get-WinEvent -LogName Application -MaxEvents 8 | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, ProviderName, LevelDisplayName

Expected result: Up to eight recent event summaries appear.

Why this command matters: A summary is safer than distributing full messages. Filter by provider and period when investigating a known incident.

Safety and troubleshooting: An error from an unrelated application is not evidence that Umicom is failing.

Step 3 — Inspect a small process snapshot

Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 8 Name, Id, CPU

Expected result: The eight processes with the highest accumulated CPU time may appear.

Why this command matters: CPU in Get-Process commonly reports accumulated processor seconds, not instant percentage utilisation. Record the metric's meaning.

Safety and troubleshooting: Avoid assuming the first row is currently consuming the most CPU.

Step 4 — Inspect system availability of free space

Get-PSDrive -PSProvider FileSystem

Expected result: Current filesystem capacity information appears.

Why this command matters: This can help correlate a write failure with a full target volume, but a single snapshot does not prove the earlier state.

Safety and troubleshooting: Do not delete logs or build evidence to create space during a forensic investigation without authorisation.

Linux — terminal practice

Run these in a Linux terminal on an authorised computer or VM. Some distributions do not install the same commands. An unavailable check should be reported as unavailable; do not assume an unobserved result is successful. No command below requires sudo.

Step 1 — Record an observation time

date -Is

Expected result: A timestamp with timezone appears.

Why this command matters: Check consistency before comparing it with Windows records.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 2 — Inspect recent journal entries

journalctl -n 10 --no-pager

Expected result: Up to ten recent messages appear when authorised.

Why this command matters: The system journal may be empty or restricted for ordinary users; record that explicitly.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 3 — Read system uptime

uptime

Expected result: Current uptime and load averages are displayed.

Why this command matters: Load average is not the same as CPU percentage and must be interpreted relative to resources and workload.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Worked Umicom support scenario

A fictional Umicom Notes service became unavailable at 10:15. The support worker records the user-visible symptom, checks the process status at 10:18, verifies the storage volume at 10:20 and reviews only the application log covering 10:10–10:22. The report says 'storage has little free space; related save errors were logged' rather than 'the disk definitely caused everything'. A proposed fix is held pending authorisation and a backup check.

A disciplined investigation sequence

  1. Describe the symptom precisely. Identify what failed and the expected result.
  2. Identify the environment. Record current account, machine class, working directory and observation time; redact private identifiers.
  3. Run the smallest relevant read-only check. Choose evidence that distinguishes two possible causes.
  4. Compare results with the requirement. Missing, blocked or outdated checks are not successful checks.
  5. Separate fact and interpretation. Label hypotheses explicitly.
  6. Propose, do not silently apply, a change. State approval, effect, rollback and validation criteria.

Common mistakes and how to respond

Incorrect assumption Better engineering response
The first red error line caused the incident. Look at provider, time, operation and dependencies before inferring causality.
More logs are always better. Focused, permitted and redacted evidence is more useful and safer than indiscriminate collection.
A snapshot metric proves what happened earlier. Historical claims need retained samples or logs from the relevant period.

Practical exercises — try these before opening the answers

  1. Create a five-row fictional incident timeline.
  2. Explain why CPU seconds are not CPU percent.
  3. Prepare a safe report for a peer.
Suggested answers and reasoning — open after attempting the exercises
  1. Create a five-row fictional incident timeline. Record time, source, observation, verification status and follow-up; mark assumptions separately.
  2. Explain why CPU seconds are not CPU percent. Accumulated process time covers a period; utilisation measures a rate over an interval.
  3. Prepare a safe report for a peer. Remove names, private IPs, tokens and home-directory identifiers while keeping reproducible commands and error categories.

Engineering connection: Umicom Framework

Framework observability should provide structured records and bounded context. Studio's Problems panel and OS monitoring should maintain separate facts for process existence, service readiness and successful business operations. Retain evidence needed for audit under approved data-governance rules.
