Stage 3 · Practical infrastructure · Chapter 48

Chapter 48 — Capstone: support and verify a fictional Umicom service

Bits to Banking · System Administration: From Zero · Umicom Foundation
Audience: beginners of any age; younger learners should use a supervised computer.
Suggested study time: 90–140 minutes.
Before this chapter: Chapters 37–47 and the Update 39 support-evidence laboratory.

The question this chapter answers

How can I understand and check this part of a computer without accidentally changing something important?

Why this matters

A learner is ready to move towards professional administration when they can investigate a problem without making it worse. This capstone combines the course's skills in one fictional incident. The Umicom Notes training application is said to be unavailable; students must establish where they are, identify their tools, inspect relevant service and storage signals, review a verified backup, and write a clear conclusion.

The exercise does not require an actual Notes server, does not touch Umicom Bank or live services and does not issue payments or trading orders. Students may use a teacher-provided fictional worksheet if they do not have permission to inspect their own machine.

A useful mental model

The task is like assembling a puzzle from evidence. One piece says a process is running; another says a required filesystem is not available; another shows a backup from an older session. The pieces can be internally consistent and still not justify release readiness. You must distinguish observations, missing evidence, a proposed action and the acceptance criteria for declaring recovery complete.

Figure 48 — The concept and its safe evidence boundary.

Key terms, explained before using them

Term Meaning
Incident An unplanned interruption or degradation of an expected service.
Scope The machine, application, user group and time interval being investigated.
Evidence A verifiable observation such as a command result or test report.
Readiness gate A required check that must pass before service can be marked ready.
Remediation An authorised action intended to address the verified cause.
Closure A documented decision that the recovery criteria and communications have been satisfied.

Read this before typing commands

Authorisation and safety: Use your own computer or an explicitly authorised learning environment. Start with an ordinary user account. Commands that install software, change access, restart services or modify networks are outside this exercise unless the text clearly identifies a harmless practice-file operation. You never need to disable a firewall or change system permissions to complete this chapter.

Reading code blocks: Open PowerShell 7 on Windows (pwsh) or a terminal on Linux. Type the line inside the block, not the example prompt. Run one command at a time. Some examples contain multiple interactive commands separated by semicolons; verify their results individually. These are interactive commands, not scripts added to Umicom.

Windows — PowerShell 7 practice

Do these steps on Windows. If you use Linux, read them for comparison and continue below. A missing command means that a tool or module may be unavailable; it is not a reason to bypass computer policy.

Step 1 — Confirm the current shell and location

$PSVersionTable.PSVersion; Get-Location

Expected result: The shell version and working directory are displayed.

Why this command matters: The assistant cannot infer your host settings. Record the actual version and path rather than copying example values into the report.

Safety and troubleshooting: Use a normal user shell. Do not elevate to bypass a missing or denied observation.

Step 2 — Check that your practice data is present

Test-Path -LiteralPath "$HOME\UmicomLearning\BackupLab\source\notes.txt"

Expected result: True if you completed Chapter 41, False otherwise.

Why this command matters: A False result is expected on a new computer and is recorded as NOT RUN or MISSING, not silently repaired by inventing evidence.

Safety and troubleshooting: Do not replace or overwrite any non-practice files.

Step 3 — Review free space

Get-PSDrive -PSProvider FileSystem

Expected result: Available volumes and free-space values appear where supported.

Why this command matters: Identify the volume containing your practice folder. A different drive's capacity does not explain a failure on the target drive.

Safety and troubleshooting: Do not delete build directories or logs solely to improve free space.

Step 4 — Inspect recent application events without changing them

Get-WinEvent -LogName Application -MaxEvents 6 | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, ProviderName, LevelDisplayName

Expected result: A small recent sample appears where available.

Why this command matters: Unless an entry has matching application identity, time and operation, do not claim it proves the Notes incident.

Safety and troubleshooting: Never share raw logs containing personal data or tokens.

Step 5 — Review an Umicom Git checkout only if it exists

git -C "C:\umicom\Umicom-Bits2Banking" status --short

Expected result: Local source changes appear or an error explains the path is missing.

Why this command matters: This is a read-only Git command. It does not fetch, stage or commit anything.

Safety and troubleshooting: If the repository is missing, do not create a new checkout in the middle of the incident simply to make the result green.

Linux — terminal practice

Run these in a Linux terminal on an authorised computer or VM. Some distributions do not install the same commands. An unavailable check should be reported as unavailable; do not assume an unobserved result is successful. No command below requires sudo.

Step 1 — Check your identity and environment

id; pwd

Expected result: Current account and working directory appear.

Why this command matters: Record the environment before interpreting service and file-access results.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 2 — Review storage capacity

df -h .

Expected result: Filesystem usage for the current directory appears.

Why this command matters: State which mount point you inspected; do not attribute an unrelated disk to the incident.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Step 3 — Read a bounded service-log sample if allowed

journalctl --user -n 6 --no-pager

Expected result: Recent user journal messages appear or the command reports restricted/unavailable access.

Why this command matters: If no appropriate source exists, record the check as NOT RUN rather than writing a fabricated error.

Safety and troubleshooting: If this command is unavailable or access is refused, record the result. Do not alter system configuration simply to make the example succeed.

Worked Umicom support scenario

A classroom worksheet supplies these fictional facts: (a) the Notes window exists, (b) its document storage is not accessible, (c) an old backup from a previous session has a matching hash, and (d) no current save-and-read test was performed. The correct outcome is BLOCKED. A running window and an old backup cannot substitute for current storage and application readiness checks. The learner writes a recovery proposal: verify permissions and storage, restore to a separate review location if approved, then rerun the actual Notes operation.

A disciplined investigation sequence

  1. Describe the symptom precisely. Identify what failed and the expected result.
  2. Identify the environment. Record current account, machine class, working directory and observation time; redact private identifiers.
  3. Run the smallest relevant read-only check. Choose evidence that distinguishes two possible causes.
  4. Compare results with the requirement. Missing, blocked or outdated checks are not successful checks.
  5. Separate fact and interpretation. Label hypotheses explicitly.
  6. Propose, do not silently apply, a change. State approval, effect, rollback and validation criteria.

Common mistakes and how to respond

Incorrect assumption Better engineering response
A successful backup hash proves the application is now ready. Backup integrity and current service readiness are distinct; the former may not establish the latter.
Git status is clean, so the failure is resolved. Version-control cleanliness does not prove runtime correctness or tests.
A missing test should be recorded as passed to complete the checklist. A missing required test blocks the claim. An honest NOT RUN is better than false assurance.

Practical exercises — try these before opening the answers

  1. Prepare a ten-line incident report.
  2. Decide READY/REVIEW/BLOCKED for the fictional worksheet.
  3. Demonstrate a non-destructive recovery plan.
Suggested answers and reasoning — open after attempting the exercises
  1. Prepare a ten-line incident report. Include incident ID, scope, observation time, symptoms, three checks, one uncertainty, proposed action and closure criteria.
  2. Decide READY/REVIEW/BLOCKED for the fictional worksheet. BLOCKED: current required storage and application checks have not passed.
  3. Demonstrate a non-destructive recovery plan. Verify backup, restore separately, test actual document read, obtain approval before replacing production state.

Engineering connection: Umicom Framework

The Update 40 service-readiness C23 lab composes the existing Update 39 observation model. It evaluates fictional service dependencies, rejects stale or missing required checks and propagates blocked prerequisites. It does not inspect the host, replace real Framework supervision or authorise any recovery. The lab demonstrates why observation quality is part of engineering correctness.

Short support-note template

Observation ID: PRACTICE-____
Observed at (include timezone):
Authorised machine or learning environment:
User-visible symptom:
Command or test (never paste credentials):
Observed result:
What remains unknown:
Proposed next safe check:
Approval required before any change:

References and further study

  • https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/
  • https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/using-git/about-git

Course progression: Chapter 47 → Chapter 48 → Advanced course index.

Safety reminder: An honest not available, not authorised or not run result is better than a fabricated pass. No real system changes or remote repository writes are required.

Stage 4 · Managed services and recovery · Chapter 49

Chapter 49 — Map managed services and their dependencies

System Administration From Zero · Stage 4 — Managed Services and Recovery
Author: Sammy Hegab · Umicom Foundation
Study time: 65–85 minutes
Before starting: Chapters 10–12, 27–28 and 45: processes, services, event logs and readiness
Safety level: observation-only on real systems; any practice writes are confined to a folder owned by the learner.

What you will achieve

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to explain map managed services and their dependencies, identify the difference between an observation and a change, and interpret at least one Windows and one Linux administration result. You will also be able to describe the evidence that an authorised Umicom support engineer would need before taking action.

Why this matters in everyday computing

When a computer starts, many programmes run without anyone clicking an icon. Some keep the clock, network, printing or logging systems available. These are services. A beginner may recognise a service as ‘running’ in Task Manager and assume it is healthy. A professional administrator asks what that service does, who depends on it, and what evidence would demonstrate that it is functioning correctly.

In this lesson we will observe standard Windows and Linux service managers. We will not start, stop, disable or restart any system services. People sharing your computer may depend on them. The practical example is a fictional Umicom Notes application that needs both document storage and an event log. If its storage requirement fails, showing a green Notes icon would be misleading.

A mental model you can remember

Think of a school library. The door may be unlocked (process running), but the catalogue may be unavailable (dependency unhealthy). The librarian cannot promise you can borrow a book until both work. Similarly, a background service has a lifecycle, dependencies and a service-level result. The operating-system service manager can report whether a process was started, while an application health check must also confirm that it can perform its assigned work.

New words, without jargon

Term Meaning
Service A programme managed by the operating system and often started automatically.
Service manager The system component that starts, tracks and stops services.
Dependency Another service or resource that must be available first.
Unit The name used by systemd for a managed service, timer or other object.
Ready A service has passed the checks required for its intended work, not merely started.
Read-only inspection A command that reports status without requesting a configuration change.

Windows practical lesson — PowerShell 7

Open Windows Terminal → PowerShell, or search for PowerShell 7. Type only the commands inside each box; the example PS C:\...> prompt is not part of a command. Unless a step explicitly says otherwise, use your normal non-administrator account. The commands are interactive teaching instructions, not a .ps1 script.

Step 1 — Open a regular PowerShell session

pwsh

Expected result: A PowerShell 7 prompt appears. If not installed, follow the installation chapter.

What it means: Do not choose Run as Administrator for this exercise. Your normal account is sufficient for many observations.

If it looks different: If pwsh is unavailable, Windows PowerShell can run the read-only commands while you arrange an approved PowerShell 7 installation.

Step 2 — Inspect the Event Log service

Get-Service -Name EventLog | Select-Object Name, DisplayName, Status, StartType

Expected result: A table appears; Status is usually Running on a normal Windows installation.

What it means: Get-Service asks the service manager for its current status; Select-Object limits the displayed properties. This does not verify that a particular event was successfully written.

If it looks different: A corporate policy may restrict which service information is visible; a refusal is evidence of a boundary, not a reason to elevate automatically.

Step 3 — Inspect several services without altering them

Get-Service | Select-Object -First 8 Name, Status

Expected result: Eight service records, or fewer on an unusual machine, are shown.

What it means: The selection avoids printing the full service catalogue. Service names are identifiers; friendly display names can vary with language.

If it looks different: The output order is not a ranked list of importance.

Step 4 — Find processes without stopping them

Get-Process | Select-Object -First 8 ProcessName, Id

Expected result: You see programme names and process IDs.

What it means: A service may run inside a shared host process. A process ID is not a stable service identity and can change after restart.

If it looks different: Do not call Stop-Process or Stop-Service in this lesson.

Linux practical comparison

On a Linux computer or an authorised virtual machine, open a terminal. These are Bash-compatible commands; do not type the $ prompt. A minimal container, Chromebook or non-systemd distribution may have a different set of tools. A missing optional tool should be recorded rather than bypassed.

Linux step 1 — List currently active services

systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running --no-pager

Expected result: Service units appear on a systemd-based Linux system.

Interpretation: A minimal Linux container or another init system may not use systemd. That is a platform difference, not a failed course.

Linux step 2 — Read one service's state

systemctl status systemd-journald.service --no-pager

Expected result: A status report appears if the unit exists and is visible.

Interpretation: This reads status only. A running logging service is useful, but it does not establish that your own application logs are complete.

Linux step 3 — Examine dependencies

systemctl list-dependencies systemd-journald.service --no-pager

Expected result: A dependency tree appears; exact names depend on the distribution.

Interpretation: The tree describes configured unit relations. It does not prove all higher-level application data dependencies are ready.

Worked support scenario — Umicom Notes

A school's Umicom Notes workstation opens normally, but cannot save a new lesson. The support volunteer sees that the Notes process is running. They check its practice storage folder and find that the folder is read-only. The correct conclusion is ‘process started, service not ready’. They record the finding and ask the authorised administrator to review permissions; they do not disable antivirus or grant broad write permissions.

Evidence record: In your own words, describe the issue, the observation time, the command used, what you actually saw, what you have not proved, and who would approve a change. Avoid copying usernames, credentials, private filenames, IP addresses or confidential logs into public notes.

Common mistakes and how to correct them

Misunderstanding Better interpretation
Running means healthy. A process can run while a database, folder or dependent service has failed.
A Windows service always has its own process. Some services share processes; do not map service to application state from a PID alone.
Restarting is the first diagnostic step. Restarting may hide evidence or interrupt another user. Observe and record first.

Guided practice and suggested responses

Exercise 1. Describe two dependencies for Notes.

Suggested response: For instance, a writable practice folder and a correctly loaded document index.

Exercise 2. Explain status versus readiness.

Suggested response: State what Get-Service proves, then name an additional functional check.

Exercise 3. Create a support note.

Suggested response: Record service name, command, time and observed status, omitting any personal identifiers.

Questions for discussion

  1. Which part of today's map managed services and their dependencies exercise was read-only, and how do you know?
  2. What does a successful command prove, and what would it not prove?
  3. Explain Service to somebody who has never opened a terminal.
  4. If an expected result does not appear, what evidence would you collect before changing anything?
  5. How would you explain this issue to a colleague without exposing private data?

Connection to Umicom Framework and software engineering

The Framework-owned lifecycle and health services should be the source of truth for real Umicom products. The Update 40 C23 readiness laboratory models how a failed prerequisite prevents a dependent service from being labelled ready. This new chapter connects that model to observation commands; it does not reimplement or change the Framework service manager.

Further reading (optional internet access)

  • https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.management/get-service
  • https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemctl.html

Learning checkpoint

You are ready to proceed if you can explain the command, its expected output, the boundary of what it proves, and a safe response to unexpected output. If the exercise needed unavailable administrator access, record not performed; do not mark it as passed.

Chapter 50 — Inspect service identities and account boundaries

System Administration From Zero · Stage 4 — Managed Services and Recovery
Author: Sammy Hegab · Umicom Foundation
Study time: 60–80 minutes
Before starting: Chapters 9, 25–26 and 34: identity, groups, least privilege and access control
Safety level: observation-only on real systems; any practice writes are confined to a folder owned by the learner.

What you will achieve

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to explain inspect service identities and account boundaries, identify the difference between an observation and a change, and interpret at least one Windows and one Linux administration result. You will also be able to describe the evidence that an authorised Umicom support engineer would need before taking action.

Why this matters in everyday computing

A service does not have to run as the same person who is looking at its window. It may use a dedicated operating-system account with access to one folder or resource. That is a useful security boundary. If the service uses an overly powerful account, one defect can affect more of the machine than necessary.

This lesson is about reading those identities safely. We will distinguish the service’s name, the user account under which it runs, and the permissions that account may hold. We will not create service accounts, change logon credentials, edit access-control lists or bypass the permissions on a school or workplace machine.

A mental model you can remember

Imagine a classroom with different keys. A student can enter the classroom, a librarian can open the book cupboard, and an administrator may manage the whole building. Giving everyone the building master key would be convenient but dangerous. Service identities are similar: grant only the keys needed for that service’s work. An identity is not itself a permission; operating-system policy and file access rules determine what it can do.

New words, without jargon

Term Meaning
Service identity The operating-system account or security principal a service runs as.
LocalSystem A highly privileged built-in Windows service identity; not a normal user account.
Service account An account assigned to a programme for controlled access to resources.
Least privilege Give each service only the rights required for its declared duties.
ACL Access-control list: rules describing who may perform operations on an object.
Access denied The operating system refusing an operation under the current effective permissions.

Windows practical lesson — PowerShell 7

Open Windows Terminal → PowerShell, or search for PowerShell 7. Type only the commands inside each box; the example PS C:\...> prompt is not part of a command. Unless a step explicitly says otherwise, use your normal non-administrator account. The commands are interactive teaching instructions, not a .ps1 script.

Step 1 — See the logged-in user

whoami

Expected result: The currently signed-in Windows account identity appears.

What it means: The user who types a command is not necessarily the account running a background service.

If it looks different: Do not post the full account name publicly without checking whether it reveals private details.

Step 2 — Find one service's configured account

Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -Filter "Name='EventLog'" | Select-Object Name, StartName, State

Expected result: The service account and current state appear if Windows exposes that record.

What it means: StartName is the configured service identity. It does not by itself prove that the account can access every required file.

If it looks different: If the query returns nothing, check the service identifier and the CIM/WMI availability. Do not change security policies.

Step 3 — Read a practice folder's access rules

Get-Acl -LiteralPath "$HOME" | Select-Object Owner, AccessToString

Expected result: A local ownership summary and access rules may appear.

What it means: This is your home directory, not a colleague's data. Do not assume the display includes all effective inheritance, privilege or network-share conditions.

If it looks different: On managed machines, some security descriptors may be restricted; record the boundary instead of using elevated tools.

Step 4 — Check the current privilege context

whoami /groups

Expected result: A list of group memberships is shown.

What it means: Membership and effective privileges are different. An administrator account running unelevated does not automatically exercise every administrative right.

If it looks different: Long output is normal; focus on the idea of groups and tokens rather than memorising names.

Linux practical comparison

On a Linux computer or an authorised virtual machine, open a terminal. These are Bash-compatible commands; do not type the $ prompt. A minimal container, Chromebook or non-systemd distribution may have a different set of tools. A missing optional tool should be recorded rather than bypassed.

Linux step 1 — See your current identity

id

Expected result: Numeric user and group IDs with names are displayed.

Interpretation: The UID and groups help explain whether a file operation may succeed. Avoid running sudo to make this exercise work.

Linux step 2 — Inspect a service's user property

systemctl show systemd-journald.service -p User -p Group -p DynamicUser --no-pager

Expected result: Property names and values appear on a systemd host; empty User can mean the default system identity.

Interpretation: A service may use more advanced security constraints. This single command is not a complete permission audit.

Linux step 3 — Inspect your own directory

ls -ld "$HOME"

Expected result: Permission bits, owner and group of your home directory appear.

Interpretation: The first character identifies the object type; the next permission characters describe traditional access modes.

Worked support scenario — Umicom Notes

A fictional Umicom Notes server needs write access only to its authorised document directory. A contributor proposes running it with full administrative privileges to fix an access error. A safer plan first confirms which identity is configured, which directory must be writable and which least-privileged permission should be approved. The contributor documents the diagnosis without changing any real access rules.

Evidence record: In your own words, describe the issue, the observation time, the command used, what you actually saw, what you have not proved, and who would approve a change. Avoid copying usernames, credentials, private filenames, IP addresses or confidential logs into public notes.

Common mistakes and how to correct them

Misunderstanding Better interpretation
The name of a service is its user account. Service names identify workloads; service identities identify the operating-system security context.
An Access Denied message means I should immediately use sudo or Run as Administrator. First establish the authorised task and ownership. Elevation may make the risk worse.
A displayed ACL is the same as effective access. Inherited rules, deny entries, security tokens and share permissions also matter.

Guided practice and suggested responses

Exercise 1. Compare two identities.

Suggested response: Explain why the service's StartName may differ from whoami.

Exercise 2. Identify an unnecessary privilege.

Suggested response: Explain why a note-taking service normally should not require permission to install drivers.

Exercise 3. Write a permissions escalation request.

Suggested response: State the exact folder, needed operation, current account and evidence, without asking for blanket administrator rights.

Questions for discussion

  1. Which part of today's inspect service identities and account boundaries exercise was read-only, and how do you know?
  2. What does a successful command prove, and what would it not prove?
  3. Explain Service identity to somebody who has never opened a terminal.
  4. If an expected result does not appear, what evidence would you collect before changing anything?
  5. How would you explain this issue to a colleague without exposing private data?

Connection to Umicom Framework and software engineering

Umicom Framework's identity, configuration and audit capabilities are responsible for real service security. Bits2Banking teaches the least-privilege analysis rather than creating service accounts through an unreviewed training tool. A future Umicom Notes service should consume Framework storage and service contracts instead of writing arbitrary locations directly.

Further reading (optional internet access)

  • https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/win32/services/service-user-accounts
  • https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/id.1.html

Learning checkpoint

You are ready to proceed if you can explain the command, its expected output, the boundary of what it proves, and a safe response to unexpected output. If the exercise needed unavailable administrator access, record not performed; do not mark it as passed.

Stage 4 · Managed services and recovery · Chapter 51

Chapter 51 — Read systemd units and understand service startup order

System Administration From Zero · Stage 4 — Managed Services and Recovery
Author: Sammy Hegab · Umicom Foundation
Study time: 70–90 minutes
Before starting: Chapters 28, 45 and 49: Linux services, dependencies and readiness
Safety level: observation-only on real systems; any practice writes are confined to a folder owned by the learner.

What you will achieve

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to explain read systemd units and understand service startup order, identify the difference between an observation and a change, and interpret at least one Windows and one Linux administration result. You will also be able to describe the evidence that an authorised Umicom support engineer would need before taking action.

Why this matters in everyday computing

When a Linux computer starts, systemd can arrange for services to start in a suitable order. Each unit has settings about dependencies, commands and restart behaviour. A system administrator often needs to understand why a service did not start or why it started before a required resource was available.

This lesson explains unit files without asking students to install a custom system service. We read existing configuration from an authorised Linux host. On Windows, we compare the similar idea through the Windows Service Control Manager. You will learn why configured startup order cannot substitute for a real application readiness check.

A mental model you can remember

A theatre performance has a sequence of events: the stage lights need power, the doors open, the actors enter, and then the show begins. ‘After’ in a unit file is like saying the actors enter after the lights are switched on. It does not necessarily mean that every seat is occupied or that the actors have learned their lines. Dependencies coordinate lifecycle events; functional readiness must still be checked separately.

New words, without jargon

Term Meaning
Unit file Configuration describing a systemd service or another managed object.
After= An ordering relation: start this unit after another when both are scheduled.
Requires= A stronger unit dependency with failure implications; details depend on the transaction.
Wants= A weaker relationship that requests another unit without the same failure coupling.
Restart= A policy controlling whether systemd retries a terminated service.
Readiness probe A functional test that decides whether the service can do its intended work.

Windows practical lesson — PowerShell 7

Open Windows Terminal → PowerShell, or search for PowerShell 7. Type only the commands inside each box; the example PS C:\...> prompt is not part of a command. Unless a step explicitly says otherwise, use your normal non-administrator account. The commands are interactive teaching instructions, not a .ps1 script.

Step 1 — Read service startup configuration

Get-Service -Name EventLog | Select-Object Name, Status, StartType

Expected result: The service's startup type appears, normally Automatic for EventLog.

What it means: Automatic means the manager is configured to start it. It does not guarantee that your application will be ready afterward.

If it looks different: Do not modify Set-Service options on a shared computer.

Step 2 — See service dependencies

Get-Service -Name EventLog | Select-Object -ExpandProperty ServicesDependedOn

Expected result: Zero or more dependent service records appear.

What it means: An empty result can be valid. A dependency graph and a process state are different observations.

If it looks different: If querying the service is restricted, keep the evidence and ask an authorised administrator.

Step 3 — Read the exact configured service name

Get-Service -Name EventLog | Format-List Name,DisplayName,Status,StartType

Expected result: The individual service properties are shown.

What it means: Format-List is a display operation, not a change to the service. In shared notes capture only fields needed for troubleshooting.

If it looks different: Do not post computer names or account identities publicly.

Linux practical comparison

On a Linux computer or an authorised virtual machine, open a terminal. These are Bash-compatible commands; do not type the $ prompt. A minimal container, Chromebook or non-systemd distribution may have a different set of tools. A missing optional tool should be recorded rather than bypassed.

Linux step 1 — Read the journal unit's configuration

systemctl cat systemd-journald.service --no-pager

Expected result: The effective unit file and any visible drop-in configuration are printed.

Interpretation: Read headings such as [Unit] and [Service]. Do not copy configuration from the example into /etc/systemd/system.

Linux step 2 — Inspect ordering relationships

systemctl show systemd-journald.service -p After -p Requires -p Wants --no-pager

Expected result: The names of related units appear as space-separated property values.

Interpretation: A listed unit is not proof that it responded successfully to an application request.

Linux step 3 — Inspect recent unit messages

journalctl -u systemd-journald.service -n 10 --no-pager

Expected result: Up to ten recent unit-related log lines are shown, subject to permissions.

Interpretation: Logs may contain private paths or identifiers. Redact before sharing with a course group.

Worked support scenario — Umicom Notes

A fictional Umicom OS Notes service is configured to start after storage mounts. Its service process launches, but its storage index is still being reconstructed. A service manager reports the process active while the Notes readiness check remains blocked. The correct design is to retain the ordering configuration and add a functional readiness gate through approved Framework supervision, not to add arbitrary sleep delays.

Evidence record: In your own words, describe the issue, the observation time, the command used, what you actually saw, what you have not proved, and who would approve a change. Avoid copying usernames, credentials, private filenames, IP addresses or confidential logs into public notes.

Common mistakes and how to correct them

Misunderstanding Better interpretation
After= means the dependent application is ready. After= primarily describes ordering, not successful completion of business work.
Restart=always solves every fault. Repeated retries may create noise or worsen failures. Diagnose underlying causes and limits.
Editing a unit is the easiest beginner experiment. An error in a real service unit can disrupt the machine; start with read-only inspection and an isolated VM for future writes.

Guided practice and suggested responses

Exercise 1. Explain two dependency types.

Suggested response: Contrast ordering and a required relationship without changing either.

Exercise 2. Find one unit setting.

Suggested response: Use systemctl cat, record a visible setting and explain it in plain language.

Exercise 3. Identify a functional probe.

Suggested response: Suggest a harmless test that would show fictional Notes storage can actually read a practice file.

Questions for discussion

  1. Which part of today's read systemd units and understand service startup order exercise was read-only, and how do you know?
  2. What does a successful command prove, and what would it not prove?
  3. Explain Unit file to somebody who has never opened a terminal.
  4. If an expected result does not appear, what evidence would you collect before changing anything?
  5. How would you explain this issue to a colleague without exposing private data?

Connection to Umicom Framework and software engineering

Umicom Framework's supervised module lifecycle and readiness contracts should remain distinct from host systemd startup ordering. A module might report started but not yet ready until its Data Server or storage requirements are available. The C23 readiness laboratory from Update 40 models that distinction without using systemd APIs or scripts.

Further reading (optional internet access)

  • https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.unit.html
  • https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.service.html

Learning checkpoint

You are ready to proceed if you can explain the command, its expected output, the boundary of what it proves, and a safe response to unexpected output. If the exercise needed unavailable administrator access, record not performed; do not mark it as passed.

Stage 4 · Managed services and recovery · Chapter 52

Chapter 52 — Inspect scheduled tasks, cron and systemd timers

System Administration From Zero · Stage 4 — Managed Services and Recovery
Author: Sammy Hegab · Umicom Foundation
Study time: 60–80 minutes
Before starting: Chapters 11, 39 and 46: services, scheduled work and maintenance planning
Safety level: observation-only on real systems; any practice writes are confined to a folder owned by the learner.

What you will achieve

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to explain inspect scheduled tasks, cron and systemd timers, identify the difference between an observation and a change, and interpret at least one Windows and one Linux administration result. You will also be able to describe the evidence that an authorised Umicom support engineer would need before taking action.

Why this matters in everyday computing

Computers can run work at a particular time: make a backup, generate a daily report or check a service. Windows uses Task Scheduler; Linux commonly uses cron or systemd timers. These tools are useful, but a scheduled job that starts is not the same as a job that finishes correctly.

This chapter teaches observation, not installing background automation. We will inspect local task catalogues safely and learn about identity, triggering conditions, last-run outcomes and what happens when a machine was switched off at the expected time.

A mental model you can remember

Imagine a wall calendar that says ‘check library returns at 17:00’. Writing the appointment does not prove somebody did the work. A scheduler records the intention to start a job. The job's output, exit status, logs and business evidence decide whether the work was completed. A reliable administrator must know who owns each job, when it should run and how an interrupted run is recovered.

New words, without jargon

Term Meaning
Trigger An event or timetable that requests a job start.
Scheduled task A Windows definition for a command launched under specified conditions.
cron Traditional Unix-like time-based job scheduler.
systemd timer A unit that triggers another systemd unit on a time or event schedule.
Exit code A number returned by a programme to indicate its completion status.
Missed run A scheduled occurrence that was not executed, for example while the computer was off.

Windows practical lesson — PowerShell 7

Open Windows Terminal → PowerShell, or search for PowerShell 7. Type only the commands inside each box; the example PS C:\...> prompt is not part of a command. Unless a step explicitly says otherwise, use your normal non-administrator account. The commands are interactive teaching instructions, not a .ps1 script.

Step 1 — List a small sample of registered tasks

Get-ScheduledTask | Select-Object -First 8 TaskName, State, TaskPath

Expected result: A sample of scheduled tasks and their states appears.

What it means: These are definitions, not proof that the associated programmes completed successfully.

If it looks different: If Get-ScheduledTask is unavailable on a non-Windows host, skip the Windows section.

Step 2 — Inspect one existing task without executing it

Get-ScheduledTask | Select-Object -First 1 TaskName, TaskPath

Expected result: One task name and path are displayed; copy them into your private study notes.

What it means: Before using Get-ScheduledTaskInfo, choose a task visible to your account and pass its actual name and path, not an invented example.

If it looks different: Do not press Run or disable a system task while learning.

Step 3 — Check the current clock

Get-Date -Format o

Expected result: An ISO-style timestamp including your local timezone offset appears.

What it means: Schedulers interpret time zones and daylight saving rules. Record both the intended timetable and effective local time.

If it looks different: The exercise does not create a task or write a script.

Step 4 — Look at the configured tasks' states

Get-ScheduledTask | Group-Object State | Select-Object Name, Count

Expected result: A count by visible task state appears.

What it means: Ready is a scheduler state, not evidence that task output was useful.

If it looks different: Counts differ across machines and organisations.

Linux practical comparison

On a Linux computer or an authorised virtual machine, open a terminal. These are Bash-compatible commands; do not type the $ prompt. A minimal container, Chromebook or non-systemd distribution may have a different set of tools. A missing optional tool should be recorded rather than bypassed.

Linux step 1 — List timer units

systemctl list-timers --all --no-pager

Expected result: The next and previous trigger times appear when systemd timers exist.

Interpretation: A timer describes scheduling; check the triggered service separately if you need completion evidence.

Linux step 2 — Inspect your own cron table

crontab -l

Expected result: Your personal cron entries appear or a message says there is no crontab.

Interpretation: An empty crontab is normal. Do not edit system crontabs or use sudo for this lesson.

Linux step 3 — Read the local date and timezone

date --iso-8601=seconds

Expected result: The current timestamp appears on GNU/Linux; another Unix may support different options.

Interpretation: Compare the timezone with the scheduler display. Do not change the system clock as an exercise.

Worked support scenario — Umicom Notes

A team expects a daily Umicom Notes report, but none appeared on Monday. The workstation was powered off on Sunday night. The support volunteer checks the scheduled trigger, the last attempted run and whether a report file was produced. They do not add an unapproved extra trigger or write an automatic rescheduling script. They document whether the issue was a missed start or a failed programme.

Evidence record: In your own words, describe the issue, the observation time, the command used, what you actually saw, what you have not proved, and who would approve a change. Avoid copying usernames, credentials, private filenames, IP addresses or confidential logs into public notes.

Common mistakes and how to correct them

Misunderstanding Better interpretation
Task State Ready means yesterday's report succeeded. Ready often means eligible to run; inspect last-run evidence and output separately.
A scheduled job always runs after a computer turns back on. Recovery and missed-run behaviour depend on scheduler and task settings.
Tasks are always safe to run manually. A job may transmit payments, modify files or contact production systems. Never trigger one without authorisation.

Guided practice and suggested responses

Exercise 1. Write a hypothetical task contract.

Suggested response: Include purpose, owner, trigger, input, output, success signal and retry policy.

Exercise 2. Explain a missed-run scenario.

Suggested response: Describe how you would distinguish a powered-off host from a failed job.

Exercise 3. Check your timezone.

Suggested response: Use the read-only date command and identify its offset without changing the clock.

Questions for discussion

  1. Which part of today's inspect scheduled tasks, cron and systemd timers exercise was read-only, and how do you know?
  2. What does a successful command prove, and what would it not prove?
  3. Explain Trigger to somebody who has never opened a terminal.
  4. If an expected result does not appear, what evidence would you collect before changing anything?
  5. How would you explain this issue to a colleague without exposing private data?

Connection to Umicom Framework and software engineering

Real scheduled processing in Umicom should use approved Framework scheduler/task services and durable event histories rather than new PowerShell or Python background scripts. A TMS end-of-day task requires business completeness, not merely a successful process start. The teaching examples never schedule real financial operations.

Further reading (optional internet access)

  • https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/scheduledtasks/get-scheduledtask
  • https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.timer.html

Learning checkpoint

You are ready to proceed if you can explain the command, its expected output, the boundary of what it proves, and a safe response to unexpected output. If the exercise needed unavailable administrator access, record not performed; do not mark it as passed.

Stage 4 · Managed services and recovery · Chapter 53

Chapter 53 — Understand configuration, environments and secret boundaries

System Administration From Zero · Stage 4 — Managed Services and Recovery
Author: Sammy Hegab · Umicom Foundation
Study time: 70–90 minutes
Before starting: Chapters 9, 34 and 46: permissions, secrets and controlled changes
Safety level: observation-only on real systems; any practice writes are confined to a folder owned by the learner.

What you will achieve

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to explain understand configuration, environments and secret boundaries, identify the difference between an observation and a change, and interpret at least one Windows and one Linux administration result. You will also be able to describe the evidence that an authorised Umicom support engineer would need before taking action.

Why this matters in everyday computing

Two copies of the same application can behave differently even when their source code is identical. One may connect to a training database while another has no configured storage directory. Settings come from configuration files, operating-system environment variables, command-line options or a managed service. Knowing which input wins is essential for repeatable administration.

Students should distinguish a configuration value, a credential and a secret reference. A path to a practice folder may be ordinary configuration. A password, private key or access token is confidential. This lesson uses only a harmless temporary variable and never asks the learner to print real environment secrets or commit credentials to Git.

A mental model you can remember

Think of a school timetable. A general term timetable is the default, a classroom notice is a local setting, and a teacher's explicitly approved change may override the normal plan. Applications likewise need a documented order of configuration sources. An administrator must know which source supplied each effective value and whether a restart or revalidation is needed. A secret is more like a key to the building: it should not be copied onto the timetable.

New words, without jargon

Term Meaning
Configuration Settings that influence a programme without changing its compiled code.
Environment variable A named value a process may inherit when it starts.
Precedence The documented rule deciding which configuration source overrides another.
Secret Sensitive information such as a password, token or private key.
Secret reference An identifier that lets an authorised provider retrieve a secret without storing it in ordinary configuration.
Process scope Settings visible to a running process and, commonly, children it launches.

Windows practical lesson — PowerShell 7

Open Windows Terminal → PowerShell, or search for PowerShell 7. Type only the commands inside each box; the example PS C:\...> prompt is not part of a command. Unless a step explicitly says otherwise, use your normal non-administrator account. The commands are interactive teaching instructions, not a .ps1 script.

Step 1 — Read your current directory

Get-Location

Expected result: PowerShell prints the folder against which relative paths are interpreted.

What it means: Many applications use an explicit work directory so that opening a shortcut from elsewhere does not change file resolution.

If it looks different: Do not assume a program writes only to the current directory.

Step 2 — Show environment variable names, not sensitive values

Get-ChildItem Env: | Select-Object -First 10 Name

Expected result: The names of ten or fewer environment variables are listed.

What it means: Displaying names is safer than publishing the entire environment. Some real variable values contain credentials.

If it looks different: Do not paste a complete environment dump into a public issue.

Step 3 — Set a harmless value in the current shell

$env:UMICOM_LEARNING_MODE = 'practice'

Expected result: The variable exists for this PowerShell process and children started afterward.

What it means: This is an interactive lesson command, not a saved PowerShell script or a permanent machine setting.

If it looks different: A new terminal window may not inherit this particular shell's temporary value.

Step 4 — Read back the practice variable

$env:UMICOM_LEARNING_MODE

Expected result: The value practice is printed.

What it means: Observe that reading a benign variable differs from exposing an authentication token.

If it looks different: If empty, rerun the preceding command in the same shell.

Step 5 — Remove only the practice variable

Remove-Item Env:UMICOM_LEARNING_MODE

Expected result: There is normally no output; the value is removed from this shell.

What it means: This is an intentionally bounded clean-up step. Do not use wildcards or remove system variables.

If it looks different: Get-ChildItem Env: helps confirm the learning variable is gone.

Linux practical comparison

On a Linux computer or an authorised virtual machine, open a terminal. These are Bash-compatible commands; do not type the $ prompt. A minimal container, Chromebook or non-systemd distribution may have a different set of tools. A missing optional tool should be recorded rather than bypassed.

Linux step 1 — Show the configured search path

printf '%s\n' "$PATH" | tr ':' '\n' | head -n 5

Expected result: A few command search directories are listed.

Interpretation: PATH is a configuration value, not automatically a secret; still consider whether paths identify private locations before sharing.

Linux step 2 — Set a temporary harmless variable

export UMICOM_LEARNING_MODE=practice

Expected result: This value becomes available in the current shell and newly launched child processes.

Interpretation: The command changes only your current shell, not a global /etc environment file.

Linux step 3 — Remove your temporary variable

unset UMICOM_LEARNING_MODE

Expected result: The practice setting is removed from the current shell.

Interpretation: Avoid modifying configuration files or setting permanent variables in this chapter.

Worked support scenario — Umicom Notes

A student starts a fictional Umicom Notes demo by clicking its icon. It cannot locate its data folder. Running from a developer terminal works. The problem might be a relative path or an environment variable available only inside the terminal. A robust solution is a Framework-owned, inspectable configuration source and a path independent of the current working directory, not a hidden script that changes PATH globally.

Evidence record: In your own words, describe the issue, the observation time, the command used, what you actually saw, what you have not proved, and who would approve a change. Avoid copying usernames, credentials, private filenames, IP addresses or confidential logs into public notes.

Common mistakes and how to correct them

Misunderstanding Better interpretation
An environment variable is always safe to print. Some values contain access tokens and passwords; inspect names or redact values deliberately.
Running a command permanently changes all user accounts. Process-scope changes normally affect only the current process and its children.
A configuration file is a place to store every credential. Sensitive secrets belong behind authorised credential-provider boundaries, not ordinary source-controlled files.

Guided practice and suggested responses

Exercise 1. Draw a configuration precedence diagram.

Suggested response: Use compiled defaults, approved application settings and an explicit per-run override, noting which source wins.

Exercise 2. Explain why shortcuts sometimes behave differently.

Suggested response: Contrast starting an application from a repository folder with starting it from a desktop icon.

Exercise 3. Identify three things never to commit.

Suggested response: Examples include tokens, passwords and private signing keys.

Questions for discussion

  1. Which part of today's understand configuration, environments and secret boundaries exercise was read-only, and how do you know?
  2. What does a successful command prove, and what would it not prove?
  3. Explain Configuration to somebody who has never opened a terminal.
  4. If an expected result does not appear, what evidence would you collect before changing anything?
  5. How would you explain this issue to a colleague without exposing private data?

Connection to Umicom Framework and software engineering

Umicom Framework owns reusable configuration, identity and secret-provider contracts. Applications should ask those services for effective settings and keep their Data Server and resource paths independent of the shell's current directory. The course uses an interactive variable only to explain the mechanism; no implementation scripts are introduced.

Further reading (optional internet access)

  • https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_environment_variables
  • https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.exec.html

Learning checkpoint

You are ready to proceed if you can explain the command, its expected output, the boundary of what it proves, and a safe response to unexpected output. If the exercise needed unavailable administrator access, record not performed; do not mark it as passed.

Stage 4 · Managed services and recovery · Chapter 54

Chapter 54 — Plan software upgrades as controlled changes

System Administration From Zero · Stage 4 — Managed Services and Recovery
Author: Sammy Hegab · Umicom Foundation
Study time: 65–85 minutes
Before starting: Chapters 8, 29 and 46: package managers and maintenance windows
Safety level: observation-only on real systems; any practice writes are confined to a folder owned by the learner.

What you will achieve

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to explain plan software upgrades as controlled changes, identify the difference between an observation and a change, and interpret at least one Windows and one Linux administration result. You will also be able to describe the evidence that an authorised Umicom support engineer would need before taking action.

Why this matters in everyday computing

Installing a new application is usually straightforward. Upgrading software used by other people is harder: a library may be incompatible, a configuration file may change meaning, or a restart may interrupt active work. Professional administration therefore separates discovery, approval, installation, verification and rollback.

This lesson teaches how to find installed tool versions and plan a change without running an upgrade. We use Git, CMake and an imaginary Umicom Notes application as examples. Installing, upgrading and uninstalling packages remain outside this chapter unless a learner has explicit permission and an isolated practice environment.

A mental model you can remember

A software update is like replacing a part in a working bicycle. You first identify the part, check compatibility, plan a safe time, keep the old part available, and test the bicycle afterward. ‘The part fits’ is not the same as ‘the bicycle is safe to ride’. Likewise, a successful installer exit code is not proof that all Umicom builds, tests and user workflows still pass.

New words, without jargon

Term Meaning
Package manager A programme that locates, installs and updates software packages.
Dependency A library or component another programme requires.
Maintenance window A planned period during which authorised changes may occur.
Compatibility matrix A record of supported combinations of tools, runtimes and versions.
Rollback plan The documented steps to return to a verified previous state after a failed change.
Smoke test A small, focused check that essential functions still work after a change.

Windows practical lesson — PowerShell 7

Open Windows Terminal → PowerShell, or search for PowerShell 7. Type only the commands inside each box; the example PS C:\...> prompt is not part of a command. Unless a step explicitly says otherwise, use your normal non-administrator account. The commands are interactive teaching instructions, not a .ps1 script.

Step 1 — Check the Windows package manager

winget --version

Expected result: The installed winget version appears if available.

What it means: --version asks only for information; it does not install or upgrade anything.

If it looks different: Some locked-down devices do not provide winget. Ask the device administrator instead of downloading random installers.

Step 2 — Check the Git version

git --version

Expected result: A Git version string appears.

What it means: Record the version in a private maintenance note before proposing a toolchain change.

If it looks different: If Git is not found, use Get-Command git to investigate installation and PATH.

Step 3 — Inspect Git's package entry

winget list --id Git.Git --exact

Expected result: A matching package entry appears if winget recognises the installed Git.

What it means: winget's available metadata depends on package sources and local detection; a missing entry is not proof that Git is absent.

If it looks different: This command is read-only; do not run winget upgrade --all on a shared machine.

Step 4 — Check compiler and build tools

cmake --version

Expected result: A CMake version and related information appear if installed.

What it means: When reporting a failed build, a version matrix (CMake, Ninja, GCC, GTK4) is more useful than guessing that the newest version fixes it.

If it looks different: Repeat with git --version and ninja --version only if those tools are installed.

Step 5 — Record installed package versions

Get-Command git,cmake,ninja -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object Name, Source

Expected result: Found tool paths are displayed without printing environment secrets.

What it means: This helps distinguish two installations of the same programme on PATH.

If it looks different: Missing optional tools should be recorded as unavailable, not labelled broken.

Linux practical comparison

On a Linux computer or an authorised virtual machine, open a terminal. These are Bash-compatible commands; do not type the $ prompt. A minimal container, Chromebook or non-systemd distribution may have a different set of tools. A missing optional tool should be recorded rather than bypassed.

Linux step 1 — Check a package's candidate version (Debian/Ubuntu)

apt-cache policy git

Expected result: Installed and candidate versions are reported on compatible distributions.

Interpretation: This is a query, not a package update. On Fedora/RHEL a comparable read-only command is dnf info git.

Linux step 2 — Read the installed compiler version

gcc --version

Expected result: The compiler version appears if GCC is installed.

Interpretation: A compiler's version is part of build evidence; do not infer compatibility from the number alone.

Linux step 3 — Read recent package activity (when permitted)

journalctl -n 10 --no-pager

Expected result: A few log entries appear, but they are not necessarily package-related.

Interpretation: For an update investigation, use the distribution's package-management logs only if authorised, and redact private entries.

Worked support scenario — Umicom Notes

The Umicom Notes teaching lab was built with one GCC and CMake configuration. A contributor suggests upgrading all developer tools before a demonstration. The maintainer first records current versions, confirms available backups, chooses a separate test host, checks whether the application still builds and runs its native C23 tests there. Only after review is a host upgrade considered. A successful upgrade must not be equated with completed validation.

Evidence record: In your own words, describe the issue, the observation time, the command used, what you actually saw, what you have not proved, and who would approve a change. Avoid copying usernames, credentials, private filenames, IP addresses or confidential logs into public notes.

Common mistakes and how to correct them

Misunderstanding Better interpretation
The newest package always works best. Compatibility with your project and other dependencies may be more important than version number alone.
If the upgrade command exits zero, users have no remaining risk. Post-change build, functional tests and recovery evidence are still required.
Rollback means copying one executable back. Changes to configuration or data schemas may require independent recovery steps and explicit approval.

Guided practice and suggested responses

Exercise 1. Prepare a two-column version baseline.

Suggested response: List each installed tool and its purpose; do not change versions as part of the exercise.

Exercise 2. Write one maintenance-window checklist.

Suggested response: Include communication, scope, backup, approval, install plan, smoke test and rollback decision.

Exercise 3. Identify a stop condition.

Suggested response: For example, required CTest cases report Not Run or a restored dataset fails reconciliation.

Questions for discussion

  1. Which part of today's plan software upgrades as controlled changes exercise was read-only, and how do you know?
  2. What does a successful command prove, and what would it not prove?
  3. Explain Package manager to somebody who has never opened a terminal.
  4. If an expected result does not appear, what evidence would you collect before changing anything?
  5. How would you explain this issue to a colleague without exposing private data?

Connection to Umicom Framework and software engineering

Real Umicom releases should use existing Framework build, deployment, test and repository-evidence services. The native course lab in Update 41 models the decision boundary without installing packages or introducing shell automation. Framework and parent application gitlinks should be qualified independently before publication.

Further reading (optional internet access)

  • https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/package-manager/winget/
  • https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/

Stage 4 · Managed services and recovery · Chapter 55

Chapter 55 — Monitor service health using baselines and sensible alerts

System Administration From Zero · Stage 4 — Managed Services and Recovery
Author: Sammy Hegab · Umicom Foundation
Study time: 65–85 minutes
Before starting: Chapters 13, 35, 38 and 45: hardware, metrics, baselines and readiness
Safety level: observation-only on real systems; any practice writes are confined to a folder owned by the learner.

What you will achieve

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to explain monitor service health using baselines and sensible alerts, identify the difference between an observation and a change, and interpret at least one Windows and one Linux administration result. You will also be able to describe the evidence that an authorised Umicom support engineer would need before taking action.

Why this matters in everyday computing

A computer may be busy for a perfectly good reason: a backup is running or an application is compiling. It may also be struggling: storage is full, memory pressure is high or an essential service has stopped responding. Looking at one number without context can lead to false alarms.

An administrator starts with a baseline: what the machine normally does at an agreed time and workload. Then they define signals that deserve investigation. This lesson shows how to observe a small set of Windows and Linux counters without installing agents or exporting logs. It avoids turning every harmless variation into an emergency.

A mental model you can remember

Imagine checking the temperature of a classroom. A single warm reading after everyone arrives has a different meaning from a long-lasting extreme temperature with a broken ventilation system. Monitoring similarly needs context: expected load, observation time, duration, threshold and functional impact. An alert is a request to investigate, not proof of root cause.

New words, without jargon

Term Meaning
Metric A numerical measurement such as available memory, disk space or process CPU time.
Baseline Measurements representing known, ordinary behaviour under stated conditions.
Threshold A value at which a measurement triggers review.
Alert A signal that an agreed threshold or check warrants attention.
False positive An alert that fires even though the relevant system is operating acceptably.
Readiness probe A check of whether a service can perform a meaningful request.

Windows practical lesson — PowerShell 7

Open Windows Terminal → PowerShell, or search for PowerShell 7. Type only the commands inside each box; the example PS C:\...> prompt is not part of a command. Unless a step explicitly says otherwise, use your normal non-administrator account. The commands are interactive teaching instructions, not a .ps1 script.

Step 1 — Record the observation time

Get-Date -Format o

Expected result: A timestamp with timezone offset appears.

What it means: Any comparison across machines needs time context; do not assume their clocks are identical.

If it looks different: Keep the output in private study notes, not a public machine-identity dump.

Step 2 — Inspect a few processes

Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 5 ProcessName, Id, CPU

Expected result: Processes with large accumulated CPU time may appear near the top.

What it means: The CPU field is cumulative CPU seconds, not an instantaneous CPU percentage. Explain this difference before drawing conclusions.

If it looks different: A short-lived process may disappear before you inspect it again.

Step 3 — Inspect available physical memory

Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem | Select-Object FreePhysicalMemory, TotalVisibleMemorySize

Expected result: Memory figures appear, generally reported by this CIM class in kibibyte-sized units.

What it means: This is a snapshot. Always record the unit and time when comparing measurements.

If it looks different: A laptop with little free memory may still be using memory effectively for cache.

Step 4 — Check drive capacity

Get-PSDrive -PSProvider FileSystem | Select-Object Name, Used, Free

Expected result: Filesystem drives and byte counts are displayed.

What it means: Large log growth or a full target filesystem may affect services even when the system drive has free capacity.

If it looks different: Do not delete logs or build folders without review.

Step 5 — Look at services without restarting them

Get-Service -Name EventLog | Select-Object Name, Status

Expected result: Service status is displayed.

What it means: A running service is one evidence item; a useful alert may also check that the application emits or consumes expected events.

If it looks different: Stop-Service and Restart-Service are deliberately excluded.

Linux practical comparison

On a Linux computer or an authorised virtual machine, open a terminal. These are Bash-compatible commands; do not type the $ prompt. A minimal container, Chromebook or non-systemd distribution may have a different set of tools. A missing optional tool should be recorded rather than bypassed.

Linux step 1 — Inspect uptime and load

uptime

Expected result: The system uptime and load averages appear on many Linux systems.

Interpretation: Load average is not the same as CPU percentage; interpret it with CPU count and workload.

Linux step 2 — Inspect available memory

free -h

Expected result: Memory statistics appear in human-readable units.

Interpretation: Available memory matters more than treating all cache as permanently unavailable.

Linux step 3 — Inspect filesystem space

df -h .

Expected result: Capacity and available space for the current filesystem are shown.

Interpretation: The dot means the current directory. A service may use another filesystem for its data, so document the target path.

Worked support scenario — Umicom Notes

A fictional Umicom Notes student reports that saving is slow. The volunteer checks the time, application readiness, free space and a baseline from the previous day. The disk is nearly full, but the Notes data directory resides on a different volume with space available. The volunteer records the difference and checks the actual service path before proposing any clean-up. Observation prevents a destructive guess.

Evidence record: In your own words, describe the issue, the observation time, the command used, what you actually saw, what you have not proved, and who would approve a change. Avoid copying usernames, credentials, private filenames, IP addresses or confidential logs into public notes.

Common mistakes and how to correct them

Misunderstanding Better interpretation
The process at the top of CPU time must be faulty. Cumulative CPU time is not a direct speed or fault measurement.
One threshold works on every computer. Workload, hardware and accepted service targets differ.
Deleting logs is a safe way to recover space. Logs may be required for audit or incident recovery; retain evidence and seek approval.

Guided practice and suggested responses

Exercise 1. Design a three-metric baseline.

Suggested response: Include measure, unit, time, expected range and reason it matters.

Exercise 2. Write an alert response.

Suggested response: Describe what you would inspect if the Notes storage volume fell below a small agreed free-space threshold.

Exercise 3. Distinguish measurement from conclusion.

Suggested response: Explain why one high CPU measurement cannot prove a regression in Notes.

Questions for discussion

  1. Which part of today's monitor service health using baselines and sensible alerts exercise was read-only, and how do you know?
  2. What does a successful command prove, and what would it not prove?
  3. Explain Metric to somebody who has never opened a terminal.
  4. If an expected result does not appear, what evidence would you collect before changing anything?
  5. How would you explain this issue to a colleague without exposing private data?

Connection to Umicom Framework and software engineering

Use Umicom Framework observability, diagnostics and health contracts when developing production monitors. The course deliberately avoids creating a second logging agent or Python polling script. Framework components should publish bounded, authorised observations and keep alerts separate from automatic actions.

Further reading (optional internet access)

  • https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.management/get-process
  • https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/uptime.1.html

Learning checkpoint

You are ready to proceed if you can explain the command, its expected output, the boundary of what it proves, and a safe response to unexpected output. If the exercise needed unavailable administrator access, record not performed; do not mark it as passed.
