Stage 4 · Managed services and recovery · Chapter 56

Chapter 56 — Check local listeners and understand network exposure

System Administration From Zero · Stage 4 — Managed Services and Recovery
Author: Sammy Hegab · Umicom Foundation
Study time: 70–90 minutes
Before starting: Chapters 15, 16, 31, 43–44 and 49: IP addresses, ports, listeners and services
Safety level: observation-only on real systems; any practice writes are confined to a folder owned by the learner.

What you will achieve

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to explain check local listeners and understand network exposure, identify the difference between an observation and a change, and interpret at least one Windows and one Linux administration result. You will also be able to describe the evidence that an authorised Umicom support engineer would need before taking action.

Why this matters in everyday computing

An application can listen only to its own computer, to one network interface, or to every available interface. These choices change who may reach it. A local teaching HTTP server often binds to 127.0.0.1 so only programmes on the same host can connect. That is much safer for an unfinished educational server than accepting traffic from a whole network.

We will inspect listeners and firewall status without opening ports, changing firewall rules or connecting to unapproved hosts. Students will learn why an open TCP port is not proof that an application is secure, authenticated or producing the expected content.

A mental model you can remember

Think of doors in a building. A door between two rooms inside one house resembles a loopback listener. A door onto the street resembles a service bound to an external network interface. A firewall resembles a guard checking whether visitors can pass. A visible door does not tell you whether everyone entering is authorised or whether the correct work happens inside.

New words, without jargon

Term Meaning
Loopback Traffic addressed to the same host, commonly 127.0.0.1 or ::1.
Listening socket A network endpoint waiting for connections.
Bind address The address on which a service accepts incoming connections.
Wildcard address An address such as 0.0.0.0 that accepts connections for multiple IPv4 interfaces.
Firewall profile A collection of traffic-control rules for a network context.
Exposure Which other computers or users may reach a service, subject to routing and policy.

Windows practical lesson — PowerShell 7

Open Windows Terminal → PowerShell, or search for PowerShell 7. Type only the commands inside each box; the example PS C:\...> prompt is not part of a command. Unless a step explicitly says otherwise, use your normal non-administrator account. The commands are interactive teaching instructions, not a .ps1 script.

Step 1 — Inspect listening TCP endpoints

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | Select-Object -First 12 LocalAddress, LocalPort, OwningProcess

Expected result: Up to twelve listening endpoints are shown, subject to system permissions.

What it means: LocalAddress shows the bind scope. 127.0.0.1 is loopback; 0.0.0.0 is a wildcard, not necessarily evidence of external reachability.

If it looks different: If Get-NetTCPConnection is not available, note your Windows environment and do not install unapproved network tools.

Step 2 — Read firewall profile state

Get-NetFirewallProfile | Select-Object Name, Enabled

Expected result: A row for each available profile shows its enabled state.

What it means: This command reads policy. It does not show every individual rule or prove a service can be reached from a different network.

If it looks different: Do not disable a firewall to troubleshoot a training service.

Step 3 — Check your own local TCP connection capability

Test-NetConnection -ComputerName 127.0.0.1 -Port 8765

Expected result: TcpTestSucceeded is True only if a listener accepts the tested connection at that moment.

What it means: No server is started by this command. A False result is expected if you have not launched the previously taught local server.

If it looks different: Do not substitute a bank, school gateway or colleague's IP without their permission.

Step 4 — Find the loopback address information

Get-NetIPAddress -AddressFamily IPv4 | Where-Object IPAddress -eq '127.0.0.1' | Select-Object InterfaceAlias, IPAddress

Expected result: A loopback record may appear.

What it means: The address 127.0.0.1 refers to the local host from the computer running the command.

If it looks different: Different interface labels are normal.

Linux practical comparison

On a Linux computer or an authorised virtual machine, open a terminal. These are Bash-compatible commands; do not type the $ prompt. A minimal container, Chromebook or non-systemd distribution may have a different set of tools. A missing optional tool should be recorded rather than bypassed.

Linux step 1 — List TCP listeners

ss -ltn

Expected result: Local addresses and ports are displayed if the ss tool is installed.

Interpretation: The -l flag requests listening sockets, -t selects TCP, and -n uses numeric addresses instead of name lookup.

Linux step 2 — Inspect one loopback listener if available

ss -ltn '( sport = :8765 )'

Expected result: A matching listener appears only if a process is actually bound to TCP 8765.

Interpretation: No output is a legitimate observation; do not create a server merely to make a screenshot match.

Linux step 3 — Read high-level firewall tool availability

command -v ufw || command -v firewall-cmd

Expected result: The name of an installed firewall front-end may appear, or neither may be present.

Interpretation: Do not change firewall policy during an introductory network exercise.

Worked support scenario — Umicom Notes

A student runs the prior Bits2Banking C23 HTTP laboratory at 127.0.0.1:8765 and it works in a browser on the same computer. Another computer cannot connect. This is the intended isolation, not necessarily a fault. To publish a production service requires approved network design, authentication, TLS, reverse-proxy policy and security review—not simply changing the bind address to 0.0.0.0.

Evidence record: In your own words, describe the issue, the observation time, the command used, what you actually saw, what you have not proved, and who would approve a change. Avoid copying usernames, credentials, private filenames, IP addresses or confidential logs into public notes.

Common mistakes and how to correct them

Misunderstanding Better interpretation
0.0.0.0 is a destination I can connect to. It is normally a wildcard bind address, not a remote server's address.
A port is open, therefore my application is healthy. A listener may accept a connection while returning errors or unauthorised data.
Disabling the firewall is a harmless test. It can expose other services. Inspect and seek approval for narrowly scoped rules instead.

Guided practice and suggested responses

Exercise 1. Classify three bind addresses.

Suggested response: Contrast 127.0.0.1, ::1 and 0.0.0.0.

Exercise 2. Explain the difference between network and application success.

Suggested response: A successful TCP connection does not prove an HTTP response is valid.

Exercise 3. Write a safe escalation note.

Suggested response: If a corporate listener must become remotely available, identify the service owner and required security review rather than changing configuration yourself.

Questions for discussion

  1. Which part of today's check local listeners and understand network exposure exercise was read-only, and how do you know?
  2. What does a successful command prove, and what would it not prove?
  3. Explain Loopback to somebody who has never opened a terminal.
  4. If an expected result does not appear, what evidence would you collect before changing anything?
  5. How would you explain this issue to a colleague without exposing private data?

Connection to Umicom Framework and software engineering

Umicom Framework's network and security contracts should govern a production listener. The earlier Bits2Banking HTTP server is a loopback educational laboratory and must not be presented as a hardened public TLS service. Keep future runtime functionality in Framework C23, with applications using existing provider contracts.

Further reading (optional internet access)

  • https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/nettcpip/get-nettcpconnection
  • https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ss.8.html

Stage 4 · Managed services and recovery · Chapter 57

Chapter 57 — Design backup retention and recovery evidence

System Administration From Zero · Stage 4 — Managed Services and Recovery
Author: Sammy Hegab · Umicom Foundation
Study time: 65–85 minutes
Before starting: Chapters 14, 33 and 41: creating a practice backup and performing a restore
Safety level: observation-only on real systems; any practice writes are confined to a folder owned by the learner.

What you will achieve

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to explain design backup retention and recovery evidence, identify the difference between an observation and a change, and interpret at least one Windows and one Linux administration result. You will also be able to describe the evidence that an authorised Umicom support engineer would need before taking action.

Why this matters in everyday computing

A backup copy is useful only if it still exists when needed and contains the information the user expects. Backup strategies therefore include where copies are stored, which copies are retained, how access is controlled and how restoration is tested. An old backup may lack recent edits; a checksum may confirm byte equality without proving a document is useful.

This lesson uses only the learner's own practice folder. We will verify files and write a simple inventory. We will not read, copy or remove data belonging to another user, and we will not connect to cloud storage, a NAS or a production database without explicit permission.

A mental model you can remember

Imagine keeping important class notes. One copy in your school bag can be damaged or lost. A second copy in the same bag does not protect against losing the entire bag. Keeping a copy elsewhere helps, but only if you can open it when needed. The familiar 3-2-1 principle is a useful starting point: three copies, on two types of media, with one off-site; modern policies may additionally require immutability, offline isolation and tested recovery.

New words, without jargon

Term Meaning
Retention How long a backup remains available before approved expiry.
Recovery point objective (RPO) The maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured backward in time.
Recovery time objective (RTO) The targeted time to restore an acceptable service.
Integrity hash A digest that helps compare file bytes when produced and trusted appropriately.
Immutable backup A backup protected from unauthorised modification or deletion under a defined policy.
Restore drill A planned test that recovers data and checks it can be used.

Windows practical lesson — PowerShell 7

Open Windows Terminal → PowerShell, or search for PowerShell 7. Type only the commands inside each box; the example PS C:\...> prompt is not part of a command. Unless a step explicitly says otherwise, use your normal non-administrator account. The commands are interactive teaching instructions, not a .ps1 script.

Step 1 — Prepare a private practice directory

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\UmicomLearning\BackupStudy"

Expected result: The folder is created if absent; existing practice material is retained.

What it means: Use the learner's home folder rather than a shared C:\ system directory.

If it looks different: If your computer restricts your home folder, choose another authorised location.

Step 2 — Write a harmless practice note

Set-Content -LiteralPath "$HOME\UmicomLearning\BackupStudy\notes.txt" -Value 'Umicom Notes practice record - version 1'

Expected result: A small text file is created in the practice directory.

What it means: Set-Content overwrites a file of the same name. Only run this command in the dedicated training directory and after checking for an existing practice file.

If it looks different: If you want to preserve a previous practice note, choose a new filename before writing.

Step 3 — Copy to a second named practice file

Copy-Item -LiteralPath "$HOME\UmicomLearning\BackupStudy\notes.txt" -Destination "$HOME\UmicomLearning\BackupStudy\notes-copy.txt"

Expected result: The second file appears; this teaches a copy, not a full backup strategy.

What it means: Both files are on the same filesystem and may be lost together. A genuine backup has independent failure boundaries.

If it looks different: If notes-copy.txt already exists, inspect it and choose a new destination instead of using -Force.

Step 4 — Compare hashes before a restore

Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 -LiteralPath "$HOME\UmicomLearning\BackupStudy\notes.txt","$HOME\UmicomLearning\BackupStudy\notes-copy.txt" | Select-Object Path, Hash

Expected result: Both hashes should match when the two files contain identical bytes.

What it means: This supports byte equality; it does not establish that the file was complete or that a database snapshot is consistent.

If it looks different: If hashes differ, do not overwrite the source. Investigate which copy contains the expected content.

Linux practical comparison

On a Linux computer or an authorised virtual machine, open a terminal. These are Bash-compatible commands; do not type the $ prompt. A minimal container, Chromebook or non-systemd distribution may have a different set of tools. A missing optional tool should be recorded rather than bypassed.

Linux step 1 — Create a private practice directory

mkdir -p "$HOME/UmicomLearning/BackupStudy"

Expected result: A directory is available under your home folder.

Interpretation: The directory should contain only the training files you own.

Linux step 2 — Create a practice note

printf '%s\n' 'Umicom Notes practice record - version 1' > "$HOME/UmicomLearning/BackupStudy/notes.txt"

Expected result: The note contains one line of fictional text.

Interpretation: Redirection overwrites an existing file, so perform this only in your known practice folder.

Linux step 3 — Copy and compare fingerprints

cp "$HOME/UmicomLearning/BackupStudy/notes.txt" "$HOME/UmicomLearning/BackupStudy/notes-copy.txt" && sha256sum "$HOME/UmicomLearning/BackupStudy/notes.txt" "$HOME/UmicomLearning/BackupStudy/notes-copy.txt"

Expected result: Two identical SHA-256 values appear if the copied bytes match.

Interpretation: The && means the checksum step runs only when the copy succeeds. Neither command provides offsite redundancy.

Worked support scenario — Umicom Notes

A volunteer maintains a fictional course catalogue with daily changes. The backup plan keeps last week's copy and yesterday's copy, but the restore requirement is to lose no more than one hour. The observed schedule cannot satisfy that RPO. Rather than claiming coverage, the volunteer reports the gap, proposes an approved higher-frequency strategy, and plans a restore drill that tests both content and permissions.

Evidence record: In your own words, describe the issue, the observation time, the command used, what you actually saw, what you have not proved, and who would approve a change. Avoid copying usernames, credentials, private filenames, IP addresses or confidential logs into public notes.

Common mistakes and how to correct them

Misunderstanding Better interpretation
Two copies on one disk satisfy disaster recovery. One disk failure can remove both copies.
A matching checksum proves business correctness. It proves selected bytes match a reference; a corrupted original can be copied perfectly.
Backups can be tested by opening a list of filenames. A successful restore requires actual usable data and checks against expected results.

Guided practice and suggested responses

Exercise 1. Choose an RPO and RTO for a fictional school portal.

Suggested response: Explain separately how much data loss and downtime are acceptable.

Exercise 2. Design a retention sketch.

Suggested response: Record a daily, weekly and off-site copy with access controls and a scheduled restore test.

Exercise 3. Verify your practice note.

Suggested response: Explain the two matching hashes and the limitations of that result.

Questions for discussion

  1. Which part of today's design backup retention and recovery evidence exercise was read-only, and how do you know?
  2. What does a successful command prove, and what would it not prove?
  3. Explain Retention to somebody who has never opened a terminal.
  4. If an expected result does not appear, what evidence would you collect before changing anything?
  5. How would you explain this issue to a colleague without exposing private data?

Connection to Umicom Framework and software engineering

The Data Server owns persistence for Umicom-managed application data, while Framework backup/recovery and audit contracts should govern production evidence. A source-code Git commit is not a substitute for restoring a database, configuration and authorised secrets. No new backup implementation or Python/PowerShell automation is introduced by the lesson.

Further reading (optional internet access)

  • https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.utility/get-filehash
  • https://www.cisa.gov/secure-our-world/back-up-your-data

Learning checkpoint

You are ready to proceed if you can explain the command, its expected output, the boundary of what it proves, and a safe response to unexpected output. If the exercise needed unavailable administrator access, record not performed; do not mark it as passed.

Stage 4 · Managed services and recovery · Chapter 58

Chapter 58 — Rehearse restoration and document rollback

System Administration From Zero · Stage 4 — Managed Services and Recovery
Author: Sammy Hegab · Umicom Foundation
Study time: 70–90 minutes
Before starting: Chapters 33, 41 and 57: checksum validation, RPO/RTO and recovery copies
Safety level: observation-only on real systems; any practice writes are confined to a folder owned by the learner.

What you will achieve

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to explain rehearse restoration and document rollback, identify the difference between an observation and a change, and interpret at least one Windows and one Linux administration result. You will also be able to describe the evidence that an authorised Umicom support engineer would need before taking action.

Why this matters in everyday computing

The phrase ‘we have a backup’ is not enough when a service fails. Administrators must know exactly how to locate the right copy, restore it safely, check permissions and decide whether the application may return to normal use. Software rollback and data restoration are related but separate. An older executable may not understand a database that was migrated by a newer release.

This lesson demonstrates a harmless file restoration into a separate practice folder. It does not replace real application files, reboot a machine, restore a system partition or execute database recovery. The focus is on evidence and decision-making.

A mental model you can remember

Imagine losing the original recipe for a class project. You have a saved copy, but before using it you check the page count and ingredients. You do not immediately throw away the damaged original. A safe data restore similarly writes into a controlled destination first, verifies content and only then considers a production cutover under approval. A rollback plan also needs to account for code, configuration, database and dependencies.

New words, without jargon

Term Meaning
Restore Bring back data from a protected copy into a chosen location.
Rollback Return a changed system to an approved previous state.
Cutover The controlled step that directs users or traffic to a newly prepared environment.
Migration A controlled transformation of stored data or schema.
Reconciliation Checking that recovered data agrees with authoritative expected records.
Restore point A specific recoverable copy identified by date, version or immutable manifest.

Windows practical lesson — PowerShell 7

Open Windows Terminal → PowerShell, or search for PowerShell 7. Type only the commands inside each box; the example PS C:\...> prompt is not part of a command. Unless a step explicitly says otherwise, use your normal non-administrator account. The commands are interactive teaching instructions, not a .ps1 script.

Step 1 — Check the practice backup exists

Test-Path -LiteralPath "$HOME\UmicomLearning\BackupStudy\notes-copy.txt"

Expected result: True means the previous chapter's practice copy is present.

What it means: A missing file is an expected condition if you have not completed Chapter 57; create only your own practice input first.

If it looks different: Never substitute a real company backup path in a public lesson.

Step 2 — Make a separate restoration directory

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$HOME\UmicomLearning\RestoreStudy"

Expected result: The new practice restore directory exists.

What it means: Restoring into a separate location prevents an unverified copy from overwriting the working document.

If it looks different: If this folder already contains valuable work, create another named training directory.

Step 3 — Restore the practice copy without overwriting data

Copy-Item -LiteralPath "$HOME\UmicomLearning\BackupStudy\notes-copy.txt" -Destination "$HOME\UmicomLearning\RestoreStudy\notes-restored.txt"

Expected result: A second practice file is created if the destination did not exist.

What it means: This is an ordinary file copy, not a system restore or application schema rollback.

If it looks different: If the destination exists, stop and inspect it; don't use -Force casually.

Step 4 — Compare the source and restored fingerprints

Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 -LiteralPath "$HOME\UmicomLearning\BackupStudy\notes-copy.txt","$HOME\UmicomLearning\RestoreStudy\notes-restored.txt" | Select-Object Path, Hash

Expected result: Matching SHA-256 values support byte equality between the two practice files.

What it means: Also open the restored note and check that its contents are what the learner expects.

If it looks different: A binary application's successful restoration requires application-level checks beyond a hash.

Step 5 — Read the restored content

Get-Content -LiteralPath "$HOME\UmicomLearning\RestoreStudy\notes-restored.txt"

Expected result: The fictional Notes sentence appears.

What it means: Keep a record of the path, restore time and verifier rather than declaring all backups safe.

If it looks different: Do not restore a real finance file or database without authorised procedures.

Linux practical comparison

On a Linux computer or an authorised virtual machine, open a terminal. These are Bash-compatible commands; do not type the $ prompt. A minimal container, Chromebook or non-systemd distribution may have a different set of tools. A missing optional tool should be recorded rather than bypassed.

Linux step 1 — Check the practice backup file

test -f "$HOME/UmicomLearning/BackupStudy/notes-copy.txt" && printf 'Backup present\n'

Expected result: The message appears when the file exists; otherwise the command exits with a nonzero status.

Interpretation: Nonzero here may simply mean the Chapter 57 practice file has not been created.

Linux step 2 — Prepare a separate restore folder

mkdir -p "$HOME/UmicomLearning/RestoreStudy"

Expected result: A separate directory exists.

Interpretation: Do not restore on top of the only remaining copy.

Linux step 3 — Copy and inspect the recovered file

cp -n "$HOME/UmicomLearning/BackupStudy/notes-copy.txt" "$HOME/UmicomLearning/RestoreStudy/notes-restored.txt" && sha256sum "$HOME/UmicomLearning/RestoreStudy/notes-restored.txt"

Expected result: The file is copied if it did not exist, and its checksum is shown.

Interpretation: -n avoids replacement where supported. Confirm whether the destination already exists before treating the command as a new restore.

Worked support scenario — Umicom Notes

A fictional Umicom Notes release includes a new database schema. The desktop crashes afterward. Rolling back the executable alone may not work against the new schema. The operations team should have an approved migration backup, a verified restoration procedure, a downtime plan and a test proving that the previous release can read the recovered data. A human change owner decides whether to recover; a CLI warning is not permission to override controls.

Evidence record: In your own words, describe the issue, the observation time, the command used, what you actually saw, what you have not proved, and who would approve a change. Avoid copying usernames, credentials, private filenames, IP addresses or confidential logs into public notes.

Common mistakes and how to correct them

Misunderstanding Better interpretation
A successful copy equals a complete restore. The recovered file also needs functional inspection, correct identity and permission checks.
Returning to the old executable always fixes the problem. Data schema or configuration may have changed incompatibly.
A failed restore should be hidden and retried silently. Report the failure and preserve the evidence; uncontrolled retries may overwrite valid information.

Guided practice and suggested responses

Exercise 1. Draw a rollback dependency table.

Suggested response: Include executable, configuration, database, compatibility and verification owners.

Exercise 2. Perform the dedicated practice restore.

Suggested response: Use the commands above and verify both hash and content.

Exercise 3. State a safe stop condition.

Suggested response: For example, recovered data fails reconciliation or the restore destination unexpectedly exists.

Questions for discussion

  1. Which part of today's rehearse restoration and document rollback exercise was read-only, and how do you know?
  2. What does a successful command prove, and what would it not prove?
  3. Explain Restore to somebody who has never opened a terminal.
  4. If an expected result does not appear, what evidence would you collect before changing anything?
  5. How would you explain this issue to a colleague without exposing private data?

Connection to Umicom Framework and software engineering

Real Umicom application data must be recovered through Data Server and authorised operational contracts. Umicom Framework should own reusable restore/report facilities rather than distributing product-specific scripts. Update 41's C23 lab can record a fictional restoration decision; it cannot restore real data or prove that a production machine is healthy.

Further reading (optional internet access)

  • https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.management/copy-item
  • https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.service.html

Stage 4 · Managed services and recovery · Chapter 59

Chapter 59 — Triage incidents and communicate with evidence

System Administration From Zero · Stage 4 — Managed Services and Recovery
Author: Sammy Hegab · Umicom Foundation
Study time: 70–90 minutes
Before starting: Chapters 12, 23, 35 and 47: logs, systematic troubleshooting and incident timelines
Safety level: observation-only on real systems; any practice writes are confined to a folder owned by the learner.

What you will achieve

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to explain triage incidents and communicate with evidence, identify the difference between an observation and a change, and interpret at least one Windows and one Linux administration result. You will also be able to describe the evidence that an authorised Umicom support engineer would need before taking action.

Why this matters in everyday computing

A technical problem may affect one user or hundreds. When somebody reports ‘Umicom Notes is down’, an administrator needs to identify the actual impact before changing settings. Is the app failing to start, unable to save, or simply slow? Has another system already changed? Which observations are factual, and which are only hypotheses?

This lesson teaches a calm, evidence-driven sequence: identify scope, record time, check current state, preserve relevant diagnostics, communicate uncertainty and escalate only to authorised owners. We do not collect confidential documents, share patient or financial data, restart services or perform unapproved forensic actions.

A mental model you can remember

Think of a doctor taking observations before choosing a treatment. ‘The patient looks tired’ is not the same as a diagnosis. Likewise, a red error banner is a symptom. The incident timeline should separate what the user reported, what the administrator observed, what changed, what was tested and what remains unknown. Clear evidence shortens recovery time and prevents a second person repeating a risky experiment.

New words, without jargon

Term Meaning
Incident An unplanned interruption or reduction in expected service quality.
Symptom What users or monitoring systems observe when something is wrong.
Hypothesis A proposed explanation that has not yet been verified.
Scope The users, components, locations and operations actually affected.
Escalation Passing responsibility to an authorised specialist or decision owner.
Timeline Time-ordered observations and actions with source, clock and outcome.

Windows practical lesson — PowerShell 7

Open Windows Terminal → PowerShell, or search for PowerShell 7. Type only the commands inside each box; the example PS C:\...> prompt is not part of a command. Unless a step explicitly says otherwise, use your normal non-administrator account. The commands are interactive teaching instructions, not a .ps1 script.

Step 1 — Record a timestamp

Get-Date -Format o

Expected result: An ISO-style timestamp with timezone offset is printed.

What it means: An incident note should use a consistent time reference. Preserve the original timezone where possible.

If it looks different: Do not change the system clock to make log times appear to match.

Step 2 — Inspect a known service without altering it

Get-Service -Name EventLog | Select-Object Name, Status

Expected result: The current service state appears.

What it means: This is one observation. Do not conclude a fictional Notes fault originates in the Windows event log service merely because you checked it.

If it looks different: Do not restart the service without authorisation.

Step 3 — Inspect a small selection of recent Windows System events

Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddMinutes(-30)} -MaxEvents 5 | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, LevelDisplayName

Expected result: Up to five recent visible events appear; there may be none or access may be restricted.

What it means: Read the event provider, time and meaning before associating it with the reported problem. Events can contain private details, so avoid copying full messages publicly.

If it looks different: If this query fails because the log is inaccessible, record that as a permission boundary.

Step 4 — Check the local source repository without changing it

git -C "C:\umicom\Umicom-Bits2Banking" status --short

Expected result: Modified or untracked paths appear if the repository exists.

What it means: This command is conditional on having the repository at that location. The result is not proof a runtime incident came from source edits.

If it looks different: On another machine, use the actual authorised repository path or skip this step.

Step 5 — Read the command help for a suspected tool

Get-Help Get-WinEvent -Examples

Expected result: Usage examples are shown when the help content is installed.

What it means: Use help to understand an unfamiliar command before changing anything.

If it looks different: If help is incomplete, Get-Help Get-WinEvent -Online opens documentation but requires network access.

Linux practical comparison

On a Linux computer or an authorised virtual machine, open a terminal. These are Bash-compatible commands; do not type the $ prompt. A minimal container, Chromebook or non-systemd distribution may have a different set of tools. A missing optional tool should be recorded rather than bypassed.

Linux step 1 — Capture the current clock

date --iso-8601=seconds

Expected result: A local timestamp is printed on GNU/Linux.

Interpretation: Record the timezone in the incident timeline.

Linux step 2 — Inspect recent journal entries

journalctl --since '30 minutes ago' -n 10 --no-pager

Expected result: Up to ten accessible entries appear, or permission restrictions are reported.

Interpretation: Log entries may contain private host details. Share only a redacted, relevant excerpt with authorised people.

Linux step 3 — Check a service's state

systemctl status systemd-journald.service --no-pager

Expected result: Systemd prints unit status if available.

Interpretation: A service can be active while the reported business function is unavailable. Compare with functional evidence.

Worked support scenario — Umicom Notes

A class tutor reports that Umicom Notes cannot save practice homework for one student. Other students can save normally. The volunteer records the error time and which account is affected, tests only the student's own practice folder under supervision, and observes that storage permissions differ. They do not reset everyone’s passwords or delete shared caches. The support note separates ‘one user affected’ from ‘all services down’ and routes the permission review to the right owner.

Evidence record: In your own words, describe the issue, the observation time, the command used, what you actually saw, what you have not proved, and who would approve a change. Avoid copying usernames, credentials, private filenames, IP addresses or confidential logs into public notes.

Common mistakes and how to correct them

Misunderstanding Better interpretation
The first error message identifies the root cause. An error can be a downstream symptom. Trace dependencies and changes.
More logs always make a better report. Share only relevant, redacted evidence. Excess logs can leak data and obscure the sequence.
An administrator should fix incidents before telling users anything. Timely, accurate scope and uncertainty updates reduce confusion and duplicate work.

Guided practice and suggested responses

Exercise 1. Create an incident record template.

Suggested response: Include unique reference, start time, affected function, observed evidence, actions, owner and next update.

Exercise 2. Write one factual and one hypothetical sentence.

Suggested response: Example: ‘Save returned an access error at 10:12’ is factual; ‘a policy change caused it’ is a hypothesis.

Exercise 3. Practice an escalation summary.

Suggested response: Explain what was checked, what was not checked and why a privileged action needs approval.

Questions for discussion

  1. Which part of today's triage incidents and communicate with evidence exercise was read-only, and how do you know?
  2. What does a successful command prove, and what would it not prove?
  3. Explain Incident to somebody who has never opened a terminal.
  4. If an expected result does not appear, what evidence would you collect before changing anything?
  5. How would you explain this issue to a colleague without exposing private data?

Connection to Umicom Framework and software engineering

Use the Framework's structured logging, diagnostic correlation and audit boundaries when producing real incident evidence. Do not grant AI agents, learning labs or thin applications unrestricted repair authority. The C23 maintenance-review lab deliberately records staged decisions and cannot change a host.

Further reading (optional internet access)

  • https://learn.microsoft.com/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.diagnostics/get-winevent
  • https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/journalctl.html

Stage 4 · Managed services and recovery · Chapter 60

Chapter 60 — Capstone: plan, review and recover a fictional Umicom Notes change

System Administration From Zero · Stage 4 — Managed Services and Recovery
Author: Sammy Hegab · Umicom Foundation
Study time: 95–120 minutes
Before starting: Chapters 37–59 and the Update 40 service-readiness demonstration
Safety level: observation-only on real systems; any practice writes are confined to a folder owned by the learner.

What you will achieve

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to explain capstone: plan, review and recover a fictional umicom notes change, identify the difference between an observation and a change, and interpret at least one Windows and one Linux administration result. You will also be able to describe the evidence that an authorised Umicom support engineer would need before taking action.

Why this matters in everyday computing

You have learned to locate an operating system, read service status, inspect permissions and network listeners, verify backups and communicate an incident. The final Stage 4 assignment joins those skills into one coherent example rather than twelve isolated commands. The situation is deliberately fictional, but the reasoning mirrors professional administration.

Your team proposes a routine Umicom Notes upgrade. Before beginning, it must confirm an authorised reviewer, backup evidence, a documented recovery route and a baseline in which Notes and storage are ready. After the simulated change, storage checks fail. The safe response is to mark the change for rollback, record an independent restored observation and leave the incident distinct from a successfully completed upgrade. No actual application, service or repository will be modified.

A mental model you can remember

Imagine a pilot checklist: before departure, confirm the aircraft and route; during flight, observe instruments; if a required safety signal fails, follow the approved contingency rather than pretending the original plan succeeded. For an administrator, each stage has its own evidence: before-change readiness, authorisation, change execution, after-change checks and, if required, restoration checks. A final green label is not credible if intermediate failures were erased.

New words, without jargon

Term Meaning
Change record A specific, reviewable description of the proposed work and its identity.
Baseline capture A numbered observation of requirements before a change.
Maker/checker A model in which one person proposes work and a different authorised person reviews it.
Verification gate A condition that must pass before a workflow can move on.
Rollback required A state indicating that failed verification needs approved recovery.
Restored A state where independently collected evidence shows a recovery condition, not a claim the upgrade succeeded.

Windows practical lesson — PowerShell 7

Open Windows Terminal → PowerShell, or search for PowerShell 7. Type only the commands inside each box; the example PS C:\...> prompt is not part of a command. Unless a step explicitly says otherwise, use your normal non-administrator account. The commands are interactive teaching instructions, not a .ps1 script.

Step 1 — Open the learning repository

Set-Location "C:\umicom\Umicom-Bits2Banking"

Expected result: The current folder becomes the learning repository if it was cloned there.

What it means: If your own repository has a different location, use it. No Git checkout or pull is required for this capstone.

If it looks different: Stop if the folder does not exist; do not create an empty imitation of the repository.

Step 2 — Check Git state without changing it

git status --short

Expected result: No output indicates the working tree is clean; otherwise edited paths are listed.

What it means: This is a source-control observation, not an application health check.

If it looks different: Do not stage, reset or clean files simply to make the output empty.

Step 3 — Prepare the C23 laboratory

cmake -S ".\labs\native\maintenance-review" -B ".\output\learning-build\maintenance-review" -G Ninja -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER="C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin\gcc.exe" -DBUILD_TESTING=ON

Expected result: CMake reports configuration and generation success if Updates 39–41 and the compiler are present.

What it means: This creates build output only; no Windows service or Git repository history is changed.

If it looks different: A missing earlier C23 laboratory must be merged rather than bypassed with placeholder code.

Step 4 — Build the executable model

cmake --build ".\output\learning-build\maintenance-review" --parallel 2

Expected result: Ninja compiles the three linked C23 teaching libraries and their test targets.

What it means: The --parallel 2 limit keeps resource use moderate for older laptops.

If it looks different: Do not continue to test if compilation fails; first read the actual error.

Step 5 — Run the verification suite

ctest --test-dir ".\output\learning-build\maintenance-review" --no-tests=error --output-on-failure

Expected result: All registered tests should pass; a failure means the batch is not accepted on that machine.

What it means: The suite includes previous evidence/readiness regression cases and the new maintenance-review cases.

If it looks different: Not Run is not the same as Passed. Preserve the output when asking for assistance.

Step 6 — Run the fictional incident demonstration

& ".\output\learning-build\maintenance-review\btb-maintenance-review-demo.exe"

Expected result: The demo reports ROLLBACK_REQUIRED, then RESTORED with distinct capture identifiers.

What it means: RESTORED is not COMPLETE: it means the simulated recovery checks passed, not that the upgrade succeeded.

If it looks different: The executable never restores files or changes a real service.

Linux practical comparison

On a Linux computer or an authorised virtual machine, open a terminal. These are Bash-compatible commands; do not type the $ prompt. A minimal container, Chromebook or non-systemd distribution may have a different set of tools. A missing optional tool should be recorded rather than bypassed.

Linux step 1 — Configure the native laboratory

cmake -S labs/native/maintenance-review -B output/learning-build/maintenance-review -G Ninja -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=gcc -DBUILD_TESTING=ON

Expected result: CMake creates a build directory when the prerequisites are present.

Interpretation: Run from the checked-out Bits2Banking root.

Linux step 2 — Build the model

cmake --build output/learning-build/maintenance-review --parallel 2

Expected result: The C23 sources are compiled.

Interpretation: No system service or package manager is involved.

Linux step 3 — Run the complete training suite

ctest --test-dir output/learning-build/maintenance-review --no-tests=error --output-on-failure

Expected result: Registered CTest cases pass or report exact failures.

Interpretation: Record the test count and compiler version as acceptance evidence.

Worked support scenario — Umicom Notes

A fictional maintenance ticket reads: ‘Upgrade Umicom Notes document storage on Friday after class’. The operator records a 40-character sample revision, a READY baseline and a verified practice backup. A different reviewer label approves the training plan. After the hypothetical change, the storage check becomes FAILURE and the Notes service is blocked through its dependency. The model refuses to mark the upgrade COMPLETE. After an independently captured passing restoration, the record becomes RESTORED. The tutor concludes that the recovery path was modelled successfully, while the upgrade remains unsuccessful and real host acceptance remains untested.

Evidence record: In your own words, describe the issue, the observation time, the command used, what you actually saw, what you have not proved, and who would approve a change. Avoid copying usernames, credentials, private filenames, IP addresses or confidential logs into public notes.

Common mistakes and how to correct them

Misunderstanding Better interpretation
Passing native tests proves production services were changed successfully. These tests cover an offline state machine, not a host upgrade or a recovered bank database.
The same person can always approve their own change. Separation of duties may be required; the classroom model uses distinct labels but does not authorise anyone.
Restored means the new version is accepted. Restored records a recovery condition after a failed update, which must stay visible.

Guided practice and suggested responses

Exercise 1. Write your complete change request.

Suggested response: Include the fictional workload, scope, source revision, backup, reviewer, before/after checks, failure condition and recovery plan.

Exercise 2. Run the native C23 test cases.

Suggested response: Explain the difference between a failed verification test and a simulation in which a failed service is correctly detected.

Exercise 3. Present a one-page support report.

Suggested response: Describe what the offline lab proves, what it cannot prove, and which steps would need real authorised Framework/OS validation later.

Questions for discussion

  1. Which part of today's capstone: plan, review and recover a fictional umicom notes change exercise was read-only, and how do you know?
  2. What does a successful command prove, and what would it not prove?
  3. Explain Change record to somebody who has never opened a terminal.
  4. If an expected result does not appear, what evidence would you collect before changing anything?
  5. How would you explain this issue to a colleague without exposing private data?

Connection to Umicom Framework and software engineering

The standalone educational C23 code must not become a parallel production change manager. Umicom Framework already owns module supervision, service configuration, security, audit and delivery contracts. The programme teaches the decision model through copied readiness evidence, preserves earlier source and leaves the actual Framework, Applications, Kernel and OS repositories untouched.

Further reading (optional internet access)

  • https://learn.microsoft.com/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/sc
  • https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemctl.html

Learning checkpoint

You are ready to proceed if you can explain the command, its expected output, the boundary of what it proves, and a safe response to unexpected output. If the exercise needed unavailable administrator access, record not performed; do not mark it as passed.

Next: Use the Stage 4 workbook and the accompanying C23 maintenance-review laboratory before progressing to professional platform administration.

Reference · Stage 3

System Administration: From Zero — Stage 3, Practical Infrastructure

Bits to Banking · Umicom Foundation · Major Update 40

This is the third stage of a single 48-chapter course, not a competing new course. Chapters 1–24 (Getting Started) and 25–36 (Intermediate Foundations) remain unchanged. This stage helps learners investigate everyday operating-system situations carefully before making changes. It is suitable for first-time learners, adults returning to computing and supervised younger students.

Choose your starting point

  • Never used a terminal? Begin at Chapter 1 and follow the beginner course index.
  • Can read basic PowerShell and create your own files? Review Chapter 24, then Chapters 25–36.
  • Comfortable with user accounts, logs, backups and DNS? Continue with Chapter 37 below.
  • Teaching a class? Read Stage 3 Instructor Guide before running practical exercises.

Stage 3 — Complete lesson sequence

  • 37. Plan a safe home administration laboratory — 55–75 minutes
  • 38. Capture an operating-system baseline and recognise drift — 50–70 minutes
  • 39. Understand accounts, groups and scheduled work — 60–80 minutes
  • 40. Understand disks, volumes, filesystems and free space — 55–80 minutes
  • 41. Make and verify a recoverable practice backup — 65–90 minutes
  • 42. Read access-control rules without changing them — 55–75 minutes
  • 43. Follow one network request from a name to a port — 65–85 minutes
  • 44. Understand firewalls and listening services without changing rules — 60–80 minutes
  • 45. Recognise service health versus process state — 65–85 minutes
  • 46. Plan software updates with approval, testing and rollback — 60–85 minutes
  • 47. Build an incident timeline from logs and metrics — 70–95 minutes
  • 48. Capstone: support and verify a fictional Umicom service — 90–140 minutes

How to study

Each lesson explains what the idea means, why administrators need it, a Windows PowerShell 7 sequence, a Linux terminal sequence, expected results, common errors, a fictional Umicom scenario, exercises and suggested answers. Terminal commands are executed interactively; no PowerShell or Python implementation scripts are introduced.

The deliberate rule is read first, change only in your own practice directory, and document the result. The course does not ask students to restart services, lower firewall security, modify other people's permissions, force-push Git history or apply system-wide updates.

Connected resources

  • Stage 3 practical workbook
  • Stage 3 glossary
  • Safe administration command reference
  • Native C23 service-readiness laboratory (reference for repository browsing; the site navigation can link the lab index separately).
  • Existing Umicom contributor guides

Reference · Stage 3

Stage 3 Practical Workbook — Read, Check, Explain

System Administration: From Zero · Chapters 37–48

Print this workbook or copy its questions into a practice notebook. Use fictional data whenever a device or organisation policy prevents access. Record real results rather than the example values.

Exercise A — Baseline (Chapters 37–38)

  1. Write your chosen practice-folder path and why it is safe.
  2. Record OS family, PowerShell/Bash environment, architecture and a timezone-aware observation time.
  3. Explain what an unavailable tool means. Can you conclude it is not installed from an unsuccessful command alone?

Evidence: one table of item / command / observed result / time / limitation.

Exercise B — Ownership and files (Chapters 39–42)

  1. Sketch identity → group → resource permission → permitted action.
  2. Draw disk → partition/volume → mount point → practice folder.
  3. Complete the practice Notes backup from Chapter 41: show source, backup and restored file paths and their SHA-256 values.
  4. Explain two reasons why access can be denied without a software defect.

Evidence: a safe storage map and a verified, non-overwriting restore.

Exercise C — Connections and security (Chapters 43–44)

  1. Trace domain name → DNS → address → TCP port → HTTP application response.
  2. What could cause a TCP connection to fail after DNS succeeds?
  3. Why is a loopback-only server preferable for a first local C23 lesson?
  4. Which observation would you collect before considering a firewall-rule change?

Evidence: one diagram and two hypotheses with distinct checks.

Exercise D — Service and updates (Chapters 45–46)

  1. Define liveness, readiness and degraded operation in your own words.
  2. Complete a fictitious maintenance proposal for a compiler upgrade: owner, old/new version, approval, baseline, tests and rollback.
  3. Explain why process Running and test PASS are different claims.

Evidence: one five-field service health checklist and one maintenance record.

Exercise E — Incident capstone (Chapters 47–48)

Fictional evidence: Notes process runs; storage check FAIL; yesterday's backup PASS; current save/read NOT RUN; DNS optional WARNING.

  1. List what is known and what is uncertain.
  2. Decide READY, REVIEW or BLOCKED and justify it.
  3. Explain which check to perform next and whose approval would be needed for a restore.
  4. Use the Update 40 C23 service-readiness demonstration to connect a blocked storage prerequisite to an application result. Do not mistake the fictional test for a real service probe.

Suggested answers

A. Missing access might mean disabled command, missing module, wrong PATH or denied permission; record the exact message rather than claiming absence.
B. Backup is not proven until hashes and a separate restore are checked.
C. DNS success does not establish listener/TCP/TLS/application health.
D. A running process can have failed dependencies or incorrect output.
E. BLOCKED: a required dependency failed, a current business-operation test was not run, and yesterday's backup is not current readiness evidence.

Marking rubric

Criterion Beginning Developing Ready for next stage
Safety Cannot identify boundary Knows to ask permission Keeps work scoped and never bypasses controls
Evidence Copies expected result Records some actual results Records actual results/time/limitations
Commands Runs without explaining Can describe basic purpose Chooses the least risky relevant command
Recovery Assumes copy is enough Verifies backup hash Restores to a separate location and verifies
Incident judgement Guesses a cause Separates some observations States facts, hypotheses, missing checks and plan

There is no required administrator access, live cloud account or production server in this workbook.

Reference · Stage 3

Stage 3 — Practical Infrastructure Glossary

Use alongside Chapters 37–48. These definitions are short enough for a first reading; the lessons give examples and important exceptions.

Term Explanation Example
Host Physical computer that runs a VM. A Windows laptop running a Linux guest.
Guest An OS inside a VM. A training Linux desktop.
Baseline Recorded system state before a change. Windows version, Git version and date.
Drift A relevant change compared with a baseline. A compiler selected from a new PATH entry.
Security principal Account or identity to which rights apply. A named user or service account.
Scheduled task Declarative job with trigger, identity and action. A daily approved report.
Volume Logical storage unit, possibly mounted as C: or /home. A project build volume.
Restore test A checked recovery using backup data. Copying an archived note to a separate folder.
ACL Ordered or platform-defined set of access rules. Read permission on a practice folder.
DNS Service mapping names to records. Resolving example.org.
TCP port Endpoint within a transport connection. Loopback port 8765 for a local lesson.
Firewall Policy controlling network traffic. Allowing selected inbound connections.
Liveness Narrow indication a process is responsive. A process still running.
Readiness Evidence a service can perform assigned work. A successful authorised Notes read.
Dependency Another component required to succeed. Notes service needs document storage.
Maintenance window Agreed time to perform a controlled change. A scheduled toolchain upgrade.
Incident timeline Ordered observations about a problem. Service error before a failed read request.
Correlation ID Identifier connecting records for one action. An operation ID shared across request and log.
Failure-atomic Invalid operation preserves prior state/output. Rejected service check does not replace report.
NOT RUN A required check was not performed. Build test not executed on Windows.
BLOCKED Required evidence is missing, stale or adverse. Storage unreadable for Notes.
REVIEW Required checks pass but a nonessential issue needs review. An optional metric is unavailable.
READY All declared checks passed in the specific model and capture. Fictional C23 readiness snapshot, not production certification.

A green training result does not grant real administrative permissions or prove production readiness. That decision belongs to the actual service owner and operational policy.

Reference · Stage 3

Stage 3 Instructor Guide — Practical Infrastructure

Audience: volunteer tutors, school technology clubs, adult learning groups and Umicom contributor mentors. Recommended approach: discussion first, safe command second, evidence and reflection last.

Safe teaching environment

  1. Use a normal, non-elevated Windows PowerShell 7 shell or an authorised Linux account. If access to a command is restricted, teach the meaning of that refusal.
  2. Do not request student accounts, passwords, personal machine serial numbers, full IP configurations, domain names or raw system logs in a shared classroom channel.
  3. Practice files belong under $HOME\UmicomLearning on Windows or $HOME/UmicomLearning on Linux. Do not enter corporate, financial, school administration or healthcare data.
  4. Screenshots should show only relevant fields. Redact usernames, hostname and network information before sharing outside the device.
  5. A supervised younger learner may inspect a shared device only with its owner's explicit permission. No system settings should be changed in this course.

Two-route delivery

Beginner route: Chapters 37–42, 45, 48. Use lab folders, Windows baseline, copy/hash/restore and discussion of services. Use teacher-supplied printed outputs for commands unavailable on a managed machine.

Expanded route: Chapters 37–48. Add Linux comparative exercises, IP/DNS/port explanation, firewall observation, update planning and incident timeline analysis.

Assessment: learner demonstrates sound judgement

The objective is not memorisation. A satisfactory learner can explain what a command reads, show one verified observation, distinguish missing evidence from a pass, preserve a sample file, and ask for approval before making a system change. Encourage short notes with command → observation → interpretation → uncertainty.

A staged 90-minute workshop

Time Activity Evidence
0–10 min Identify shell and working directory A redacted shell/location note
10–25 min Baseline operating system and storage Three factual fields + timestamp
25–45 min Complete practice-file copy/hash/restore Equal hashes and separate destination
45–60 min Distinguish process status and service readiness A drawn dependency chain
60–80 min Work fictional Notes outage capstone Timeline + READY/REVIEW/BLOCKED explanation
80–90 min Peer review and next step One supported conclusion and one remaining question

Answer integrity

A learner who writes “NOT RUN — Windows cmdlet unavailable here” has met the reporting requirement when they explain why. Do not award invented green checks. Exercises are not operational authorisations and do not qualify actual Umicom production systems.

Guide provenance

This stage reuses the established Bits2Banking curriculum and points to the existing Creating a New Umicom Application beginner guide delivered with Update 38. That original document should remain unchanged; its planned automatic-discovery design must not be presented as implemented code.

Reference · Stage 3

Safe Windows PowerShell and Linux Administration — Quick Reference

This sheet summarises interactive commands. No .ps1 or .py files are delivered. Do not type PS C:\> or $ prompts displayed in examples. Commands marked practice write act only on folders owned by the learner.

Question Windows PowerShell 7 Linux terminal Note
Where am I? Get-Location or pwd pwd Reads working directory
What shell? $PSVersionTable.PSVersion echo $SHELL These identify different things
What OS? Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object WindowsProductName, OsVersion, OsArchitecture cat /etc/os-release Choose only needed fields
What CPU? Get-CimInstance Win32_Processor | Select-Object Name, NumberOfCores lscpu Availability varies
Disk capacity? Get-PSDrive -PSProvider FileSystem df -h . Check the volume containing your project
Who am I? whoami id Avoid sharing full account info
File ACL? Get-Acl -LiteralPath $HOME ls -ld "$HOME" Observe; do not grant rights
Services? Get-Service | Select-Object -First 10 Name, Status systemctl --user list-units --type=service --all Stopped need not be broken
Recent log? Get-WinEvent -LogName Application -MaxEvents 6 journalctl --user -n 6 --no-pager Redact messages
Name lookup? Resolve-DnsName example.org getent ahosts example.org Optional internet connection
TCP port? Test-NetConnection 127.0.0.1 -Port 8765 ss -lnt No service: refusal may be expected
Firewall summary? Get-NetFirewallProfile command -v nft Never disable rules for a class exercise
Package versions? winget --version cat /etc/os-release These describe different systems
Available updates? winget upgrade apt list --upgradable List only; do not install
File digest? Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 -LiteralPath PATH sha256sum PATH Use real paths you own
Git working tree? git status --short git status --short Reads local changes only
Native test report? ctest --test-dir BUILD --output-on-failure Same command Does not prove all suites were run

Before any real change

Verify: permission → target → expected behaviour → backup/rollback → approval → actual acceptance test. If any required condition is unknown, stop and ask the owner. The default purpose of this course is inspection, not system modification.

Bits to Banking · Umicom Foundation · Chapters 49–60 · UK English

Stage 4 builds on the 48 previously published chapters. You do not need to be an expert to follow it: start with the service and identity concepts, then build confidence with scheduling, configuration and administration evidence, and finish with a C23 simulation that cannot change a real computer.

Study route

Recommended learning method

  1. Read the new words and mental model before entering any command.
  2. Keep the command line and result visible together. Do not type a PS C:\> or $ prompt.
  3. State whether the command observes, writes inside your practice folder, or would require administrator approval.
  4. Record what happened on your machine, including unexpected results and commands that could not be run.
  5. Complete the exercises and explain one situation in which the command would not be sufficient proof.
  6. Use the Stage 4 workbook and the C23 maintenance-review laboratory as your practical assessment.

Safety and source rules

Windows examples are interactive PowerShell 7 commands; Linux examples use a terminal. No PowerShell or Python implementation scripts are introduced. Do not change production accounts, scheduled tasks, firewall rules, systemd units, package versions or real repositories merely to reproduce a classroom screenshot. Reusable software capability belongs in Umicom Framework and is not duplicated here.

Source and prerequisite evidence

The previous course chapters and the originally supplied new-project beginner guide are retained in earlier updates. This batch adds files only. The maintenance-review lab links Update 40, which links Update 39, so a valid checkout must include both prerequisites.
