Audience: older children with an adult mentor, adult beginners, returning professionals and Umicom contributors. Equipment: non-administrator PowerShell 7 or an authorised Linux terminal, ordinary practice files and (for the capstone) a checked-out Bits2Banking repository with Updates 39–41.

Observation log template

Field Student note
Time and timezone
Host category (do not publish host identifier) Windows / Linux / training VM
Command / tool
Expected result
Actual result
What it proves
What it does not prove
Was the step read-only?
Next authorised owner

Exercises by chapter

For each exercise, run no more than the read-only steps supplied in the chapter and keep a short note of the result. Written explanations are acceptable when the OS/tool is not available.

| Chapter | Exercise | What earns credit | |---|---| | 49 | Describe two dependencies for Notes. | For instance, a writable practice folder and a correctly loaded document index. | | 50 | Compare two identities. | Explain why the service's StartName may differ from whoami. | | 51 | Explain two dependency types. | Contrast ordering and a required relationship without changing either. | | 52 | Write a hypothetical task contract. | Include purpose, owner, trigger, input, output, success signal and retry policy. | | 53 | Draw a configuration precedence diagram. | Use compiled defaults, approved application settings and an explicit per-run override, noting which source wins. | | 54 | Prepare a two-column version baseline. | List each installed tool and its purpose; do not change versions as part of the exercise. | | 55 | Design a three-metric baseline. | Include measure, unit, time, expected range and reason it matters. | | 56 | Classify three bind addresses. | Contrast 127.0.0.1, ::1 and 0.0.0.0. | | 57 | Choose an RPO and RTO for a fictional school portal. | Explain separately how much data loss and downtime are acceptable. | | 58 | Draw a rollback dependency table. | Include executable, configuration, database, compatibility and verification owners. | | 59 | Create an incident record template. | Include unique reference, start time, affected function, observed evidence, actions, owner and next update. | | 60 | Write your complete change request. | Include the fictional workload, scope, source revision, backup, reviewer, before/after checks, failure condition and recovery plan. |

Applied exercise A — Why the report did not arrive

A scheduled fictional Notes report was expected at 17:00 but is missing. The machine was offline earlier. Explain the difference between scheduler configuration, attempt evidence and business output; note which commands from Chapters 52, 55 and 59 would be safe. Prepare a short incident note with a confidence label on every hypothesis. No real scheduled job should be run.

Suggested answer: Read the timetable and last-run evidence, compare with the host availability timeline, check whether the expected report artefact exists in an authorised training directory, then escalate to the job owner. A configured trigger proves neither an attempt nor successful report production.

Applied exercise B — Restore a fictional note into a separate folder

Use Chapters 57 and 58 to write a private practice note, copy it, verify SHA-256, restore the copy to another private folder, compare the digests and read the restored content. No production backup, school data or bank account is used.

Suggested answer: Both selected files should have identical byte hashes and the restored text should match the expected sentence. Record that one disk containing multiple copies does not satisfy a disaster-recovery policy.

Applied exercise C — C23 change-window simulation

Read the three public headers in sysadmin-evidence, service-readiness and maintenance-review. Build the new C23 target, run the full CTest suite and the standalone demonstration. Record the exact number passed, compiler version and output showing ROLLBACK_REQUIRED followed by RESTORED. Explain why neither the demo nor the tests prove that an actual OS service was changed.

Suggested answer: The three libraries share ownership through linked C23 contracts. The planned change cannot finish after blocked post-change evidence. A distinct restored observation changes the educational state, not the host. Real approval, backups, runtime metrics and independent test evidence would be needed before production release.

Assessment rubric (100 points)

Area Points
Correctly explains terminology without guessing 20
Commands used within authorised, safe scope 20
Writes accurate expected versus actual observations 20
Distinguishes scope, hypothesis and proof 20
Explains recovery and Framework ownership 20

Pass guidance: 70+ points, with no unauthorised system modification. A student who declines an unsafe step and explains why should receive credit for good judgement rather than be marked down.

Reference · Stage 4

Stage 4 Glossary — Managed Services and Recovery

Definitions are written for beginners; terms may have additional meanings in particular products. Always consult the installed system documentation for platform-specific behaviour.

Term Plain-English meaning
Access denied The operating system refusing an operation under the current effective permissions.
ACL Access-control list: rules describing who may perform operations on an object.
After= An ordering relation: start this unit after another when both are scheduled.
Alert A signal that an agreed threshold or check warrants attention.
Baseline Measurements representing known, ordinary behaviour under stated conditions.
Baseline capture A numbered observation of requirements before a change.
Bind address The address on which a service accepts incoming connections.
Change record A specific, reviewable description of the proposed work and its identity.
Compatibility matrix A record of supported combinations of tools, runtimes and versions.
Configuration Settings that influence a programme without changing its compiled code.
cron Traditional Unix-like time-based job scheduler.
Cutover The controlled step that directs users or traffic to a newly prepared environment.
Dependency Another service or resource that must be available first.
Environment variable A named value a process may inherit when it starts.
Escalation Passing responsibility to an authorised specialist or decision owner.
Exit code A number returned by a programme to indicate its completion status.
Exposure Which other computers or users may reach a service, subject to routing and policy.
False positive An alert that fires even though the relevant system is operating acceptably.
Firewall profile A collection of traffic-control rules for a network context.
Hypothesis A proposed explanation that has not yet been verified.
Immutable backup A backup protected from unauthorised modification or deletion under a defined policy.
Incident An unplanned interruption or reduction in expected service quality.
Integrity hash A digest that helps compare file bytes when produced and trusted appropriately.
Least privilege Give each service only the rights required for its declared duties.
Listening socket A network endpoint waiting for connections.
LocalSystem A highly privileged built-in Windows service identity; not a normal user account.
Loopback Traffic addressed to the same host, commonly 127.0.0.1 or ::1.
Maintenance window A planned period during which authorised changes may occur.
Maker/checker A model in which one person proposes work and a different authorised person reviews it.
Metric A numerical measurement such as available memory, disk space or process CPU time.
Migration A controlled transformation of stored data or schema.
Missed run A scheduled occurrence that was not executed, for example while the computer was off.
Package manager A programme that locates, installs and updates software packages.
Precedence The documented rule deciding which configuration source overrides another.
Process scope Settings visible to a running process and, commonly, children it launches.
Read-only inspection A command that reports status without requesting a configuration change.
Readiness probe A functional test that decides whether the service can do its intended work.
Ready A service has passed the checks required for its intended work, not merely started.
Reconciliation Checking that recovered data agrees with authoritative expected records.
Recovery point objective (RPO) The maximum acceptable amount of data loss measured backward in time.
Recovery time objective (RTO) The targeted time to restore an acceptable service.
Requires= A stronger unit dependency with failure implications; details depend on the transaction.
Restart= A policy controlling whether systemd retries a terminated service.
Restore Bring back data from a protected copy into a chosen location.
Restore drill A planned test that recovers data and checks it can be used.
Restore point A specific recoverable copy identified by date, version or immutable manifest.
Restored A state where independently collected evidence shows a recovery condition, not a claim the upgrade succeeded.
Retention How long a backup remains available before approved expiry.
Rollback Return a changed system to an approved previous state.
Rollback plan The documented steps to return to a verified previous state after a failed change.
Rollback required A state indicating that failed verification needs approved recovery.
Scheduled task A Windows definition for a command launched under specified conditions.
Scope The users, components, locations and operations actually affected.
Secret Sensitive information such as a password, token or private key.
Secret reference An identifier that lets an authorised provider retrieve a secret without storing it in ordinary configuration.
Service A programme managed by the operating system and often started automatically.
Service account An account assigned to a programme for controlled access to resources.
Service identity The operating-system account or security principal a service runs as.
Service manager The system component that starts, tracks and stops services.
Smoke test A small, focused check that essential functions still work after a change.
Symptom What users or monitoring systems observe when something is wrong.
systemd timer A unit that triggers another systemd unit on a time or event schedule.
Threshold A value at which a measurement triggers review.
Timeline Time-ordered observations and actions with source, clock and outcome.
Trigger An event or timetable that requests a job start.
Unit The name used by systemd for a managed service, timer or other object.
Unit file Configuration describing a systemd service or another managed object.
Verification gate A condition that must pass before a workflow can move on.
Wants= A weaker relationship that requests another unit without the same failure coupling.
Wildcard address An address such as 0.0.0.0 that accepts connections for multiple IPv4 interfaces.

Five distinctions to remember

  • Started is not necessarily ready.
  • Scheduled is not necessarily completed.
  • A copied file is not necessarily a recoverable backup.
  • A reviewer label in a training model is not production approval.
  • RESTORED after a failed upgrade is not COMPLETE.

Reference · Stage 4

Stage 4 Instructor Guide — Managed Services and Recovery

Umicom Foundation · Bits to Banking · Chapters 49–60

Audience and teaching standard

This stage is suitable for a school technology club, adult beginners, a community workshop or a technical refresher group. Explanations are professional but assume no prior administration vocabulary. Define each term before using it and demonstrate a command in a normal user shell before discussing privileges or exceptions.

Four 90-minute teaching sessions

Session Chapters Shared practical activity Evidence to retain
1 — What starts and who owns it? 49–52 Read service states, identities, unit files and scheduled tasks Distinguish service name, owner, scheduler and readiness
2 — What configuration is effective? 53–54 Use one harmless temporary variable; record installed tool versions Explain scope, precedence and a reviewed maintenance plan
3 — Is the service healthy and recoverable? 55–58 Observe metrics/listeners; restore a practice note to a separate directory Separate observation, network exposure and recovery verification
4 — How should we respond to change failure? 59–60 Incident timeline and C23 maintenance simulation Full CTest transcript, fictional recovery outcome and escalation note

Allow additional time for keyboard practice. Students should not be penalised for slow typing. Encourage them to repeat the meaning of a command before pressing Enter.

Safety requirements

Use a non-elevated Windows PowerShell 7 session or an authorised Linux account. A young learner should use a supervised device and practise only inside an explicitly named private directory. Do not use production service accounts, customer records, bank data, patient data, live trading environments, package upgrades, firewall changes or system-wide scheduled tasks for demonstrations. For Linux-only systemd activities, a tutor may show a recorded walkthrough where a student's machine lacks systemd.

The two practice-write exercises are explicitly confined to the student's own UmicomLearning folders. Check destination filenames before creating or copying text. Do not use wildcards, force overwrites or deletion as teaching shortcuts.

Explain failed commands correctly

A missing systemctl in a container, a restricted Windows Event Log query or no task returned by crontab -l is not evidence that the student has failed. Teach how to identify environmental prerequisites and record not performed, not available, restricted, passed and failed separately.

Guide the C23 lab

The new maintenance-review project composes the unchanged Update 40 service-readiness library, which composes unchanged Update 39 sysadmin-evidence. Compile it with CMake + Ninja and require an actual CTest report. Discuss the difference between a test passing when it rejects bad input and a real service failing verification. Show the demo's ROLLBACK_REQUIRED and RESTORED outputs; explain why the second does not mean the upgrade succeeded.

Sample mentoring questions

Ask learners to explain why 0.0.0.0 is a bind wildcard rather than a secure destination; why a scheduled report is not proof of execution; why a service account should have fewer rights than a local administrator; why a copied file is not a tested backup; and what evidence a real Umicom OS operator would need before updating a Framework gitlink.

Source and publication standards

Preserve the original guide and all earlier chapters. New C23 teaching source must not become a duplicate of Umicom Framework's security, VCS, service or deployment implementation. PowerShell is for interactive commands only; no new .ps1 or .py implementation files. Peer-review the standalone HTML course, Markdown and MkDocs navigation before publication. The Windows build and the hosted site require independent verification.

Reference · Stage 4

Stage 4 — Safe command reference

Commands below are typed interactively in PowerShell 7 or a Linux terminal. No .ps1 or .py scripts are delivered. Commands that write are confined to learner-owned practice folders. Read the relevant chapter first; this sheet is a reminder, not a substitute for understanding.

Purpose Windows PowerShell 7 Linux terminal Important limitation
Where am I? Get-Location pwd Directory, not service state
Current time Get-Date -Format o date --iso-8601=seconds Note timezone
Check a known service Get-Service -Name EventLog systemctl status systemd-journald.service --no-pager Process status does not prove application readiness
Service configured identity Get-CimInstance Win32_Service -Filter "Name='EventLog'" systemctl show systemd-journald.service -p User -p Group Identity is not permission proof
List scheduled work Get-ScheduledTask \| Select-Object -First 8 TaskName,State systemctl list-timers --all --no-pager A trigger is not completed work
Inspect available drives Get-PSDrive -PSProvider FileSystem df -h . Check the actual data volume
Check tool version cmake --version cmake --version Versions do not prove compatibility
List listeners Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen ss -ltn Bind scope is not full security posture
Firewall profile (read) Get-NetFirewallProfile \| Select-Object Name,Enabled command -v ufw \|\| command -v firewall-cmd Do not disable/change firewall rules
Check Git without mutation git status --short git status --short Run inside actual repository
Hash a practice file Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 -LiteralPath .\notes.txt sha256sum ./notes.txt Hash equality is not database recovery
Validate C23 learning lab ctest --test-dir .\output\learning-build\maintenance-review --no-tests=error --output-on-failure ctest --test-dir output/learning-build/maintenance-review --no-tests=error --output-on-failure Only tests already configured and built

Never use git reset --hard, git clean -fd, an unreviewed force push, Stop-Service, systemctl stop, firewall disabling or system-wide package upgrades as a short-cut to make an introductory exercise pass. Record unexpected results and ask the system owner before making changes.

Stage 5 · Virtual machines and deployment · Chapter 61

Chapter 61 — Understand virtual machines, hosts and guests

Bits to Banking · System Administration From Zero · Stage 5 · Umicom Foundation
Audience: First-time computer users, older learners, new contributors and returning professionals.
Practical mode: Read-only observation by default; any exercise that writes uses a clearly identified private training directory.
Implementation policy: New Umicom executable functionality uses C23 or Assembly. PowerShell and Linux terminal commands here are interactive instructions, not implementation scripts.

The problem we are solving

How can a beginner practise operating-system administration without risking the computer they use every day?

A virtual machine (VM) is a simulated computer with its own operating system, virtual disk and network devices. The actual computer is called the host. The virtual computer is the guest. A hypervisor or emulator provides the guest's virtual hardware. An application running in the guest normally cannot change the host's ordinary files unless you deliberately share storage or grant other access. This is useful for learning, but it is not an absolute security boundary.

A VM is not the same as a folder, a Git repository or a shell window. A folder stores data; a repository tracks versions; a shell runs commands in the current operating system. A VM runs another operating system instance. A container, by contrast, normally shares its host's operating-system kernel. We introduce containers only after learners can explain the host–guest boundary.

Imagine teaching a new Umicom contributor how to install Linux. Doing that on the family computer's real disk would risk existing files. In a VM, the learner can inspect a simulated disk and return to a known snapshot. This is why the course uses isolated, disposable guests for administration experiments.

Words you need before you continue

  • Host — Your real computer and its operating system.
  • Guest — A separate system running in virtual hardware.
  • Hypervisor — Software that creates or supervises virtual machines.
  • Snapshot — A recorded VM state that may support returning to an earlier point; not a backup of the host.

Worked Umicom example

An Umicom Kernel learner needs to understand boot output. They can run a separately prepared RISC-V teaching image in QEMU, read serial output and stop the guest, while retaining the Windows or Linux host intact. They must distinguish a QEMU process starting successfully from proof that the Umicom kernel actually booted and reached its expected state.

Before touching your computer

Read each command all the way through. Check the directory or filename first. A command is something you type in the terminal; the command output is the evidence you interpret. If a step requires a file or application that is not installed, record not available and continue with the conceptual part. Do not invent a result and do not try a more powerful command merely to make the exercise appear to pass.

Safety boundary: For the first exercise do not create a virtual disk or launch an installer. A snapshot may not protect a host folder shared into the guest. Never point a VM disk command at a physical drive containing personal files.

Windows — PowerShell 7, step by step

Start Windows Terminal and select PowerShell, or use PowerShell 7 directly. Confirm with $PSVersionTable.PSVersion. The prompt ending in > is where you enter the command; do not type the prompt itself. Commands are shown exactly, except for placeholders such as YOUR_APPROVED_LINUX.iso, which must be replaced with a real filename before execution.

1. See your machine architecture

Get-CimInstance Win32_ComputerSystem | Select-Object Manufacturer, Model, HypervisorPresent
Get-CimInstance Win32_Processor | Select-Object Name, NumberOfCores, NumberOfLogicalProcessors

Expected result and interpretation: The manufacturer, model and logical processor count are displayed. HypervisorPresent may be false on an otherwise virtualisation-capable PC.

2. Check whether QEMU is already installed

Get-Command qemu-system-x86_64, qemu-system-riscv64 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object Name, Source

Expected result and interpretation: A missing command produces no listing. Do not assume QEMU is installed simply because Windows supports virtualisation.

Linux — terminal, step by step

Open the distribution's Terminal application. The examples assume an ordinary, non-root account. Linux paths use / and case-sensitive names on most filesystems; a Windows path beginning C:\ must not be pasted unchanged into Linux commands.

1. Identify the host and potential hypervisor

uname -s
uname -m
lscpu

Expected result and interpretation: Look for the architecture and, when supported, virtualisation information. Some commands might be unavailable in a minimal guest.

2. Check QEMU without starting a guest

command -v qemu-system-x86_64
command -v qemu-system-riscv64

Expected result and interpretation: A printed path means the executable is discoverable. No VM starts.

Guided practice laboratory

  1. Draw two boxes labelled Host and Guest. Put PowerShell or Terminal in the host box and a hypothetical Linux service in the guest box.
  2. Run the read-only hardware commands; write down your CPU architecture without publishing personal computer identifiers.
  3. Explain in your own words why a guest snapshot and an ordinary file backup solve different problems.
  4. Describe one boundary that would be weakened by mapping the host Documents folder into an untrusted guest.

Keep evidence: Note the date, selected environment, commands entered, expected outcomes and actual outcomes. Omit passwords, tokens, private patient/customer details and unnecessary machine identifiers. A missing or failed step belongs in your report; it is not a reason to hide the error.

Common problems and how to investigate

Symptom Safe investigation
HypervisorPresent is False This does not by itself prove the processor lacks virtualisation support. Consult hardware specifications and firmware settings before changing anything.
QEMU command is not recognised The tool is not installed or its directory is not on PATH. Continue with theory and postpone VM creation.

Never substitute git reset --hard, git clean -fd, broad permission changes, service shutdown or force-push for diagnosis. Those operations can discard unrelated work.

Review questions with suggested answers

  1. What is the host?

    Answer: The physical machine and operating system that run the virtualisation software.

  2. Does a snapshot replace backups?

    Answer: No. Snapshots are tied to the VM environment and may not protect other storage or survive host failure.

  3. Can a guest access host folders?

    Answer: Sometimes, if sharing was explicitly configured; do not assume isolation of shared data.

How this fits into Umicom

We keep the responsibilities clear. Umicom Kernel owns privileged boot and hardware behaviour. Umicom OS composes the operating-system environment. Umicom Framework owns reusable C23/Assembly services, build, VCS, security and application lifecycle contracts. Bits2Banking owns the teaching material and isolated laboratories. A lesson should not be mistaken for proof that a production system is ready.

Stage 5 · Virtual machines and deployment · Chapter 62

Chapter 62 — Prepare a disposable virtual-machine laboratory

Bits to Banking · System Administration From Zero · Stage 5 · Umicom Foundation
Audience: First-time computer users, older learners, new contributors and returning professionals.
Practical mode: Read-only observation by default; any exercise that writes uses a clearly identified private training directory.
Implementation policy: New Umicom executable functionality uses C23 or Assembly. PowerShell and Linux terminal commands here are interactive instructions, not implementation scripts.

The problem we are solving

What should be checked before downloading an operating-system image or making a virtual disk?

A safe VM laboratory begins with a plan, not an installation command. Choose a host folder you own, a trustworthy operating-system source, a reasonable memory budget, a virtual disk that contains no personal data, and a method of saving your progress. Keep a plain-text record of the image filename, its download source, the published checksum if one exists, the guest architecture, and when the image was acquired.

An ISO image is commonly a representation of installation media. A virtual disk image is where a guest stores its installed system and data. These are different objects. An ISO is often read-only in normal use. A guest disk is mutable and should be a separate file created for practice. A checksum can detect accidental corruption; comparing a hash with a checksum displayed on the same untrusted page does not, by itself, prove origin or authenticity. Prefer the distributor's official download and verification instructions.

Avoid enabling host-folder sharing, USB passthrough, clipboard integrations or bridged networking by default. Every additional connection gives the guest access to more of the real system. You can enable a specific capability after understanding and approving it.

Words you need before you continue

  • ISO image — A file containing installation-media content.
  • Virtual disk — A file the guest sees as a disk drive.
  • SHA-256 — A cryptographic digest used to compare file contents.
  • Network mode — A setting controlling how the guest connects to networks and the host.

Worked Umicom example

A trainee plans a small guest used to test a fictional Umicom Notes service. They write a one-page checklist: host architecture x86-64; approved guest OS; download hash recorded; private virtual disk; no shared folders; disposable account; snapshots and backups clearly distinguished. The checklist itself prevents accidental installation onto the family computer.

Before touching your computer

Read each command all the way through. Check the directory or filename first. A command is something you type in the terminal; the command output is the evidence you interpret. If a step requires a file or application that is not installed, record not available and continue with the conceptual part. Do not invent a result and do not try a more powerful command merely to make the exercise appear to pass.

Safety boundary: Never use a bare disk device path (/dev/sda, \.\PhysicalDrive0) in an educational exercise. Do not execute commands that partition, format or write a real disk. Ask an adult or system owner before changing firmware settings on a shared computer.

Windows — PowerShell 7, step by step

Start Windows Terminal and select PowerShell, or use PowerShell 7 directly. Confirm with $PSVersionTable.PSVersion. The prompt ending in > is where you enter the command; do not type the prompt itself. Commands are shown exactly, except for placeholders such as YOUR_APPROVED_LINUX.iso, which must be replaced with a real filename before execution.

1. Prepare a named practice location

Set-Location "$HOME"
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path "UmicomLearning" -Force | Out-Null
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path "$HOME\UmicomLearning\VMs" -Force | Out-Null
Get-ChildItem "$HOME\UmicomLearning"

Expected result and interpretation: The VMs folder exists beneath your own profile. No system directory or service was changed.

2. Check an image only if you have obtained it safely

Test-Path "$HOME\Downloads\YOUR_APPROVED_LINUX.iso"
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 -LiteralPath "$HOME\Downloads\YOUR_APPROVED_LINUX.iso"

Expected result and interpretation: Run the second command only when the first returns True and replace the placeholder with a real filename. Compare the hash against the distributor’s official value.

Linux — terminal, step by step

Open the distribution's Terminal application. The examples assume an ordinary, non-root account. Linux paths use / and case-sensitive names on most filesystems; a Windows path beginning C:\ must not be pasted unchanged into Linux commands.

1. Prepare a private workspace

mkdir -p "$HOME/UmicomLearning/VMs"
ls -ld "$HOME/UmicomLearning/VMs"

Expected result and interpretation: A private learning location exists. Check the permissions printed by ls.

2. Inspect a previously downloaded image

sha256sum "$HOME/Downloads/YOUR_APPROVED_LINUX.iso"

Expected result and interpretation: Replace the placeholder; do not run it for a nonexistent path. The digest should match the official download record.

Guided practice laboratory

  1. Create only the practice directory; do not create a disk image yet.
  2. Write a checklist with source URL, expected SHA-256, guest architecture, planned RAM, guest disk path and network mode.
  3. Identify which checklist values need checking again if the machine changes.
  4. Explain why choosing an ISO matching x86-64 does not automatically make it bootable in a RISC-V guest.

Keep evidence: Note the date, selected environment, commands entered, expected outcomes and actual outcomes. Omit passwords, tokens, private patient/customer details and unnecessary machine identifiers. A missing or failed step belongs in your report; it is not a reason to hide the error.

Common problems and how to investigate

Symptom Safe investigation
Get-FileHash: path does not exist Check Get-Location, Downloads directory and exact filename. No need to use administrator privileges.
Published hash does not match Do not boot or install the image. Check the source and redownload from an authoritative publisher.

Never substitute git reset --hard, git clean -fd, broad permission changes, service shutdown or force-push for diagnosis. Those operations can discard unrelated work.

Review questions with suggested answers

  1. What is the difference between ISO and guest disk?

    Answer: The ISO typically provides installation media; the guest disk stores the guest’s changing installation and data.

  2. Why choose a private practice directory?

    Answer: It prevents exercise files from being confused with system data and makes cleanup reviewable.

  3. Does a matching hash prove a file is trustworthy?

    Answer: It proves equality with that hash; the hash source itself must be authenticated.

How this fits into Umicom

We keep the responsibilities clear. Umicom Kernel owns privileged boot and hardware behaviour. Umicom OS composes the operating-system environment. Umicom Framework owns reusable C23/Assembly services, build, VCS, security and application lifecycle contracts. Bits2Banking owns the teaching material and isolated laboratories. A lesson should not be mistaken for proof that a production system is ready.

Next: 63 — Understand QEMU and the Umicom Kernel boot boundary.

Stage 5 · Virtual machines and deployment · Chapter 63

Chapter 63 — Understand QEMU, RISC-V and the Umicom boot boundary

Bits to Banking · System Administration From Zero · Stage 5 · Umicom Foundation
Audience: First-time computer users, older learners, new contributors and returning professionals.
Practical mode: Read-only observation by default; any exercise that writes uses a clearly identified private training directory.
Implementation policy: New Umicom executable functionality uses C23 or Assembly. PowerShell and Linux terminal commands here are interactive instructions, not implementation scripts.

The problem we are solving

Why does an emulator start even when a guest operating system cannot boot?

QEMU can emulate hardware devices and processors. The RISC-V virt machine is a standard virtual board useful for operating-system education. Its firmware or bootloader sets up the machine and transfers control to a kernel. The kernel then initialises memory, exceptions and drivers before any ordinary user-space service can run. These are separate stages with separate evidence.

For Umicom, the Linux kernel and the minimal recovery layer are distinct from the reusable application Framework. A successful C23 unit test on the host proves a specific native component test; it does not prove that the compiled kernel boots under QEMU. Likewise, QEMU displaying a window or console is not evidence that the guest filesystem or user-space application started.

Architectures are important. An x86-64 host executable does not become a RISC-V guest kernel merely because the filename ends in .elf. Build the intended target with a compatible toolchain, inspect its architecture, and boot using the exact documented profile. This lesson is read-only until the learner has the vetted boot artefacts from the Umicom Kernel project.

Words you need before you continue

  • Emulator — Software that reproduces the behaviour of a machine architecture or its devices.
  • RISC-V — An instruction-set architecture used by real and virtual processors.
  • Firmware — Early code that prepares a machine for its next boot stage.
  • Guest kernel — The privileged core that runs within the emulated or virtual machine.

Worked Umicom example

An engineer sees QEMU print a firmware banner but no Umicom prompt. This narrows the problem: the emulator and firmware ran, but the next boot phase may have failed. They capture the serial output and exact kernel SHA rather than declaring the whole OS operational. A later GTK desktop test proves a different layer.

Before touching your computer

Read each command all the way through. Check the directory or filename first. A command is something you type in the terminal; the command output is the evidence you interpret. If a step requires a file or application that is not installed, record not available and continue with the conceptual part. Do not invent a result and do not try a more powerful command merely to make the exercise appear to pass.

Safety boundary: Do not guess a -kernel path or boot flags from an unrelated tutorial. The exact Umicom Kernel QEMU runbook and output should be reviewed against the checked-out source revision. Keep guest storage and host storage separate.

Windows — PowerShell 7, step by step

Start Windows Terminal and select PowerShell, or use PowerShell 7 directly. Confirm with $PSVersionTable.PSVersion. The prompt ending in > is where you enter the command; do not type the prompt itself. Commands are shown exactly, except for placeholders such as YOUR_APPROVED_LINUX.iso, which must be replaced with a real filename before execution.

1. Check that RISC-V QEMU is installed

Get-Command qemu-system-riscv64 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
qemu-system-riscv64 --version

Expected result and interpretation: The version is printed if QEMU is installed and on PATH. If it is missing, postpone the boot exercise.

2. List supported machines without booting

qemu-system-riscv64 -machine help

Expected result and interpretation: Look for a machine named virt. This lists emulated machine types without opening a virtual disk.

Linux — terminal, step by step

Open the distribution's Terminal application. The examples assume an ordinary, non-root account. Linux paths use / and case-sensitive names on most filesystems; a Windows path beginning C:\ must not be pasted unchanged into Linux commands.

1. Check QEMU and possible machine names

command -v qemu-system-riscv64
qemu-system-riscv64 -machine help

Expected result and interpretation: The machine list may include virt, and no guest is launched.

2. Inspect an existing ELF with a trusted native tool

file ./YOUR_VERIFIED_KERNEL.elf

Expected result and interpretation: Only run when you have a verified local artefact; check that the reported target architecture matches the intended guest.

Guided practice laboratory

  1. Identify the host architecture using uname -m or PowerShell processor queries.
  2. Write the expected order: QEMU machine → firmware → kernel → recovery/user space → Framework applications.
  3. From the real Umicom Kernel documentation, note the name and output of a boot smoke test without executing unverified flags.
  4. Explain two types of evidence required before saying the guest actually booted.

Keep evidence: Note the date, selected environment, commands entered, expected outcomes and actual outcomes. Omit passwords, tokens, private patient/customer details and unnecessary machine identifiers. A missing or failed step belongs in your report; it is not a reason to hide the error.

Common problems and how to investigate

Symptom Safe investigation
QEMU shows no output This may indicate the wrong console flags, architecture, firmware, kernel or a genuine kernel problem. Inspect the target-specific runbook; do not guess.
file identifies an x86-64 executable The file is not a RISC-V guest kernel. Rebuild for the correct target rather than renaming it.

Never substitute git reset --hard, git clean -fd, broad permission changes, service shutdown or force-push for diagnosis. Those operations can discard unrelated work.

Review questions with suggested answers

  1. Does a QEMU process existing prove guest readiness?

    Answer: No. It proves only that the emulator process started.

  2. Why separate Kernel and Framework?

    Answer: A kernel owns privilege, hardware and core OS concerns; Framework supplies reusable user-space application services.

  3. What is a safe first emulator command?

    Answer: A version or machine-help command, because it starts no guest and writes no disk.

How this fits into Umicom

We keep the responsibilities clear. Umicom Kernel owns privileged boot and hardware behaviour. Umicom OS composes the operating-system environment. Umicom Framework owns reusable C23/Assembly services, build, VCS, security and application lifecycle contracts. Bits2Banking owns the teaching material and isolated laboratories. A lesson should not be mistaken for proof that a production system is ready.

Stage 5 · Virtual machines and deployment · Chapter 64

Chapter 64 — Identify an operating system and architecture without guessing

Bits to Banking · System Administration From Zero · Stage 5 · Umicom Foundation
Audience: First-time computer users, older learners, new contributors and returning professionals.
Practical mode: Read-only observation by default; any exercise that writes uses a clearly identified private training directory.
Implementation policy: New Umicom executable functionality uses C23 or Assembly. PowerShell and Linux terminal commands here are interactive instructions, not implementation scripts.

The problem we are solving

How do you know which instructions and installer belong to the computer or VM in front of you?

An operating system has a name, a release, an architecture and an environment. Windows 11 on x86-64 and Linux on RISC-V may both offer a command line, but they require different executables, package sources and service managers. Even within one machine, the host and a virtual guest can report different operating-system versions.

A 64-bit processor may execute some 32-bit programs, but that does not imply all binary formats, drivers and shared libraries are compatible. Never choose a downloadable package solely because its filename says “64-bit”. A package may also depend on the correct operating system, runtime libraries and toolchain ABI.

Collect a baseline before installing or troubleshooting. An OS baseline records only the useful technical identifiers: OS release, architecture, command interpreter version and selected tools. Do not copy machine serial numbers, network credentials or other identifiers into a public issue report.

Words you need before you continue

  • Architecture — The processor family targeted by executable instructions.
  • ABI — Rules for how compiled code calls functions and exchanges values.
  • Distribution — A packaged Linux operating system with a specific software-management ecosystem.
  • Baseline — A short record of known system properties and versions.

Worked Umicom example

A contributor tries an x86-64 Windows GCC package inside an aarch64 Linux VM. The file cannot run because both the operating-system and architecture expectations are wrong. The correct diagnosis begins with uname -m, /etc/os-release and the intended toolchain, not with disabling security controls.

Before touching your computer

Read each command all the way through. Check the directory or filename first. A command is something you type in the terminal; the command output is the evidence you interpret. If a step requires a file or application that is not installed, record not available and continue with the conceptual part. Do not invent a result and do not try a more powerful command merely to make the exercise appear to pass.

Safety boundary: Only record information relevant to troubleshooting. Do not post full system inventories to public forums without checking for personal, private or business details.

Windows — PowerShell 7, step by step

Start Windows Terminal and select PowerShell, or use PowerShell 7 directly. Confirm with $PSVersionTable.PSVersion. The prompt ending in > is where you enter the command; do not type the prompt itself. Commands are shown exactly, except for placeholders such as YOUR_APPROVED_LINUX.iso, which must be replaced with a real filename before execution.

1. Read operating-system information

Get-ComputerInfo | Select-Object WindowsProductName, OsVersion, OsArchitecture
$PSVersionTable.PSVersion

Expected result and interpretation: You should see a Windows name, version, architecture and PowerShell version. These are read-only observations.

2. Locate the command that will run

Get-Command pwsh, git, gh, cmake -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object Name, Source

Expected result and interpretation: Source identifies the selected executable, helping diagnose unexpected older versions.

Linux — terminal, step by step

Open the distribution's Terminal application. The examples assume an ordinary, non-root account. Linux paths use / and case-sensitive names on most filesystems; a Windows path beginning C:\ must not be pasted unchanged into Linux commands.

1. Read kernel and distribution separately

uname -s
uname -m
cat /etc/os-release

Expected result and interpretation: uname reports the running kernel and architecture; /etc/os-release identifies the distribution.

2. Inspect the shell and tools

printf '%s\n' "$SHELL"
command -v cmake
command -v gcc

Expected result and interpretation: A shell path and any installed tool paths are displayed.

Guided practice laboratory

  1. Create a baseline note with OS, release, architecture and PowerShell or shell version.
  2. Compare your output with the instructions for the current Umicom repository.
  3. Explain what would change if the work moved into a virtual Linux guest.
  4. Check that Get-Command or command -v resolves the tool you expected.

Keep evidence: Note the date, selected environment, commands entered, expected outcomes and actual outcomes. Omit passwords, tokens, private patient/customer details and unnecessary machine identifiers. A missing or failed step belongs in your report; it is not a reason to hide the error.

Common problems and how to investigate

Symptom Safe investigation
A command is missing Different editions and minimal images ship different tools. Note the absence rather than installing a random replacement.
Two versions of GCC appear Check the resolved executable path. PATH order, toolchain profile and ABI must agree.

Never substitute git reset --hard, git clean -fd, broad permission changes, service shutdown or force-push for diagnosis. Those operations can discard unrelated work.

Review questions with suggested answers

  1. Does PowerShell 7 make Windows into Linux?

    Answer: No. A shell runs on an operating system; changing shells does not replace the kernel.

  2. Why keep the OS release alongside architecture?

    Answer: Software depends on both, plus ABI and library versions.

  3. Why avoid sharing serial numbers in a bug report?

    Answer: They are usually unnecessary and can disclose identifiable system details.

How this fits into Umicom

We keep the responsibilities clear. Umicom Kernel owns privileged boot and hardware behaviour. Umicom OS composes the operating-system environment. Umicom Framework owns reusable C23/Assembly services, build, VCS, security and application lifecycle contracts. Bits2Banking owns the teaching material and isolated laboratories. A lesson should not be mistaken for proof that a production system is ready.

Implementation policy: New Umicom executable functionality uses C23 or Assembly. PowerShell and Linux terminal commands here are interactive instructions, not implementation scripts.

The problem we are solving

What is stored in a disk-image file, and why must beginners never confuse one with their computer’s real disk?

A disk image is a file holding disk-like data. It may contain a partition table, one or more filesystems and data. A filesystem organises files and directories; a root filesystem holds the operating system’s user-space directories and configuration. A kernel is not the same thing as the root filesystem. A RAM-based root filesystem may exist only during the running guest session.

Formats such as raw, qcow2 and VHDX are not interchangeable. Some use metadata for snapshots or sparse allocation; others represent a linear sequence of sectors. A reported virtual size can exceed the image’s physical file size when sparse allocation is used. This does not grant the real disk unlimited space.

For the first exercise, we inspect ordinary files and existing image metadata. We do not partition, format, mount, write, expand or repair any disk. A learner who can explain the difference between C:\umicom\guest.qcow2 and C: is much less likely to lose data in a later administration task.

Words you need before you continue

  • Partition — A named region of a disk using a partition-table scheme.
  • Filesystem — The format that organises file data and metadata.
  • Root filesystem — The primary directory hierarchy for a running Linux system.
  • Sparse disk image — An image that allocates host storage as guest data is written.

Worked Umicom example

A student sees a qcow2 image reporting a 20 GB virtual size while the host file occupies only 1 GB. They should not infer 19 GB of free physical storage. They should check the host filesystem’s remaining space and remember that the guest may grow the image when saving new data.

Before touching your computer

Read each command all the way through. Check the directory or filename first. A command is something you type in the terminal; the command output is the evidence you interpret. If a step requires a file or application that is not installed, record not available and continue with the conceptual part. Do not invent a result and do not try a more powerful command merely to make the exercise appear to pass.

Safety boundary: Do not run mkfs, fdisk, diskpart clean, Remove-Disk, dd of=/dev/..., or qemu-img convert in a beginner lesson. These can overwrite storage. This chapter is deliberately read-only.

Windows — PowerShell 7, step by step

Start Windows Terminal and select PowerShell, or use PowerShell 7 directly. Confirm with $PSVersionTable.PSVersion. The prompt ending in > is where you enter the command; do not type the prompt itself. Commands are shown exactly, except for placeholders such as YOUR_APPROVED_LINUX.iso, which must be replaced with a real filename before execution.

1. Inspect your practice directory

Get-ChildItem "$HOME\UmicomLearning\VMs" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object Name, Length

Expected result and interpretation: The listed values describe files in your practice folder only.

2. Check image information only for an existing image

Get-Command qemu-img -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
qemu-img info "C:\PATH\TO\YOUR-EXISTING-PRACTICE-IMAGE.qcow2"

Expected result and interpretation: Replace the placeholder with a verified personal practice image. The command is read-only; do not run it against real device paths.

Linux — terminal, step by step

Open the distribution's Terminal application. The examples assume an ordinary, non-root account. Linux paths use / and case-sensitive names on most filesystems; a Windows path beginning C:\ must not be pasted unchanged into Linux commands.

1. Inspect filesystem capacity without modifying it

df -h "$HOME"
ls -lh "$HOME/UmicomLearning/VMs"

Expected result and interpretation: df reports remaining space on the filesystem; ls reports file sizes.

2. Inspect image metadata if QEMU tools exist

qemu-img info "$HOME/UmicomLearning/VMs/EXISTING-PRACTICE-IMAGE.qcow2"

Expected result and interpretation: The report distinguishes virtual size and disk size if the file and utility exist.

Guided practice laboratory

  1. Draw file → disk image metadata → virtual blocks → guest partitions → guest filesystem.
  2. Inspect the size of a harmless local practice file using Get-Item or ls -lh.
  3. Explain why a read-only qemu-img info command is safer than converting or formatting an image.
  4. Name the evidence required before a storage image can be claimed to boot under QEMU.

Keep evidence: Note the date, selected environment, commands entered, expected outcomes and actual outcomes. Omit passwords, tokens, private patient/customer details and unnecessary machine identifiers. A missing or failed step belongs in your report; it is not a reason to hide the error.

Common problems and how to investigate

Symptom Safe investigation
Image format cannot be recognised Confirm that the file is actually a supported image and was downloaded or created by a trusted source.
Guest reports disk full despite free host space The guest filesystem and the host filesystem have separate capacities; diagnose both before changing a disk.

Never substitute git reset --hard, git clean -fd, broad permission changes, service shutdown or force-push for diagnosis. Those operations can discard unrelated work.

Review questions with suggested answers

  1. Can a file represent a disk?

    Answer: Yes. That is the purpose of a disk-image file.

  2. Are virtual size and physical usage always equal?

    Answer: No, especially with sparse formats.

  3. Does a readable disk image prove the OS boots?

    Answer: No. Boot, filesystem and service readiness require independent evidence.

We keep the responsibilities clear. Umicom Kernel owns privileged boot and hardware behaviour. Umicom OS composes the operating-system environment. Umicom Framework owns reusable C23/Assembly services, build, VCS, security and application lifecycle contracts. Bits2Banking owns the teaching material and isolated laboratories. A lesson should not be mistaken for proof that a production system is ready.

Stage 5 · Virtual machines and deployment · Chapter 66

Chapter 66 — Design safe learner accounts and permission boundaries

Bits to Banking · System Administration From Zero · Stage 5 · Umicom Foundation
Audience: First-time computer users, older learners, new contributors and returning professionals.
Practical mode: Read-only observation by default; any exercise that writes uses a clearly identified private training directory.
Implementation policy: New Umicom executable functionality uses C23 or Assembly. PowerShell and Linux terminal commands here are interactive instructions, not implementation scripts.

The problem we are solving

Why do professional administrators avoid practising every command as an administrator?

A user account identifies a human or service. Permissions specify what that identity may read or change. An administrator can usually alter system-wide settings, installed services and sensitive files. These powers are useful for maintenance but inappropriate for routine study. Least privilege means granting only the capabilities required for a task.

For a safe Umicom learning laboratory, ordinary commands should run using an ordinary account inside a directory owned by that user. Virtual machines can have distinct learner accounts. A student can practise inspecting files, using Git, compiling C23 and running local demonstrations without system-level privileges.

Identity is not the same as process name. A service may run as a system account or as a restricted user even when its executable is identical. Before changing permissions, ask which identity will execute the process, who owns the files and which exact action is blocked. Changing access for “Everyone” or setting broad executable permissions should never be a reflexive workaround.

Words you need before you continue

  • Principal — An identity that can be granted permissions.
  • Least privilege — Giving an identity only the access it needs.
  • ACL — Access-control list describing permissions for users and groups.
  • Elevation — Temporarily gaining stronger privileges for a permitted operation.

Worked Umicom example

Umicom Notes displays “access denied” when writing to C:\Program Files. This does not mean the application needs administrator mode. The right solution is to identify the intended writable user-data location, the calling identity and the Framework path contract.

Before touching your computer

Read each command all the way through. Check the directory or filename first. A command is something you type in the terminal; the command output is the evidence you interpret. If a step requires a file or application that is not installed, record not available and continue with the conceptual part. Do not invent a result and do not try a more powerful command merely to make the exercise appear to pass.

Safety boundary: Do not use sudo, runas, icacls /grant, chmod -R 777, registry permission changes or account-creation commands as a beginner exercise. Read first; obtain permission for an authorised change later.

Windows — PowerShell 7, step by step

Start Windows Terminal and select PowerShell, or use PowerShell 7 directly. Confirm with $PSVersionTable.PSVersion. The prompt ending in > is where you enter the command; do not type the prompt itself. Commands are shown exactly, except for placeholders such as YOUR_APPROVED_LINUX.iso, which must be replaced with a real filename before execution.

1. Identify the current account

whoami
whoami /groups

Expected result and interpretation: You should see your account name and group memberships. This does not change permissions.

2. Inspect permissions on your practice folder

Get-Acl "$HOME\UmicomLearning" | Format-List Owner, Access

Expected result and interpretation: The owner and access rules are shown for the named folder. It is safe to stop if the folder does not exist.

Linux — terminal, step by step

Open the distribution's Terminal application. The examples assume an ordinary, non-root account. Linux paths use / and case-sensitive names on most filesystems; a Windows path beginning C:\ must not be pasted unchanged into Linux commands.

1. Read the identity and group memberships

id
groups

Expected result and interpretation: UID, primary group and supplementary groups are displayed.

2. Inspect a private directory

Expected result and interpretation: Ownership, mode and metadata are reported; no rights are changed.

Guided practice laboratory

  1. Record your current identity privately; do not publish account or group details unnecessarily.
  2. Inspect permissions on one folder you own.
  3. Explain why an application binary and its user-data directory usually need different write permissions.
  4. Design an account policy for a fictional Notes service: read installation files, write only private user data, no administrator privileges.

Keep evidence: Note the date, selected environment, commands entered, expected outcomes and actual outcomes. Omit passwords, tokens, private patient/customer details and unnecessary machine identifiers. A missing or failed step belongs in your report; it is not a reason to hide the error.

Common problems and how to investigate

Symptom Safe investigation
Get-Acl cannot locate the path Create or use your own existing practice directory; do not switch to a system folder.
Linux group list looks different than Windows They are different security models. Compare ownership and effective access, not just group names.

Never substitute git reset --hard, git clean -fd, broad permission changes, service shutdown or force-push for diagnosis. Those operations can discard unrelated work.

Review questions with suggested answers

  1. What is least privilege?

    Answer: Allow only the specific operations necessary for the task.

  2. Does access denied mean permissions should be opened widely?

    Answer: No. Diagnose the intended identity and storage location first.

  3. Why avoid compiling as root?

    Answer: Compiler mistakes and build tools would gain unnecessary control over the host.

Stage 5 · Virtual machines and deployment · Chapter 67

Chapter 67 — Configure reproducible C23 toolchains and build directories

Bits to Banking · System Administration From Zero · Stage 5 · Umicom Foundation
Audience: First-time computer users, older learners, new contributors and returning professionals.
Practical mode: Read-only observation by default; any exercise that writes uses a clearly identified private training directory.
Implementation policy: New Umicom executable functionality uses C23 or Assembly. PowerShell and Linux terminal commands here are interactive instructions, not implementation scripts.

The problem we are solving

Why can the same source code compile on one contributor’s computer and fail on another?

A toolchain is the collection of compilers, linkers, build systems and libraries required to turn source into executable code. CMake describes targets and configuration; Ninja executes generated build steps; GCC or Clang compiles C23 source. The versions and the target ABI matter.

For Umicom projects, Windows contributors commonly use MSYS2 UCRT64. Mixing tools from different compiler environments can create dependency problems even when each command works separately. A CMake preset records a known configuration, but it does not automatically install the correct compiler or prove that the source is correct.

Source directory and build directory must remain separate. Generated object files and logs belong under a build/output location, not in the source tree. A successful configure step is not the same as a successful compile, and a compiled program has not necessarily passed its tests. This distinction is central to professional troubleshooting.

Words you need before you continue

  • C23 — The 2023 ISO C language revision used for new native Umicom code.
  • Preset — Named CMake configuration that captures chosen options and build location.
  • Build artefact — A generated object, library, executable or package.
  • ABI — Binary-level contract governing function calls and data layout.

Worked Umicom example

A student opens PowerShell with an older GCC first on PATH while the Umicom project expects MSYS2 UCRT64. gcc --version alone identifies a version, not necessarily the one CMake has already cached. Get-Command gcc and CMakeCache.txt reveal which executable is being used.

Before touching your computer

Read each command all the way through. Check the directory or filename first. A command is something you type in the terminal; the command output is the evidence you interpret. If a step requires a file or application that is not installed, record not available and continue with the conceptual part. Do not invent a result and do not try a more powerful command merely to make the exercise appear to pass.

Safety boundary: Never solve a toolchain mismatch by deleting source files or changing public Framework APIs. Record the full compiler path, version, preset, first error and target before attempting a repair.

Windows — PowerShell 7, step by step

Start Windows Terminal and select PowerShell, or use PowerShell 7 directly. Confirm with $PSVersionTable.PSVersion. The prompt ending in > is where you enter the command; do not type the prompt itself. Commands are shown exactly, except for placeholders such as YOUR_APPROVED_LINUX.iso, which must be replaced with a real filename before execution.

1. Check which build tools are selected

Get-Command cmake, ninja, gcc -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object Name, Source
cmake --version
ninja --version

Expected result and interpretation: Note the returned paths and versions. A missing tool should be installed only from an approved source.

2. Check the UCRT64 GCC executable directly

& "C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin\gcc.exe" --version
Get-Command "C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin\gcc.exe" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Expected result and interpretation: This calls the selected compiler, bypassing ambiguity in PATH. If it is missing, follow the established MSYS2 setup lesson.

Linux — terminal, step by step

Open the distribution's Terminal application. The examples assume an ordinary, non-root account. Linux paths use / and case-sensitive names on most filesystems; a Windows path beginning C:\ must not be pasted unchanged into Linux commands.

1. Identify compiler and build tools

command -v cc
cc --version
cmake --version
ninja --version

Expected result and interpretation: The installed versions and paths are shown. Do not assume cc selects GCC.

2. Inspect supported CMake presets in a checked-out project

cmake --list-presets

Expected result and interpretation: Run at the root of a project containing CMakePresets.json. The output lists named configurations.

Guided practice laboratory

  1. Inspect your toolchain paths; note missing tools rather than installing everything at once.
  2. Explain which files a cmake -S ... -B ... command reads and creates.
  3. Identify the native laboratory in Update 42 and its separate output/learning-build/deployment-rehearsal directory.
  4. Describe the difference between Configure, Build, Test and Install in one sentence each.

Keep evidence: Note the date, selected environment, commands entered, expected outcomes and actual outcomes. Omit passwords, tokens, private patient/customer details and unnecessary machine identifiers. A missing or failed step belongs in your report; it is not a reason to hide the error.

Common problems and how to investigate

Symptom Safe investigation
CMake reports compiler not found Check whether the expected compiler exists and whether the correct path was supplied; do not mix MSYS2 environments.
Compiler warning appears during build Read the specific warning, identify affected file and review before editing. Do not suppress warnings globally.

Never substitute git reset --hard, git clean -fd, broad permission changes, service shutdown or force-push for diagnosis. Those operations can discard unrelated work.

Review questions with suggested answers

  1. Does CMake compile C code by itself?

    Answer: It primarily configures and generates a build; the build step invokes a compiler.

  2. Why separate source and build directories?

    Answer: It protects source files and makes generated artefacts easier to inspect and replace.

  3. Is a successful compile a passing test?

    Answer: No. Tests must run and report their own results.

Stage 5 · Virtual machines and deployment · Chapter 68

Chapter 68 — Stage a release in a private directory without system-wide installation

Bits to Banking · System Administration From Zero · Stage 5 · Umicom Foundation
Audience: First-time computer users, older learners, new contributors and returning professionals.
Practical mode: Read-only observation by default; any exercise that writes uses a clearly identified private training directory.
Implementation policy: New Umicom executable functionality uses C23 or Assembly. PowerShell and Linux terminal commands here are interactive instructions, not implementation scripts.

The problem we are solving

How can learners practise installation while keeping their actual operating system unchanged?

In software delivery, staging means placing a built application into a controlled directory before wider release. A prefix specifies the destination root for files installed by a CMake project. A private installation places them under a folder you own, not under Windows system directories or Linux /usr/local.

The new Update 42 laboratory provides a small executable with an explicit CMake install rule. It deliberately does not register a Windows service, create Start-menu shortcuts, change the registry or write global configuration. Students can observe what CMake copies and prove that the program runs from the staged location.

Before staging, verify the build and tests. After staging, inspect the exact files created and run the relocated demonstration. This is stronger evidence than a console message saying “installed”: a real running executable at the chosen location is a separate observation. It still does not qualify an enterprise installer or prove other operating systems will run the binary.

Words you need before you continue

  • Stage — A controlled copy of build output prepared for review.
  • Install prefix — The root directory where an installer or build tool places files.
  • Relocation — Running software correctly after moving it to its installation location.
  • Portable — Designed to run without relying on undeclared machine-specific state.

Worked Umicom example

A student gets all automated tests passing, stages the teaching executable to C:\umicom\learning-stage-update42\bin and launches it by its full path. They then record which executable ran and what it printed. A successful staging exercise is not evidence that an Umicom Studio Windows installer bundles every GTK DLL or that Umicom OS boots.

Before touching your computer

Read each command all the way through. Check the directory or filename first. A command is something you type in the terminal; the command output is the evidence you interpret. If a step requires a file or application that is not installed, record not available and continue with the conceptual part. Do not invent a result and do not try a more powerful command merely to make the exercise appear to pass.

Safety boundary: The cmake --install command writes files. Run it only against the named practice prefix, which you have verified is appropriate. Do not use a system prefix or administrator rights for this exercise.

Windows — PowerShell 7, step by step

Start Windows Terminal and select PowerShell, or use PowerShell 7 directly. Confirm with $PSVersionTable.PSVersion. The prompt ending in > is where you enter the command; do not type the prompt itself. Commands are shown exactly, except for placeholders such as YOUR_APPROVED_LINUX.iso, which must be replaced with a real filename before execution.

1. Build the native Update 42 laboratory

Set-Location "C:\umicom\Umicom-Bits2Banking"
$env:Path = "C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin;$env:Path"
cmake -S ".\labs\native\deployment-rehearsal" -B ".\output\learning-build\deployment-rehearsal" -G Ninja -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER="C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin\gcc.exe" -DBUILD_TESTING=ON
cmake --build ".\output\learning-build\deployment-rehearsal" --parallel 2
ctest --test-dir ".\output\learning-build\deployment-rehearsal" --no-tests=error --output-on-failure

Expected result and interpretation: The build finishes and CTest reports the full test count with no failures before the install exercise.

2. Stage only inside a named practice prefix

Test-Path "C:\umicom\learning-stage-update42"
cmake --install ".\output\learning-build\deployment-rehearsal" --prefix "C:\umicom\learning-stage-update42"
Get-ChildItem "C:\umicom\learning-stage-update42\bin"

Expected result and interpretation: Check the path first. If it already contains unrelated material, choose a different practice prefix instead of overwriting it.

Linux — terminal, step by step

Open the distribution's Terminal application. The examples assume an ordinary, non-root account. Linux paths use / and case-sensitive names on most filesystems; a Windows path beginning C:\ must not be pasted unchanged into Linux commands.

1. Configure, build and verify

cmake -S labs/native/deployment-rehearsal -B output/learning-build/deployment-rehearsal -G Ninja -DBUILD_TESTING=ON
cmake --build output/learning-build/deployment-rehearsal --parallel 2
ctest --test-dir output/learning-build/deployment-rehearsal --no-tests=error --output-on-failure

Expected result and interpretation: The local executable and tests are built and run without sudo.

2. Stage into your own home directory

cmake --install output/learning-build/deployment-rehearsal --prefix "$HOME/umicom-learning-stage"
ls -l "$HOME/umicom-learning-stage/bin"

Expected result and interpretation: A copy of the demonstration appears in the private bin folder.

Guided practice laboratory

  1. Confirm CTest passes before the install command.
  2. Read the exact destination prefix aloud and check that it is a private training directory.
  3. Stage the program, list installed files and run the staged demonstration.
  4. Explain how installing to /usr/local or C:\Program Files would change the safety and permission requirements.

Keep evidence: Note the date, selected environment, commands entered, expected outcomes and actual outcomes. Omit passwords, tokens, private patient/customer details and unnecessary machine identifiers. A missing or failed step belongs in your report; it is not a reason to hide the error.

Common problems and how to investigate

Symptom Safe investigation
cmake --install: no install target The CMake project must declare install rules. Check the laboratory’s CMakeLists.txt; do not improvise copying unknown binary dependencies.
Staged executable cannot start Record the exact error, check runtime dependencies and never assume that a successful copy establishes portability.

Never substitute git reset --hard, git clean -fd, broad permission changes, service shutdown or force-push for diagnosis. Those operations can discard unrelated work.

Review questions with suggested answers

  1. What does an install prefix do?

    Answer: Sets the root location for installation outputs.

  2. Should the student use Run as administrator?

    Answer: No, not for a private staging exercise.

  3. Are passed tests enough to claim deployment success?

    Answer: No. Staging, runtime and operational checks provide separate evidence.

Stage 5 · Virtual machines and deployment · Chapter 69

Chapter 69 — Inspect runtime dependencies and test relocation

Bits to Banking · System Administration From Zero · Stage 5 · Umicom Foundation
Audience: First-time computer users, older learners, new contributors and returning professionals.
Practical mode: Read-only observation by default; any exercise that writes uses a clearly identified private training directory.
Implementation policy: New Umicom executable functionality uses C23 or Assembly. PowerShell and Linux terminal commands here are interactive instructions, not implementation scripts.

The problem we are solving

Why can a program work in a build folder but fail when opened from another computer or folder?

A compiled executable may depend on shared libraries such as DLL files on Windows or .so files on Linux. It may also depend on data files, fonts, schemas, environment variables and a working directory. Merely copying the executable does not guarantee these resources follow it.

A static library normally contributes code to the linked program. A dynamic library is loaded at run time. A relocatable application can find the resources it needs even when the installation folder differs from the build folder. Umicom Framework owns reusable Windows runtime packaging and application-startup policy; thin products should consume those facilities instead of introducing separate copying scripts.

Professional diagnosis starts by distinguishing three phases: linking, operating-system loader startup, and later application initialisation. Missing DLL errors occur before ordinary application code may run. A missing icon, schema or configuration can be a later resource-resolution failure. Test each boundary separately and record the exact message.

Words you need before you continue

  • DLL — Windows dynamic-link library loaded at run time.
  • Shared object — Common Linux shared-library file, often ending in .so.
  • Loader — Operating-system component that loads an executable and its dependencies.
  • Working directory — Directory from which relative file paths are interpreted.

Worked Umicom example

Umicom Trader launches from a PowerShell window but fails when double-clicked. One plausible cause is that PowerShell configured C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin on PATH, while the desktop shortcut does not. The proper fix is Framework-owned runtime staging and relocatable paths, tested by icon launch—not telling end users to open a development shell.

Before touching your computer

Read each command all the way through. Check the directory or filename first. A command is something you type in the terminal; the command output is the evidence you interpret. If a step requires a file or application that is not installed, record not available and continue with the conceptual part. Do not invent a result and do not try a more powerful command merely to make the exercise appear to pass.

Safety boundary: Do not download random DLLs from search results to silence loader errors. Do not modify PATH globally or copy SDK files into Windows system directories without an approved package policy.

Windows — PowerShell 7, step by step

Start Windows Terminal and select PowerShell, or use PowerShell 7 directly. Confirm with $PSVersionTable.PSVersion. The prompt ending in > is where you enter the command; do not type the prompt itself. Commands are shown exactly, except for placeholders such as YOUR_APPROVED_LINUX.iso, which must be replaced with a real filename before execution.

1. Inspect the staged executable first

Get-Item "C:\umicom\learning-stage-update42\bin\btb-deployment-review-demo.exe" | Select-Object FullName, Length

Expected result and interpretation: The file exists and its size is reported. If absent, return to the staging lesson.

2. Inspect declared Windows DLL imports, if objdump is installed

& "C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin\objdump.exe" -p "C:\umicom\learning-stage-update42\bin\btb-deployment-review-demo.exe" | Select-String 'DLL Name'

Expected result and interpretation: The list shows named import dependencies; it does not prove every dependency resolves on another machine.

Linux — terminal, step by step

Open the distribution's Terminal application. The examples assume an ordinary, non-root account. Linux paths use / and case-sensitive names on most filesystems; a Windows path beginning C:\ must not be pasted unchanged into Linux commands.

1. Inspect the dynamic section of your own build

readelf -d "$HOME/umicom-learning-stage/bin/btb-deployment-review-demo" | grep NEEDED

Expected result and interpretation: Only works when the binary and readelf are available. A fully static binary may have no dynamic section.

2. Run the staged program from another working directory

cd "$HOME"
"$HOME/umicom-learning-stage/bin/btb-deployment-review-demo"

Expected result and interpretation: A successful relocation run is evidence that this particular demonstration does not depend on its original build CWD.

Guided practice laboratory

  1. Read the executable path and imported libraries for a known training build.
  2. Try running the staged demo from a different current directory.
  3. Document which dependencies the loader provides and which resources the application must locate itself.
  4. Explain why working on your machine does not prove that a release is distributable.

Keep evidence: Note the date, selected environment, commands entered, expected outcomes and actual outcomes. Omit passwords, tokens, private patient/customer details and unnecessary machine identifiers. A missing or failed step belongs in your report; it is not a reason to hide the error.

Common problems and how to investigate

Symptom Safe investigation
objdump.exe is not found Install or select an approved toolchain; do not substitute a random internet executable.
A library is listed but still cannot load The loader may not find the right architecture, ABI or dependent libraries. Capture the exact message and inspect the package.

Never substitute git reset --hard, git clean -fd, broad permission changes, service shutdown or force-push for diagnosis. Those operations can discard unrelated work.

Review questions with suggested answers

  1. What happens before main() starts?

    Answer: The operating system locates and loads the executable and needed runtime libraries.

  2. Can CWD changes break a program?

    Answer: Yes, when code incorrectly relies on relative paths.

  3. Who should own shared runtime deployment?

    Answer: Umicom Framework, with thin applications using its tested facilities.
