Next: 70 — Understand application startup and shutdown supervision.

Stage 5 · Virtual machines and deployment · Chapter 70

Chapter 70 — Understand supervised application startup, shutdown and readiness

Bits to Banking · System Administration From Zero · Stage 5 · Umicom Foundation
Audience: First-time computer users, older learners, new contributors and returning professionals.
Practical mode: Read-only observation by default; any exercise that writes uses a clearly identified private training directory.
Implementation policy: New Umicom executable functionality uses C23 or Assembly. PowerShell and Linux terminal commands here are interactive instructions, not implementation scripts.

The problem we are solving

How do we tell the difference between a process existing and an application being ready to serve users?

A process is a running program. A service is a managed background workload. A service manager may supervise starting, stopping and restarting services, but not every application is installed as a service. A health check asks whether a process or capability is functioning; a readiness check asks whether it is safe to accept new work.

Imagine an Umicom Notes API with a local data store. Its process may start successfully but fail to open the store. The service exists, yet it should not report readiness. Conversely, a process intentionally shutting down may remain alive while draining work; its readiness should change before it exits. These are normal states, not contradictions.

Keep startup order, dependency failure and graceful shutdown distinct. The Umicom Framework Master Controller and Slave Controllers own application lifecycle policy. The OS service manager owns process supervision. A GUI button does not override a shared service's authoritative state. The beginner exercises below only inspect, never stop services.

Words you need before you continue

  • Liveness — Evidence that a process responds or is running.
  • Readiness — Evidence that required dependencies are ready to accept work.
  • Service manager — Operating-system component that supervises configured services.
  • Drain — Stop accepting new work while completing or cancelling existing work safely.

Worked Umicom example

The GUI reports “Umicom Notes ready,” but a required file provider failed. The correct report is NOT READY. Update 40’s educational service-readiness graph models this distinction: dependent work must remain blocked until its required provider passes.

Before touching your computer

Read each command all the way through. Check the directory or filename first. A command is something you type in the terminal; the command output is the evidence you interpret. If a step requires a file or application that is not installed, record not available and continue with the conceptual part. Do not invent a result and do not try a more powerful command merely to make the exercise appear to pass.

Safety boundary: Do not execute Stop-Service, Restart-Service, systemctl stop, kill, or service restart as an introductory exercise. A shared machine may depend on these workloads.

Windows — PowerShell 7, step by step

Start Windows Terminal and select PowerShell, or use PowerShell 7 directly. Confirm with $PSVersionTable.PSVersion. The prompt ending in > is where you enter the command; do not type the prompt itself. Commands are shown exactly, except for placeholders such as YOUR_APPROVED_LINUX.iso, which must be replaced with a real filename before execution.

1. Observe a familiar application process

Get-Process | Select-Object -First 10 Name, Id, CPU

Expected result and interpretation: The sample shows running processes with their identifiers and CPU time. The result alone does not establish readiness.

2. Read service state, not change it

Get-Service -Name Spooler -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object Name, Status, StartType

Expected result and interpretation: The Print Spooler service may be absent, stopped or disabled. This is an observation, not a suggested change.

Linux — terminal, step by step

Open the distribution's Terminal application. The examples assume an ordinary, non-root account. Linux paths use / and case-sensitive names on most filesystems; a Windows path beginning C:\ must not be pasted unchanged into Linux commands.

1. Observe user services

systemctl --user --no-pager list-units --type=service --state=running

Expected result and interpretation: The user service manager lists running units when available. A minimal container may lack systemd.

2. Read current process information

ps -eo pid,comm,stat --sort=pid | head -n 12

Expected result and interpretation: Process states are displayed; do not infer application-level health solely from the STAT column.

Guided practice laboratory

  1. Find a running process without changing it.
  2. Find a service and note whether its displayed status is running, stopped or unknown.
  3. Draw the dependency chain: process alive → data store ready → Notes API ready → user request admitted.
  4. Describe how a graceful shutdown changes readiness before the process exits.

Keep evidence: Note the date, selected environment, commands entered, expected outcomes and actual outcomes. Omit passwords, tokens, private patient/customer details and unnecessary machine identifiers. A missing or failed step belongs in your report; it is not a reason to hide the error.

Common problems and how to investigate

Symptom Safe investigation
systemctl --user cannot connect to bus The environment may not run systemd as a user manager. Record that the check was unavailable instead of assuming the service is dead.
A process shows CPU zero It may be idle or waiting. CPU time alone is not a failure diagnosis.

Never substitute git reset --hard, git clean -fd, broad permission changes, service shutdown or force-push for diagnosis. Those operations can discard unrelated work.

Review questions with suggested answers

  1. Does Running mean Ready?

    Answer: No; a service may lack required dependencies.

  2. What does drain mean?

    Answer: Stop new admissions and resolve existing work under the component’s ownership policy.

  3. Why have one controller responsible for lifecycle?

    Answer: So multiple views cannot independently and inconsistently change authoritative service state.

How this fits into Umicom

We keep the responsibilities clear. Umicom Kernel owns privileged boot and hardware behaviour. Umicom OS composes the operating-system environment. Umicom Framework owns reusable C23/Assembly services, build, VCS, security and application lifecycle contracts. Bits2Banking owns the teaching material and isolated laboratories. A lesson should not be mistaken for proof that a production system is ready.

Next: 71 — Diagnose a failed launch and choose safe recovery.

Stage 5 · Virtual machines and deployment · Chapter 71

Chapter 71 — Diagnose a failed launch and plan recovery without guesswork

Bits to Banking · System Administration From Zero · Stage 5 · Umicom Foundation
Audience: First-time computer users, older learners, new contributors and returning professionals.
Practical mode: Read-only observation by default; any exercise that writes uses a clearly identified private training directory.
Implementation policy: New Umicom executable functionality uses C23 or Assembly. PowerShell and Linux terminal commands here are interactive instructions, not implementation scripts.

The problem we are solving

What should you do when an installed application fails immediately or starts but is unusable?

A professional incident investigation starts with the earliest reliable evidence. Record what was attempted, which executable and revision were involved, what actually happened, and which stage failed. Avoid making multiple changes at once; otherwise you cannot tell which action helped or harmed.

Classify the failure: (1) command/executable not found, (2) loader cannot find a library, (3) application initialisation fails, (4) a dependency is unavailable, (5) the program works but its interface is unusable, or (6) tests fail despite a successful launch. Each category has different evidence and a different owner.

A rollback is not simply copying an old file over a new file. It requires a known earlier release, compatible state, a safe change procedure and independent post-recovery checks. In a database-backed system, schema and data compatibility can prevent a trivial binary rollback. Our lessons practise planning and evidence collection, not automatic restoration of real services.

Words you need before you continue

  • Incident — An unexpected condition affecting a service or expected operation.
  • Root cause — The underlying reason for a failure, distinguished from an observed symptom.
  • Mitigation — An action that limits impact before a full repair.
  • Rollback — A controlled return to an approved earlier state, verified afterward.

Worked Umicom example

Umicom Studio fails when launched by desktop icon. Its debug-shell launch works because a toolchain folder is on PATH. Record the exact launch method, environment differences and missing DLL message. Fix packaging in the shared Framework and verify by double-click after installing a tested release; do not instruct every user to use PowerShell.

Before touching your computer

Read each command all the way through. Check the directory or filename first. A command is something you type in the terminal; the command output is the evidence you interpret. If a step requires a file or application that is not installed, record not available and continue with the conceptual part. Do not invent a result and do not try a more powerful command merely to make the exercise appear to pass.

Safety boundary: Do not solve a failing launch by disabling antivirus, relaxing directory permissions, deleting configuration, force-resetting Git or overwriting runtime DLLs. Escalate changes to the responsible system owner.

Windows — PowerShell 7, step by step

Start Windows Terminal and select PowerShell, or use PowerShell 7 directly. Confirm with $PSVersionTable.PSVersion. The prompt ending in > is where you enter the command; do not type the prompt itself. Commands are shown exactly, except for placeholders such as YOUR_APPROVED_LINUX.iso, which must be replaced with a real filename before execution.

1. Record the currently selected executable

Get-Command pwsh, git, cmake -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object Name, Source

Expected result and interpretation: This records selected tool paths and can reveal an unexpected installation.

2. Inspect recent Application events without changing Windows

Get-WinEvent -LogName Application -MaxEvents 8 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object TimeCreated, Id, ProviderName, LevelDisplayName

Expected result and interpretation: Any visible recent events may help establish a timeline. Absence of an event is not proof that no failure occurred.

Linux — terminal, step by step

Open the distribution's Terminal application. The examples assume an ordinary, non-root account. Linux paths use / and case-sensitive names on most filesystems; a Windows path beginning C:\ must not be pasted unchanged into Linux commands.

1. Read recent user journal records

journalctl --user -n 12 --no-pager

Expected result and interpretation: When a user journal is available, the most recent entries appear. Logs are evidence, not permission to take action.

2. Inspect a trusted executable path

command -v cmake
file "$(command -v cmake)"

Expected result and interpretation: The tool and file type are reported if the commands are available.

Guided practice laboratory

  1. Write an incident report for a fictional Notes executable that cannot find a DLL.
  2. Identify the likely failure stage (loader before application main).
  3. List the non-destructive checks you would run first: path, revision, imports, private stage and event logs.
  4. Propose a rollback plan with a named baseline and independent readiness verification.

Keep evidence: Note the date, selected environment, commands entered, expected outcomes and actual outcomes. Omit passwords, tokens, private patient/customer details and unnecessary machine identifiers. A missing or failed step belongs in your report; it is not a reason to hide the error.

Common problems and how to investigate

Symptom Safe investigation
No obvious event log entry Look for process output, program-specific logs and build provenance. An absent log is still useful evidence but not closure.
Old version also fails The root cause may be a shared dependency, data incompatibility or environment condition; do not claim a successful rollback.

Never substitute git reset --hard, git clean -fd, broad permission changes, service shutdown or force-push for diagnosis. Those operations can discard unrelated work.

Review questions with suggested answers

  1. Which error should be investigated first?

    Answer: The earliest reliable failure at a specific boundary, not simply the last message on screen.

  2. Does restoring a binary prove a service is recovered?

    Answer: No. Run independent functional/readiness checks.

  3. Why record exact revision IDs?

    Answer: So the reported behaviour can be reproduced against known code and dependency versions.

How this fits into Umicom

We keep the responsibilities clear. Umicom Kernel owns privileged boot and hardware behaviour. Umicom OS composes the operating-system environment. Umicom Framework owns reusable C23/Assembly services, build, VCS, security and application lifecycle contracts. Bits2Banking owns the teaching material and isolated laboratories. A lesson should not be mistaken for proof that a production system is ready.

Next: 72 — Capstone: staged Umicom Notes deployment.

Stage 5 · Virtual machines and deployment · Chapter 72

Chapter 72 — Capstone: rehearse a verified private Umicom Notes deployment

Bits to Banking · System Administration From Zero · Stage 5 · Umicom Foundation
Audience: First-time computer users, older learners, new contributors and returning professionals.
Practical mode: Read-only observation by default; any exercise that writes uses a clearly identified private training directory.
Implementation policy: New Umicom executable functionality uses C23 or Assembly. PowerShell and Linux terminal commands here are interactive instructions, not implementation scripts.

The problem we are solving

Can you prepare, review and explain a software release without modifying any shared machine settings?

This capstone combines the entire Stage 5 sequence. You will identify the host, confirm a native toolchain, build a harmless training executable, run automated tests, stage a private copy, inspect its dependencies, run it from a different working directory and produce a short evidence report. No real Umicom OS service is changed.

The update's C23 BtbDeploymentReview consumes the previous BtbMaintenanceReview model. It holds claimed package and configuration digests, staging observations and a source revision. It does not hash real artefacts, query Git, sign packages or operate an installer. Its value lies in teaching failure-closed review: a missing dependency, stale capture or incomplete maintenance state prevents the fictional deployment from being labelled QUALIFIED.

The most important professional habit is separating three statements: I built it, I tested it, and I deployed it successfully. These are different claims. Include the command, environment, source revision and evidence for each; report “not verified” if the observation was not performed.

Words you need before you continue

  • Release evidence — Records showing how a particular version was built and checked.
  • Change approval — Authorisation to carry out a change under a defined policy.
  • Drift — An unapproved difference between expected and actual state.
  • Qualification gate — A stated condition that must be satisfied before declaring a result acceptable.

Worked Umicom example

A learner completes the build and test but forgets to inspect runtime dependencies. The educational release gate reports BLOCKED rather than passing. The learner then records the missing check, performs a harmless inspection and explains why a new capture must be fresher than the old observation. This is the correct mindset for enterprise software.

Before touching your computer

Read each command all the way through. Check the directory or filename first. A command is something you type in the terminal; the command output is the evidence you interpret. If a step requires a file or application that is not installed, record not available and continue with the conceptual part. Do not invent a result and do not try a more powerful command merely to make the exercise appear to pass.

Safety boundary: Perform this only in your own training checkout. If the intended stage directory already contains valuable files, choose a different empty prefix. Do not create production Git commits, change network permissions or deploy Umicom OS from this capstone.

Windows — PowerShell 7, step by step

Start Windows Terminal and select PowerShell, or use PowerShell 7 directly. Confirm with $PSVersionTable.PSVersion. The prompt ending in > is where you enter the command; do not type the prompt itself. Commands are shown exactly, except for placeholders such as YOUR_APPROVED_LINUX.iso, which must be replaced with a real filename before execution.

1. Run the complete native learning test suite

Set-Location "C:\umicom\Umicom-Bits2Banking"
$env:Path = "C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin;$env:Path"
cmake -S ".\labs\native\deployment-rehearsal" -B ".\output\learning-build\deployment-rehearsal" -G Ninja -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER="C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin\gcc.exe" -DBUILD_TESTING=ON
cmake --build ".\output\learning-build\deployment-rehearsal" --parallel 2
ctest --test-dir ".\output\learning-build\deployment-rehearsal" --no-tests=error --output-on-failure

Expected result and interpretation: Record the actual CTest summary. Do not write “all passed” if any test failed or did not run.

2. Stage and launch the exercise binary

cmake --install ".\output\learning-build\deployment-rehearsal" --prefix "C:\umicom\learning-stage-update42"
& "C:\umicom\learning-stage-update42\bin\btb-deployment-review-demo.exe"
git status --short

Expected result and interpretation: The stage contains the training executable, its demonstration prints fictional decisions, and Git shows any uncommitted repository changes.

Linux — terminal, step by step

Open the distribution's Terminal application. The examples assume an ordinary, non-root account. Linux paths use / and case-sensitive names on most filesystems; a Windows path beginning C:\ must not be pasted unchanged into Linux commands.

1. Configure, test and stage only in your own directory

cmake -S labs/native/deployment-rehearsal -B output/learning-build/deployment-rehearsal -G Ninja -DBUILD_TESTING=ON
cmake --build output/learning-build/deployment-rehearsal --parallel 2
ctest --test-dir output/learning-build/deployment-rehearsal --no-tests=error --output-on-failure
cmake --install output/learning-build/deployment-rehearsal --prefix "$HOME/umicom-learning-stage"

Expected result and interpretation: Do not use sudo. Record the exact test count from your environment.

2. Run the staged demonstration and inspect Git

"$HOME/umicom-learning-stage/bin/btb-deployment-review-demo"
git status --short

Expected result and interpretation: The demonstration is separate from any actual service deployment.

Guided practice laboratory

  1. Write a preflight table with OS/architecture, source revision, toolchain versions and intended private stage directory.
  2. Run the C23 configure/build/test commands in order and record their actual results.
  3. Stage only under an approved private prefix and confirm the staged executable launches.
  4. Run the negative CTest cases missing-runtime, stale-verification, rollback and restored, explaining their different outcomes.
  5. Prepare a support note: what was proven, what remained unverified, and whether anyone authorised a real deployment (answer: no).

Keep evidence: Note the date, selected environment, commands entered, expected outcomes and actual outcomes. Omit passwords, tokens, private patient/customer details and unnecessary machine identifiers. A missing or failed step belongs in your report; it is not a reason to hide the error.

Common problems and how to investigate

Symptom Safe investigation
Test suite reports failure Do not proceed to staging. Save the first failing test and the associated source revision.
Private prefix contains unrelated files Do not overwrite them. Choose a fresh practice directory and state that choice in the evidence report.

Never substitute git reset --hard, git clean -fd, broad permission changes, service shutdown or force-push for diagnosis. Those operations can discard unrelated work.

Review questions with suggested answers

  1. What does QUALIFIED mean in the C23 lab?

    Answer: Only that fictional supplied evidence passed the teaching policy; it is not production certification.

  2. Why is RESTORED_ONLY distinct from QUALIFIED?

    Answer: The old state may have been recovered after a failed change; the new release did not succeed.

  3. What are the three separate claims?

    Answer: Built, tested and deployed successfully, each with its own evidence.

How this fits into Umicom

We keep the responsibilities clear. Umicom Kernel owns privileged boot and hardware behaviour. Umicom OS composes the operating-system environment. Umicom Framework owns reusable C23/Assembly services, build, VCS, security and application lifecycle contracts. Bits2Banking owns the teaching material and isolated laboratories. A lesson should not be mistaken for proof that a production system is ready.

Update 42 · Stage 5 overview

System Administration From Zero — Stage 5

Virtual machines, reproducible builds and safe service deployment

Umicom Foundation · Update 42 · Chapters 61–72

This stage assumes only the basic vocabulary introduced in Chapters 1–60. Absolute beginners can enter here after the introductory stages. Each chapter provides a clear problem, definitions, a real-world Umicom scenario, separate interactive Windows PowerShell 7 and Linux terminal commands, expected results, troubleshooting, exercises and answers.

Chapter Main question Practice boundary
61 What is a VM and why do we use it? Observe architecture and tools only
62 How do we prepare a disposable guest? Own directory and verified downloads
63 What does QEMU actually prove? Read machine help, no guest start
64 Which architecture and OS am I using? Read-only platform inspection
65 How does a disk image differ from a real disk? Read-only image metadata
66 Which identity should run administration tools? Read-only account/permission checks
67 How do I select the correct C23 toolchain? Version and preset inspection
68 How do I stage a private copy of a program? Practice-prefix CMake install
69 Why does an executable fail after relocation? Observe declared runtime dependencies
70 Why is a running process not always ready? Read-only service observation
71 How do I investigate a failed launch? Diagnostics, no forced recovery
72 Can I complete an end-to-end release rehearsal? Private copy and fictional evidence

Suggested schedule: Twelve guided sessions of 60–90 minutes, with optional deeper exercises for experienced learners. The dedicated practice workbook supplies assignments and marking criteria. The child/young-learner path uses only read-only observations and private directory exercises with adult supervision; deeper service and VM configuration is reserved for approved training machines.

Teaching conventions

  • Type: the literal command only, not the PowerShell prompt shown to the left of it.
  • Check: what should appear and what it actually means.
  • Record: any error without hiding it, avoiding passwords, account secrets and private data.
  • Stop: if a step names a file that does not exist, asks for elevated privileges or could overwrite unrelated work.
  • Distinguish: Windows uses C:\ style paths and PowerShell; Linux uses / style paths and its terminal shell.

This stage does not add a new production deployment subsystem. The new labs/native/deployment-rehearsal exercise composes the prior C23 administration, readiness and maintenance models, and the course calls existing Umicom Framework development facilities where appropriate.

Update 42 · Stage 5 workbook

Stage 5 learner workbook — Virtualisation and deployment evidence

Umicom Foundation · Update 42 · Suitable for supervised beginners and adult learners

Section A — Foundation checks (20 marks)

  1. (2) Draw host and guest. Identify which contains your own files by default.
  2. (2) Explain why an ISO is not the same as a mutable guest disk.
  3. (2) State why qemu-system-riscv64 -machine help is a safer first command than an unreviewed -kernel command.
  4. (3) Write Windows and Linux commands to read processor architecture and OS release.
  5. (3) Explain virtual disk size versus physical host disk usage.
  6. (3) Name three conditions under which VM isolation may be weakened.
  7. (5) Describe the difference between a guest snapshot, a copied file and a verified backup restore.

Section B — Safe system observation (20 marks)

  1. (5) Record a sanitised, read-only platform baseline: OS family, release, architecture, shell version and compiler version. Provide the commands you used.
  2. (5) Read permissions of a folder you own. Explain why an application usually should not run as administrator.
  3. (5) Compare one process observation and one service observation. Why are neither sufficient to prove readiness?
  4. (5) Given “application launches from terminal, but not from icon”, propose a read-only investigation plan with at least three steps.

Section C — Native training laboratory (30 marks)

  1. (5) Configure Update 42 with the chosen C23 compiler and a separate build directory.
  2. (5) Run the full CTest suite; write the actual number of passed, failed and not-run cases.
  3. (5) Check that C:\umicom\learning-stage-update42 or $HOME/umicom-learning-stage is an appropriate private destination before staging.
  4. (5) Run the staged demonstration; report exactly what it prints and what it does not prove.
  5. (5) Run missing-runtime, stale-verification, rollback and restored. Describe the difference between the four outcomes.
  6. (5) Locate the imported existing maintenance model in the source and explain how duplicate implementation was avoided.

Section D — Incident and recovery case study (30 marks)

A fictional Umicom Notes update is built and staged. After startup it can no longer read the document store. An independent recovery check confirms the previous version works again.

  1. (5) Which layer failed: build, stage, loader or service dependency? Explain your evidence.
  2. (5) Why does a green git status not close the incident?
  3. (5) What must be recorded before trying another candidate release?
  4. (5) Should the newer release be labelled QUALIFIED, BLOCKED, ROLLBACK_REQUIRED or RESTORED_ONLY after independent restoration? Explain.
  5. (5) Which Umicom components own real package integrity, build, process supervision and release controls?
  6. (5) Prepare a clear five-line status report for the instructor, distinguishing observed evidence from assumptions.

Suggested answers (instructor use)

Section A: The host contains the actual user environment; the guest has separately presented virtual hardware. ISO and guest disks have different roles; help commands enumerate options without booting. Windows: Get-ComputerInfo ...; Linux: uname -m and /etc/os-release. VM sharing, USB passthrough and permissive networking weaken isolation. Snapshots do not replace off-VM tested backups.

Section B: Use commands demonstrated in Chapters 64, 66 and 70. Read-only observations do not change accounts or services. A service can be running without its data store. Desktop startup may differ from a terminal's PATH or working directory.

Section C: Cite your actual CTest count. On a fully merged Updates 39–42 lab, the reference Linux build registered 79 tests. Do not copy that number if your host reports something different. The demonstration uses fictional values; it does not hash real files or install an OS service.

Section D: The dependency/readiness stage failed, not necessarily compilation. A clean Git working tree proves no pending local changes, not operational success. Record revision, package, diagnosis, evidence and the approved next step. After independent restoration the status is RESTORED_ONLY, not successful deployment. Production reuse belongs to Umicom Framework's existing VCS, build, packaging, security, logging and lifecycle facilities.

Assessment standard: A learner earns full credit for honest “not installed”, “not run” or “cannot verify” statements when supported by observation. Fabricated evidence and dangerous operations invalidate the affected practical task.

Update 42 · Stage 5 glossary

Stage 5 glossary — Virtual machines and safe deployments

Architecture — Processor instruction set required by an executable, such as x86-64 or RISC-V64.
ABI — Rules for how compiled components interact at the binary boundary.
Artifact — A result produced by a build, such as an executable or packaged file.
Baseline — A recorded known state used to interpret later changes.
Build directory — Location of generated CMake, compiler, linker and test files.
Capture ID — A classroom identifier that orders observations; it is not a trusted timestamp or signature.
Configuration drift — A difference between expected and actual settings.
CMake preset — A named set of project build settings.
DLL — Windows shared library loaded at run time.
Emulator — Software that reproduces a machine's hardware behaviour.
Guest — Operating system instance running inside a VM or emulator.
Host — The real computer and operating system running the virtual machine.
Hypervisor — Technology that supervises virtual machines.
Image — A file representing installation media, a disk, a filesystem or other system artefact.
Install prefix — Destination root for installed build output.
Liveness — Evidence that a process is active or responding, not necessarily useful.
Least privilege — Limit an identity to permissions necessary for its task.
QEMU — Emulator and virtualisation program used in Umicom kernel laboratories.
Readiness — Evidence that required dependencies are available so work can be accepted.
Relocation — Starting an application from an installation location different from its original build folder.
Rollback — A controlled return to a previously accepted system state with later verification.
Root filesystem — Main user-space directory tree used by a Linux system.
SHA-256 — Cryptographic digest algorithm; comparing an independently trusted checksum can detect changes.
Snapshot — Recorded VM state; not an automatic substitute for host backups.
Staging — Copying built files into a controlled location before wider release.
Toolchain — Compiler, linker and build tools needed for a target.
Virtual disk — File presented to a guest operating system as storage.
VM — Virtual machine with virtual hardware and a guest OS.

A claimed hash is not a computed hash. Update 42's native evidence model receives claimed values; its tests never claim to have checked a real on-disk package.

Update 42 · Stage 5 instructor guide

Stage 5 instructor guide — Virtual machines, reproducibility and private staging

Umicom Foundation · Course owner: Bits2Banking · Update 42

Audience and preparation

This course teaches the same foundational system concepts to teenagers, adults and experienced engineers returning for a refresher. Do not assume learners know the difference between a shell window, an operating system, an executable or a file path. Students can perform read-only exercises without special privileges. A younger learner should use a supervised account and never install a guest OS on shared hardware without adult/owner approval.

Before the session, verify whether each machine has PowerShell 7, Git, CMake, Ninja and an approved C23 toolchain. The absence of QEMU is acceptable for the initial conceptual lessons. Do not ask participants to download guest images from a random site or run unverified firmware/installer commands during class.

Recommended session structure

  • 10 minutes: Define the problem and introduce four new terms with a diagram.
  • 15 minutes: Instructor demonstration of only the read-only commands; point out the prompt and explain that the prompt itself is not typed.
  • 20 minutes: Learners repeat on their own workspaces; the instructor checks actual outputs instead of collecting personal machine identifiers.
  • 15 minutes: Troubleshooting: what happens when the tool is absent, path differs or an OS behaves differently?
  • 15 minutes: Practical independent exercise and a short evidence log.
  • 5 minutes: Questions and recap; name the next dependency.

Learning-specific teaching notes

Chapters 61–63: Draw host, guest, emulator, firmware and kernel as separate boxes. A running QEMU process is not evidence of successful guest boot. Treat guest snapshots and backups as different tools.

Chapters 64–66: Demonstrate identity, architecture and permissions using commands that do not modify system state. Always state why privilege escalation is not needed for observation.

Chapters 67–69: Walk through configure, build, test and stage as separate gates. Have learners inspect an executable in a private prefix; do not stage into Program Files or /usr/local.

Chapters 70–72: Teach Running versus Ready, incident stages and recovery. Use the supplied fictional Umicom Notes evidence, not an actual production service.

Common misconceptions

  • “I saw a command prompt, therefore I am running PowerShell 7.” — Run $PSVersionTable.PSVersion to identify the shell.
  • “The emulator opened, therefore the kernel booted.” — Review guest serial/boot evidence separately.
  • “The file is 1 GB, therefore its guest disk cannot grow.” — Sparse virtual sizes can be larger.
  • “Green CMake output means all tests passed.” — Configure, compile, test and staging must be checked independently.
  • “The review says QUALIFIED, therefore we installed successfully.” — It is an offline educational model with supplied fictional evidence.
  • “A rollback restored the old version, therefore the upgrade succeeded.” — A recovered baseline is RESTORED_ONLY.

Assessment and safeguarding

Record only a learner's commands, reasoning and pass/fail outcomes. Do not demand screenshots containing private user names, tokens, hardware serials or customer information. Correctly identifying “not verified” should be rewarded. Do not ask students to run destructive Git, package, disk, firewall, permission or service commands merely to reproduce a failure.

The complete C23 implementation is in labs/native/deployment-rehearsal. It requires previous Updates 39–41. Prefer a shared classroom starter repository with those prior labs already present. Run the included native CTest suite on the class toolchain, and distinguish its actual results from the reference Linux validation report.
