Git changes git status --short git status --short No
Git revision git rev-parse HEAD git rev-parse HEAD No
Native tests ctest --test-dir <build> --output-on-failure Same Test executables may write under a private build tree
Private staging cmake --install <build> --prefix C:\umicom\learning-stage-update42 cmake --install <build> --prefix "$HOME/umicom-learning-stage" Yes, private prefix only

Never run as a shortcut: git reset --hard, git clean -fd, git push --force, Stop-Service, systemctl stop, chmod -R 777, mkfs, diskpart clean, or a system-wide package upgrade. These operations may be appropriate only in separately authorised professional work, never as a generic beginner troubleshooting step.

If a command is unavailable, say “not installed” rather than fabricate a result. If a path is missing, check the current directory and correct it before doing anything else. If a step would write files, verify that the destination is a practice folder you own and that its existing contents are not important.

System Administration · Stage 6 · Chapter 73

Chapter 73 — What remote administration means, and why permission comes first

Bits to Banking · System Administration From Zero · Stage 6 · Umicom Foundation
Audience: Absolute beginners, school-age learners with supervision, adults and returning professionals.
Starting point: You can open PowerShell 7 or a Linux terminal and run Get-Location or pwd.
Safety: Read-only first; there is no connection to an unfamiliar server in this lesson.

Why a system administrator needs this skill

Imagine the Umicom Notes application is running on a computer in another room. You see its screen when you stand beside it, but how could an authorised administrator check it from a different machine? Remote administration means inspecting or managing another computer through a network. It can be convenient, but it crosses a security boundary: the remote machine must recognise who is requesting access, which device they mean and what they are allowed to do.

This chapter is about understanding that boundary, not opening it. No one should try a remote login just because an address or username appears in a tutorial. For class exercises, use a training VM you own or one explicitly provided by your instructor.

Vocabulary in ordinary language

Word Meaning Umicom example
Local computer The machine you are using. Your Windows laptop.
Remote host Another machine reached over a network. An approved Linux VM running a Notes demonstration.
Client Software that asks another system for a service. The ssh command on your laptop.
Server Software that answers a particular kind of request. An SSH server on the approved VM.
Account A named identity with specific access rights. notes-operator, not a shared administrator account.
Authentication Checking that the requester controls their claimed identity. A permitted SSH key or other supported factor.
Authorisation Deciding what that identity can do. Read service status, but not modify payments or production data.
Host identity Evidence that you reached the intended computer. A previously verified SSH host-key fingerprint.

The difference between authentication and authorisation is especially important. Being able to log in does not mean someone may change files, restart a service or access an unrelated repository.

Windows — start from a familiar prompt

Step 1. Open Windows Terminal and select PowerShell. If only Windows PowerShell appears, you may use it for these read-only commands. Check your shell:

$PSVersionTable.PSVersion
Get-Location

Expected: A version number and the directory you are currently in. You do not type the PS C:\...> prompt itself.

Step 2. Ask the computer for its own name. This does not contact another machine:

$env:COMPUTERNAME

Expected: Your Windows computer's name. It may differ from the label printed on its case.

Step 3. Check whether an SSH client is installed, without making a connection:

Get-Command ssh -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object Name, Source
ssh -V

Expected: If present, the command location and an OpenSSH version. Some OpenSSH versions print their version to the error stream; that is not by itself a login failure. If the command is missing, record SSH client not installed and do not guess a replacement executable.

Linux — use an ordinary account

Open Terminal, then type:

pwd
hostname
command -v ssh
ssh -V

pwd shows your current folder, hostname prints the local machine name, and command -v checks whether an SSH client exists. No command here attempts a login. Never use sudo merely to inspect the client version.

Worked example: the wrong host

A teacher says the exercise server is notes.training.invalid. That name is deliberately fictional: .invalid is reserved for names that should not resolve in normal public DNS. Before doing anything, the student must establish the actual authorised host name or address and the identity-checking procedure. Typing a random address into ssh is not a substitute.

A professional access request records the purpose, accountable owner, authorised identity, permitted resources, start/end time, host identity method and a plan to stop or recover from errors. In Umicom, a Master Controller may coordinate a service, but application permission and security decisions remain with their authorised Framework and operating-system owners.

Practice without a server

Draw three boxes labelled your computer, network and approved server. Put an ssh client in the first box and an SSH server in the last. Mark two checks: verify remote host identity and authenticate your own account. Now add a third check: authorise a specific read-only task. Explain which checks you must complete before you could inspect a real Umicom service.

Problems and safe responses

What you see What it might mean Safe next action
ssh is not recognised Client missing or not on PATH. Check Get-Command ssh or command -v ssh; do not install a server accidentally.
You do not know the remote hostname The target has not been identified. Ask the owner; do not scan arbitrary hosts.
You see a request to run as Administrator/root The example requires more privilege. Stop; this lesson needs none.

Check your understanding

  1. Recall: Does successful login automatically give permission to edit other people's data? Answer: No; authorisation is a separate decision.
  2. Explain: Why must the remote machine prove its identity? Answer: Otherwise you might provide credentials to the wrong host.
  3. Apply: What is the safer first step if a server address is missing? Answer: Obtain the approved address and verification procedure from its owner.

Record: The commands you ran, actual output (without sensitive identifiers if sharing), and whether a client was installed. Next: Chapter 74 — recognising ports and listening processes.

System Administration · Stage 6 · Chapter 74

Chapter 74 — Understand ports, listeners and the local host

Bits to Banking · System Administration From Zero · Stage 6 · Umicom Foundation
Prerequisite: Chapter 73; familiarity with a terminal prompt.
Safety: Only inspect your own machine; do not scan networks or change firewall rules.

The problem: one computer can offer many services

A computer can display a website, accept an SSH connection and host a database at the same time. An IP address identifies a network endpoint; a port number helps the operating system deliver a connection to a particular service on that endpoint. Think of an office building: the street address gets you to the building, while the room number directs you to a specific office. A port is not a password and opening one does not automatically make the service secure.

A process that is ready to accept connections is called a listener. 127.0.0.1 is the IPv4 loopback address: connections to it remain on the local computer. 0.0.0.0 as a listening address means the process accepts IPv4 connections on all its local interfaces, subject to firewall and routing rules. The difference matters before turning a teaching web server into a network service.

Terms to learn

Term Plain-language definition Example
TCP A transport for a reliable ordered stream of bytes. SSH and many HTTPS connections.
Listener Program waiting for connections on an address and port. A local Umicom learning HTTP server.
Loopback Network path to the same computer. 127.0.0.1:8765.
Established connection A two-way TCP conversation that exists now. Browser to local training server.
PID Process identifier assigned by the operating system. The number shown beside a listening process.

A TCP listener is not proof that the application is healthy. It may accept a connection but fail to read configuration, find its database or finish a user's request.

Windows — read listening TCP endpoints

Step 1. Open PowerShell 7. Check the command first:

Get-Command Get-NetTCPConnection -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

If it exists, list a few local TCP listeners:

Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen |
    Select-Object -First 12 LocalAddress, LocalPort, OwningProcess

Expected: A table of addresses, ports and process IDs. Some machines restrict some network details; an access-denied result is evidence to record, not a reason to use Administrator rights automatically.

Step 2. Ask which process owns one PID you observed. Replace 1234 with an actual displayed number:

Get-Process -Id 1234 | Select-Object Id, ProcessName

Expected: A process name. A process can exit between the two commands; a not found response can therefore be normal.

Step 3. Check one specific local port only if you know that a practice service is intentionally running on it:

Test-NetConnection -ComputerName 127.0.0.1 -Port 8765

TcpTestSucceeded: False means no TCP connection was made; it is not proof of a broken computer. A listener may simply be absent. True proves TCP connection establishment, not business readiness or identity.

Linux — inspect your own sockets

ss -ltn

-l means listening, -t means TCP and -n means numeric addresses and ports. A non-root user may not see the owning process name. Resist the temptation to add sudo until you have an authorised reason.

To observe a specifically permitted local port:

ss -ltn '( sport = :8765 )'

An empty result is expected if the teaching server is not running. These commands do not install or enable a service.

Worked Umicom scenario

A student starts the previously built C23 loopback HTTP laboratory on port 8765. The browser reaches the teaching page using http://127.0.0.1:8765/. Another laptop cannot connect, because the process was deliberately bound to loopback. Do not change the binding to 0.0.0.0 simply to make it accessible. Exposing a service requires an approved threat model, authentication, transport protection, firewall review and operational ownership.

Guided exercise

Write down three observations: a local listening address, a port number, and whether a process name was available. Identify whether the listener is loopback-only or potentially accessible on other interfaces. If no suitable practice listener exists, record not observed; do not create a public listener just to complete the worksheet.

Troubleshooting

Observation Interpretation Next safe check
Port appears but the application fails TCP listener is not a readiness guarantee. Inspect authorised application logs and dependency health.
Connection refused Nothing accepted the connection at that endpoint. Check the intended address and whether the service was meant to start.
Timed out No timely response; path or firewall could be involved. Check DNS, route and approved firewall policy without changing them.
0.0.0.0 appears Wildcard listener across local IPv4 interfaces. Flag for security review; do not assume internet reachability.

Review questions with answers

  1. What does 127.0.0.1 mean? Answer: The local computer's IPv4 loopback address.
  2. Does a successful TCP connection prove SSH host identity? Answer: No.
  3. Why does an unrecognised port deserve investigation? Answer: It could be unexpected exposure or a legitimate service; identify the owner before acting.

Next: Chapter 75 — understanding SSH host identity before connecting.

System Administration · Stage 6 · Chapter 75

Chapter 75 — SSH clients, host keys and safe first contact

Bits to Banking · System Administration From Zero · Stage 6 · Umicom Foundation
Prerequisite: Chapters 73–74.
Safety: Do not connect to an unknown host. Only use an authorised training server whose identity was independently provided.

What SSH actually provides

Secure Shell (SSH) is a protocol commonly used for secure terminal sessions, file transfer and controlled administration. An SSH client (such as ssh) runs on your computer; a server such as sshd runs on the remote host. SSH encrypts their conversation, but encryption alone is insufficient if the client connects to an impostor.

For that reason, the server presents a host key, and the client associates the host's identity with that key. The short fingerprint displayed by SSH helps an administrator compare the host's key with a trusted value obtained through a separate reliable channel, such as a secured asset register or direct confirmation from the authorised owner. Merely copying a fingerprint from the same unverified connection does not independently establish identity.

Terms that are often confused

Term What it proves or represents
SSH host key Identity of the remote SSH server, when independently verified.
User authentication key Your own account authentication key pair, if that method is enabled.
known_hosts Your client's remembered host-key observations. It is not the server's user database.
authorized_keys One server-side mechanism permitting specific public keys for a user.
Password / passphrase A secret that may authenticate an account or protect a private key.

Host authentication occurs before you should trust a remote login prompt. If a known host's key changes unexpectedly, stop. It can mean a legitimate server rebuild, an administrator-initiated rotation, a DNS problem or an attempted interception. Do not automatically bypass the warning.

Windows PowerShell — practise without connecting

Step 1. See whether the OpenSSH client is available:

Get-Command ssh, ssh-keygen -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object Name, Source
ssh -V

Expected: Executable paths and a version if installed. You need not enable the OpenSSH Server Windows feature for this lesson.

Step 2. Ask SSH to display how it would interpret a fictional destination without opening a network connection:

ssh -G learner@notes.training.invalid |
    Select-String -Pattern '^(hostname|user|port|stricthostkeychecking) '

-G prints the effective configuration and exits. This example uses a non-real .invalid domain. Config values reflect your installed OpenSSH and user configuration. Do not publish the full output if it contains private paths or host aliases.

Step 3. If you already have a known_hosts file, find its path but do not alter it:

Test-Path "$HOME\.ssh\known_hosts"

No file is required for completion. Absence is normal on a machine that has never made a trusted SSH connection.

Linux terminal — read configuration

command -v ssh
ssh -V
ssh -G learner@notes.training.invalid | grep -E '^(hostname|user|port|stricthostkeychecking) '

These commands use your current SSH configuration. Never replace a known host-key mismatch with -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no, and never delete known_hosts wholesale as a workaround.

Optional instructor-supervised connection

Only after an instructor supplies an actual approved hostname, expected host-key fingerprint, and a student account, the command shape is:

ssh student@APPROVED_TRAINING_HOST

APPROVED_TRAINING_HOST is a placeholder; do not paste this line unchanged and expect a login. If prompted to trust a new host, independently compare its fingerprint with the approved one. If they differ or the trusted fingerprint is unknown, cancel. Successful host verification does not grant permission to use sudo or change configuration.

Why ssh-keyscan is not enough

ssh-keyscan can fetch what a network endpoint claims is its host key. The tool does not prove the response came from the intended host. It may be useful to inventory keys once independent trust exists, but it must not be used alone to suppress the first-connection identity check.

Practice and expected answers

Describe the difference between an SSH client's identity and the server's host identity. Explain what you would do if the connection reports REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED. Correct answer: stop, record the observed warning without sensitive values, contact the responsible operator through a separate channel, and follow an approved host-key rotation procedure. Do not delete all known host keys.

Next: Chapter 76 — protecting SSH authentication keys in a private practice directory.

System Administration · Stage 6 · Chapter 76

Chapter 76 — SSH public keys, private keys and safe handling

Bits to Banking · System Administration From Zero · Stage 6 · Umicom Foundation
Prerequisite: Chapter 75.
Safety: Create only a disposable training key in a separate practice directory you own. Never upload the private key to GitHub.

Why key pairs are useful

Some SSH deployments authenticate a user with public-key cryptography. The user holds a private key, and the remote service stores or otherwise trusts the corresponding public key. The private key is like a unique signing tool: it must remain secret, even if an attacker knows the public key. A passphrase encrypts the private-key file at rest; it does not replace account authorisation, MFA policy or host verification.

A public key is intended for distribution to approved access systems. A private key is not. Never copy it into a repository, a support ticket, a screenshot, a classroom assignment or a chat message.

Vocabulary

Word Meaning
Ed25519 A widely used public-key signature algorithm supported by modern OpenSSH installations.
Private key Secret key material; only you or an approved secure key manager should have access.
Public key Corresponding data that can be given to an authorised server.
Fingerprint Short identifier derived from a key; compare against a trusted source.
Passphrase A secret protecting a locally stored private key.
Key rotation Replacing credentials using an authorised, recorded process.

Windows — create a disposable example in your own folder

Step 1. Open PowerShell 7 and create a learning folder if appropriate:

$Practice = Join-Path $HOME "UmicomLearning\ssh-keys"
Test-Path -LiteralPath $Practice
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $Practice -Force
Get-Location

New-Item writes to your home directory. Check the chosen path first. It is not a system configuration command.

Step 2. Check that the proposed key filename does not exist:

$Key = Join-Path $Practice "practice_ed25519"
Test-Path -LiteralPath $Key
Test-Path -LiteralPath "$Key.pub"

Both should report False before proceeding. If either exists, stop and choose a fresh name rather than overwrite it.

Step 3. Create the new practice key pair:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f $Key -C "umicom-training-only"

OpenSSH may ask for a passphrase twice. Use a passphrase you can remember for this short-lived practice exercise; do not paste a real work credential. If Ed25519 is unsupported by your approved environment, stop and consult the instructor; do not weaken security to complete the worksheet.

Step 4. Inspect only the public key's fingerprint:

ssh-keygen -lf "$Key.pub"
Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $Practice | Select-Object Name, Length

Expected: one practice_ed25519 private file and one practice_ed25519.pub public file. Never run Get-Content $Key to paste private-key content into documentation.

Linux — the same isolation idea

From a normal terminal:

mkdir -p "$HOME/UmicomLearning/ssh-keys"
ls -la "$HOME/UmicomLearning/ssh-keys"

Verify that practice_ed25519 and practice_ed25519.pub are absent. If they are, create the new training pair:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f "$HOME/UmicomLearning/ssh-keys/practice_ed25519" -C "umicom-training-only"
ssh-keygen -lf "$HOME/UmicomLearning/ssh-keys/practice_ed25519.pub"

OpenSSH normally creates private-key files with restrictive permissions. Observe permissions using ls -l rather than applying broad recursive changes.

Do not confuse key creation with server access

A key pair on your laptop does not grant remote access by itself. The remote owner must approve the account, key, target machine, and allowed activity. The server's own host key must be checked separately. There is no step in this lesson for copying the practice public key into a real server; that is an authorised administration task for a later supervised environment.

Git and Umicom warning

Before any git add -A, check whether you accidentally created keys inside a Git repository:

git status --short

This command works only if your current folder is inside a Git repository. Training keys should stay outside it. .gitignore is not a guarantee that a previously committed secret has disappeared from history. If you accidentally publish a real credential, stop and contact the responsible administrator for immediate revocation and replacement.

Review questions

  1. Which file may an authorised remote account receive? Answer: The public key, not the private key.
  2. Why use a separate training directory? Answer: To prevent accidental Git commits and avoid touching production credentials.
  3. Does a passphrase replace permission checks? Answer: No.
  4. Should you run ssh-keygen using Administrator/root for this exercise? Answer: No.

Next: Chapter 77 — dedicated service identities and least privilege.

System Administration · Stage 6 · Chapter 77

Chapter 77 — Service identities, least privilege and audit responsibility

Bits to Banking · System Administration From Zero · Stage 6 · Umicom Foundation
Prerequisite: Chapters 73–76.
Practical mode: Read-only observation; do not create or modify operating-system accounts.

Why services have identities

A person opening Umicom Notes has one identity. The Notes storage service may run under a different service identity. Separating them limits what each process can access and allows incidents to be traced back to their source. For example, a Notes API needs to read its own configuration and save notes through an approved store; it should not have unrestricted authority over banking ledgers, browser files or other users' documents.

The principle of least privilege means providing only the permissions required for a specified function. It is not a command to make every file unreadable. The administrator must first understand the application's actual work, files and dependencies, then grant the smallest sufficient rights. Permissions should be reviewed whenever that work changes.

Human account versus service account

Dimension Human account Service identity
Purpose Person uses interactive tools. Application runs an approved workload.
Typical login Interactive with MFA when supported. Often non-interactive, subject to platform policy.
Rights Based on staff role and task. Based on the narrow service contract.
Audit Who made a change and when. Which workload performed an operation.
Lifecycle Joiner, role change, leaver. Deployment, rotation, revocation, retirement.

A shared administrator account makes accountability difficult. A student's convenient default of “run everything as administrator” is especially dangerous on systems with real data.

Windows — inspect your current identity

Open PowerShell 7:

whoami
whoami /groups
Get-Process -Id $PID | Select-Object ProcessName, Id

whoami reports the account associated with the current process. /groups shows its group memberships and may produce many entries. This reveals capabilities associated with your own session; do not assume a group name alone proves a particular operation will succeed. $PID refers to the current PowerShell process.

If available, inspect the name and state only of a familiar service:

Get-Service | Select-Object -First 10 Name, Status, DisplayName

This does not reveal its complete service security configuration or effective file permissions. Reading that properly may require specific system rights and documented tooling.

Linux — read your account and process identity

whoami
id
ps -p $$ -o pid,user,comm

id lists your numeric user/group identifiers and their names. These values are not passwords. ps shows the current terminal shell process. Services may run under a different non-interactive account such as notes-service; do not assume that a Linux process with a familiar name runs as the same user as your shell.

For services on systems using systemd, a read-only example is:

systemctl --user list-units --type=service --no-pager

This lists your user-managed services; it does not start, stop or enable anything. Some environments may have no user systemd instance.

Worked Umicom scenario

Consider a fictional Notes system with three roles: a person who writes notes, a service that saves approved notes, and a support operator who reads service health. They should not all have the same authority. The writer needs access to their documents, the service needs narrowly scoped storage operations, and support needs logs and diagnostics without access to note contents. The Framework Data Server remains the authoritative persistence boundary for Umicom-owned state; frontends must not bypass it.

Now imagine a support technician wants to investigate a slow service. If they are allowed to read status and logs, do not automatically give them permission to delete database files or turn off audit logging. A reviewable change request records who requested access and who independently approved it.

Guided practical exercise

Create a permissions matrix on paper or in a text document:

Task Notes user Notes service Support operator
Read their own note Yes When authorised for processing No
Write a validated note through the service Yes Yes No
Read service readiness Maybe Yes Yes
Modify global security rules No No Only a separately authorised administrator

Challenge the matrix: what happens if a temporary support account is never removed? How could audit records distinguish the three roles?

Common mistakes

Using Administrator/root as a universal repair technique hides permissions defects, increases blast radius and may produce files owned by the wrong account. Making directories world-writable (chmod -R 777) is not a diagnostic tool. Creating a service identity is an approved provisioning change, not a default classroom exercise.

Review questions

  1. What does least privilege mean? Answer: Only the access actually required for the task.
  2. Why avoid a shared support login? Answer: It weakens accountability and controlled revocation.
  3. Do group memberships prove a service has correct filesystem access? Answer: Not completely; actual resource policies and access-control entries also matter.

Next: Chapter 78 — firewall rules and network exposure.

System Administration · Stage 6 · Chapter 78

Chapter 78 — Firewalls, network profiles and controlled exposure

Bits to Banking · System Administration From Zero · Stage 6 · Umicom Foundation
Prerequisite: Chapter 74: IP addresses, ports and listeners.
Safety: All commands are observations. Do not disable a firewall or open ports for this exercise.

A firewall is a policy gate, not an application login

A firewall decides which network traffic is permitted according to its policy: addresses, protocols, ports, interfaces and sometimes application identities. It does not normally verify that a human has permission to edit Umicom configuration or access a treasury record. An administrator must consider firewall policy alongside authentication, host identity, service privileges, application controls and logging.

Consider a local HTTP teaching service bound to 127.0.0.1:8765. Even if a firewall allows external TCP on that port, a loopback-only listener is not a service listening on the public interface. Conversely, a service bound to a wildcard address may be exposed through other routes unless appropriate controls prevent access. Listener, route and firewall are separate questions.

Important words

Term Meaning
Inbound rule Controls traffic arriving at an interface or host.
Outbound rule Controls traffic leaving an interface or host.
Network profile Category such as Domain, Private or Public used by Windows firewall policy.
Allowlist Explicit set of permitted identities, sources, ports or actions.
Deny by default Unlisted requests are refused rather than quietly granted.
Egress Traffic leaving a network or device.

A rule set can be complex and overlapping. The first rule a novice sees is not necessarily the effective rule for a connection.

Windows PowerShell — inspect without changing settings

Step 1. Inspect the firewall profiles:

Get-NetFirewallProfile |
    Select-Object Name, Enabled, DefaultInboundAction, DefaultOutboundAction

Expected: Typically one row for each Windows firewall profile. Do not infer a complete risk assessment from these four columns; third-party filters, enterprise policies and network placement can also affect traffic. Some environments may deny read access to certain settings.

Step 2. Check which network profiles Windows currently recognises:

Get-NetConnectionProfile |
    Select-Object Name, NetworkCategory, InterfaceAlias

Expected: Local interface details. A Public network category is not an error; changing it to Private merely to make something reachable is unsafe.

Step 3. If you are authorised to inspect a specific rule, query it by its actual name instead of dumping thousands of rules:

Get-NetFirewallRule | Select-Object -First 10 DisplayName, Enabled, Direction, Action

This is a read-only inventory, not proof that a connection is reachable from a particular source.

Linux — know your distribution before choosing tools

Different distributions may use nftables, firewalld, ufw or another policy manager. Inspect installed commands first:

command -v nft
command -v firewall-cmd
command -v ufw

An absent command is normal on some systems. Where policy allows read-only inspection by the current account, try:

nft list ruleset

This may return permission denied. Record that result rather than automatically escalating with sudo. Enterprise firewall policies may also be enforced on a separate gateway or cloud network security group.

A practical network-exposure decision

Imagine a classroom Notes system that needs to be accessed only from the student's own laptop. The correct solution may be to keep it on loopback and use the local browser. Publishing an open port on a school or office network would add risk without advancing the lesson.

If a team later needs remote access, its change proposal must name the requesting group, approved source addresses, destination interface, exact protocol/port, application authentication, expected logging, expiry and rollback. A firewall change alone must never become the approval for all those concerns.

Guided exercise

Without changing any settings, list one firewall profile, one local listener from Chapter 74, and whether it binds to loopback, a private address or a wildcard. Write a short assessment with known and unknown facts. Example: “The service listens on loopback. I have not performed an external reachability test. I cannot claim it is reachable from other devices.”

Problems and safer answers

Symptom Avoid Better observation
Connection timed out Turning the firewall off. Verify target, DNS, listener, routes and authorised rules separately.
nft missing Installing random firewall packages. Read your distribution's approved policy documentation.
Service works on localhost but not a phone Binding publicly without review. Determine whether remote access is intended at all.

Review questions

  1. Does permitting TCP 22 authorise any SSH user to log in? No: SSH authentication and OS authorisation still apply.
  2. Why does the Public network profile exist? Answer: It supplies a security posture suitable for untrusted networks.
  3. Should a beginner disable a firewall to test a tutorial? No.

Next: Chapter 79 — distinguish DNS resolution, routing and TCP connectivity.

System Administration · Stage 6 · Chapter 79

Chapter 79 — Trace DNS, routes and a TCP connection without guessing

Bits to Banking · System Administration From Zero · Stage 6 · Umicom Foundation
Prerequisite: Chapters 74 and 78.
Safety: Use read-only local checks and approved test destinations; do not sweep or probe unrelated networks.

One symptom can have many different causes

A browser says “This site can't be reached.” The problem might be a mistyped address, DNS lookup failure, network route, firewall restriction, service not listening, TLS certificate error or a functioning service that rejects your application request. Changing one setting without locating the failing stage can make matters worse.

Think of a letter's journey: first find the recipient's address (DNS); then find a route to that address (IP routing); then establish the intended conversation (TCP); then verify the server identity and encryption (TLS for HTTPS); finally ask the application to do useful work (HTTP/service readiness).

Vocabulary and evidence

Stage What it asks What it does not prove
DNS Can a name be resolved to address records? That the service is up.
Routing Is there a path for packets to the destination? That the correct application answers.
TCP connect Did a listener accept a connection? That TLS or application login is valid.
TLS Can the connection establish authenticated encryption? That the application transaction succeeds.
Application response Did the requested operation return a meaningful result? That all business processing is healthy.

Windows PowerShell — three small read-only checks

Step 1. Read a DNS record for a public example domain:

Resolve-DnsName example.org -Type A

example.org is reserved for documentation. An internet connection is required for a live public lookup; if none is available, note network lookup not run instead of claiming success.

Step 2. Read your computer's routing summary:

Get-NetRoute -AddressFamily IPv4 |
    Select-Object -First 12 DestinationPrefix, NextHop, InterfaceAlias

A 0.0.0.0/0 route is the general default IPv4 route. You are reading a snapshot, not installing or changing routes.

Step 3. Test a known HTTPS port only when internet access is permitted:

Test-NetConnection -ComputerName example.org -Port 443

If TcpTestSucceeded is false, continue diagnosis in order. Do not conclude which intermediate control blocked the connection from that single result.

Linux — equivalent observations

getent ahostsv4 example.org
ip -4 route

getent uses configured name-resolution facilities; ip route shows the IPv4 routing table. For a permitted public HTTPS check, one option is:

curl -I --connect-timeout 5 https://example.org/

curl may not be installed, and some networks require a proxy. -I sends a HEAD request; some servers handle HEAD differently from GET. A successful HTTPS response proves only that this particular request path worked at that moment.

A useful diagnostic ladder for Umicom Notes

Suppose the Notes teaching website is intended to run locally at http://127.0.0.1:8765/. First inspect the process and listening socket on your own computer. Next request that specific loopback URL. If the service is absent, look at its startup output. Do not inspect public DNS for 127.0.0.1, as it is already a numeric address. Do not change a firewall rule before checking the listener.

If a later authorised deployment uses a DNS name and HTTPS, also check the certificate host name, expiry and issuing chain (Chapter 80). A reachable port with a mismatched certificate remains a failure, not a partial success to suppress.

Guided exercise

Write a short incident report for this fictional observation:

DNS resolves the expected hostname. TCP times out. The operator has not checked the remote listener or the approved firewall policy.

Correct conclusion: DNS was observed working, TCP was not established, and the failure could lie in routes, filters, host reachability or listening state. Request the missing evidence; do not disable the firewall or restart a service on a guess.

Common mistakes

Avoid assuming ping must succeed; many hosts intentionally refuse ICMP echo requests. Avoid treating a DNS address as a trusted identity. Avoid pasting raw diagnostic output publicly when it includes internal names, addresses or network topology.

Review questions

  1. Does DNS resolution prove a service is healthy? No.
  2. What does a route describe? How traffic is directed toward an address range.
  3. Why collect evidence in order? Each step separates plausible failure categories and prevents unnecessary changes.

Next: Chapter 80 — HTTPS certificates, identities and expiry.

System Administration · Stage 6 · Chapter 80

Chapter 80 — Understand HTTPS, TLS certificates and trust

Bits to Banking · System Administration From Zero · Stage 6 · Umicom Foundation
Prerequisite: Chapter 79: DNS, TCP and application responses.
Safety: Inspect public documentation domains or a permitted training endpoint; never disable certificate validation as a shortcut.

Why a padlock is not the entire security story

When a browser uses an https:// address, it normally establishes a Transport Layer Security (TLS) connection. TLS protects network traffic and, when correctly validated, authenticates the server identity for the requested hostname. A certificate is a signed document binding key information to names and validity dates under a chain of trust. The user's browser or client still needs to enforce hostname matching, certificate validity and trusted issuing authorities.

An HTTPS padlock does not prove that the website is honest, authorised to receive your organisation's data or correctly implements Umicom payments. It indicates properties of the connection, not the business or its operator.

Terms to remember

Term Beginner explanation
Certificate Signed identity information presented for a service.
Certificate authority (CA) Trusted issuer that signs certificates under defined policies.
Common Name / SAN Names listed in a certificate; clients primarily use Subject Alternative Name.
Expiry Date beyond which a certificate should no longer be accepted as valid.
Private key Secret material corresponding to the certificate's public key.
TLS handshake Initial exchange that agrees on encryption and establishes identities.

The SSH host key studied earlier serves a related identity purpose but uses different trust and certificate mechanisms. Do not confuse an SSH host-key fingerprint with a website certificate chain.

Windows — inspect a known HTTPS URL

Open PowerShell 7 and check that curl.exe exists:

Get-Command curl.exe -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

Now, only if external network checks are permitted, request the HTTP response headers for the public example domain:

curl.exe --head --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 15 https://example.org/

If it succeeds, curl.exe has completed an HTTPS connection under its configured TLS trust policy and returned response headers. A network proxy or security appliance may affect the path. A failure could reflect DNS, TCP, TLS, proxy policy or the HTTP server. Do not append -k / --insecure to silence a certificate error.

For a web browser, inspect the site-information or connection-information panel. Modern browsers present the certificate details differently; look for the actual hostname, issuer, validity dates and security warnings.

Linux — inspect without saving secrets

command -v curl
curl --head --connect-timeout 5 --max-time 15 https://example.org/

Optionally, if an approved OpenSSL executable is available, a qualified instructor can demonstrate certificate inspection. Be aware that openssl s_client reports handshake details but does not necessarily fail its process exit code on all certificate-verification errors unless verification options are specified correctly. Do not use its output alone as proof of complete endpoint verification.

A fictional Umicom example

The Umicom Notes training service is published at https://notes.example.org in a lesson diagram. This is a documentation-style name, not an actual deployed service. If the certificate is valid for www.example.org but not the requested notes.example.org, the connection should fail hostname validation. The correct response is to repair the server certificate or DNS configuration through an approved change—not teach students to ignore warnings.

If a TLS certificate changes during scheduled renewal, retain evidence of the planned change, valid new certificate, service restart (if required), and a fresh connection test. A certificate renewal that disrupts application readiness remains an operational incident even if the new certificate is cryptographically valid.

Guided exercise

Sketch four gates for an HTTPS connection: resolve the name, connect over TCP, validate TLS identity, then receive an application response. Write a different possible failure for each gate. For TLS, use “certificate expired” or “name mismatch”, not “server down”.

Troubleshooting table

Symptom Safe explanation Next step
Certificate has expired Validity time failed. Ask the service owner for a controlled renewal.
Name mismatch Certificate does not represent the requested hostname. Check approved hostname and certificate configuration.
curl: (60) Trust or certificate verification problem. Keep validation enabled; retain the exact error without secrets.
HTTPS succeeds but Notes operation fails Application or business workflow may be broken. Inspect authorised application health separately.

Review questions

  1. Why is curl --insecure not a routine fix? It removes server-certificate verification and hides identity failures.
  2. Does HTTPS prove an organisation is trustworthy? No.
  3. Which name should be checked? The hostname requested by the client.

Next: Chapter 81 — careful SFTP and approved file transfer.

System Administration · Stage 6 · Chapter 81

Chapter 81 — SFTP, file transfer and source/destination ownership

Bits to Banking · System Administration From Zero · Stage 6 · Umicom Foundation
Prerequisite: SSH identity and public/private keys (Chapters 75–76).
Safety: Default to a local practice copy. Remote transfer is an optional, explicitly authorised exercise.

The difference between copying and transferring

You already know how to copy a file from one folder to another. A remote transfer copies bytes between machines. The same safety questions remain: where are the source and destination, which account may read and write them, how do we detect an accidental overwrite, and how do we verify that the received data is complete?

SFTP stands for SSH File Transfer Protocol. It operates through SSH and is distinct from the old plain-text FTP protocol. Although both transfer files, they do not use the same trust or security model. SFTP does not automatically provide backup history, business approval or permission to export confidential data.

Terms and boundaries

Word Meaning
Source The file you intend to copy.
Destination The new path that receives the bytes.
Overwrite Replacing a file already present at the destination.
Integrity hash A calculated digest used to compare file contents.
Remote account A separately authorised identity on the destination host.
Transfer log A record of what was attempted and observed, excluding secrets.

We will rehearse everything locally first. This avoids touching production servers or transmitting personal information during basic lessons.

Windows PowerShell — safe local rehearsal

Step 1. Create a practice folder inside your own profile:

$Root = Join-Path $HOME "UmicomLearning\transfer-practice"
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $Root -Force
Set-Location $Root

Step 2. Create a fictional non-sensitive report with your editor:

notepad .\notes-status.txt

Enter Umicom Notes training status: READY TO REVIEW and save. If a file already exists, inspect it before editing or choose a new practice folder.

Step 3. Make a separate receive directory and check before copying:

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path ".\received" -Force
Test-Path ".\received\notes-status.txt"

Only if the result is False, copy the training document:

Copy-Item -LiteralPath ".\notes-status.txt" -Destination ".\received\notes-status.txt"

Step 4. Compute both SHA-256 hashes:

Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 -LiteralPath ".\notes-status.txt"
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 -LiteralPath ".\received\notes-status.txt"

Expected: Two identical hashes if the files contain the same bytes. A matching hash demonstrates content equality under that algorithm; it does not prove that you were authorised to copy the file.

Linux terminal — equivalent private practice

mkdir -p "$HOME/UmicomLearning/transfer-practice/received"
cd "$HOME/UmicomLearning/transfer-practice"

Use your editor to create notes-status.txt. Before copying, check whether the destination already exists:

ls -l notes-status.txt
ls -l received/

Only if the destination is vacant, use:

cp -n notes-status.txt received/notes-status.txt
sha256sum notes-status.txt received/notes-status.txt

cp -n requests no overwrite; implementation and error behaviour can vary slightly by platform. The important rule remains: verify the destination before any copy.

What a real authorised SFTP session looks like

When the teacher provides an approved host, SSH host-key fingerprint, individual account and remote practice directory, an example command shape is:

sftp student@APPROVED_TRAINING_HOST

That placeholder is not an actual target and must be replaced only with an approved name. The SFTP session has its own commands such as pwd, lpwd, ls and lls for remote/local directories. Do not upload a file before checking which side each directory belongs to. A typical controlled workflow is to list the remote directory, upload one harmless training file into an explicitly assigned path, list it again, and compare contents via an approved integrity procedure.

Failure examples

Symptom Meaning or risk Action
Permission denied Account lacks required rights, or target is not correct. Verify the approved destination; do not escalate privileges.
Host-key change warning Remote identity may have changed. Stop and verify independently.
File already exists Overwrite risk. Choose a new training filename or request an approved versioning strategy.
Same filename, different hash Bytes differ. Preserve both copies; investigate before publishing or acting on them.

Questions and answers

  1. Why is SFTP different from old plain FTP? It uses SSH's authenticated, encrypted transport.
  2. Does a matching hash prove authorisation? No, only matching content for the compared files.
  3. When should you stop before a transfer? When the host identity, target, permissions or overwrite policy is unknown.

Next: Chapter 82 — safely separating service configuration from deployed program files.

System Administration · Stage 6 · Chapter 82

Chapter 82 — Configure a service safely in a private staging environment

Bits to Banking · System Administration From Zero · Stage 6 · Umicom Foundation
Prerequisite: Chapter 68 (private staging), 70 (readiness) and 77 (least privilege).
Safety: No registry edits, service installation, firewall changes, real passwords or production deployment.

Why application files and configuration are different

A compiled program contains operations the developer built into it. Configuration tells an installation which permitted options to use—for example, a listening address, a local notes directory or a log level. Two installations can run the same executable with different configuration. But configuration is not automatically safe: a single wildcard listener or database URL could expose sensitive functionality.

Umicom Framework provides reusable native configuration, security and application lifecycle contracts. A thin Umicom application should consume those services instead of creating its own configuration parser or introducing a PowerShell/Python setup script. This chapter is about the administrator's responsibilities: examining a configuration change, staging it privately, preserving the last known-good version, and testing the new state.

Separate five pieces of a release

Item Why it exists Good practice
Program binary Executable implementation. Hash and identify the tested revision.
Configuration file Deployment-specific settings. Validate schema and retain approved history.
Secret reference Points to credential storage. Do not store the secret directly in the repository.
Service definition Describes process start, account and restart policy. Review privileges and dependencies.
Verification evidence Shows what was actually tested and observed. Tie results to the exact staged revision.

Windows PowerShell — read-only plan and private directory

Start with a check of your current location and a safe candidate prefix:

Get-Location
$Stage = Join-Path $HOME "UmicomLearning\private-stage"
Test-Path -LiteralPath $Stage

If True, examine the existing contents before any writing:

Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $Stage -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

For a harmless Markdown configuration sketch, create a separate text file under a new training folder using Notepad:

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path "$HOME\UmicomLearning\service-config-training" -Force
notepad "$HOME\UmicomLearning\service-config-training\notes-configuration-review.md"

Write a short proposal, not a production configuration: listen address = 127.0.0.1, purpose = read-only Notes demonstration, owner = training, and secrets = none. Save and inspect it:

Get-Content "$HOME\UmicomLearning\service-config-training\notes-configuration-review.md"

This is training documentation. It is not a valid .ini, .yaml or Umicom application manifest, and nobody should use it as operational input.

Linux terminal — equivalent review

pwd
ls -la "$HOME/UmicomLearning"

If appropriate, create a new personal course folder and open its Markdown review document with your chosen text editor. An editor may be absent; do not install one as root merely to finish this lesson. Keep the simulated configuration outside production locations such as /etc.

How to review a genuine service definition (read-only)

On a Linux system with systemd and an authorised practice service, use a name actually provided by the instructor:

systemctl --user cat APPROVED_PRACTICE_SERVICE.service

This displays user-service unit content without enabling it. The name is a placeholder. If no approved unit exists, record not available. On Windows, Get-Service displays status but does not show the complete executable command or protected credentials; additional inspections must follow authorised procedures.

A staged change can still be blocked

Suppose the Notes executable was built and tested, but its new configuration points to a database that is unavailable. The process might start and show a PID while failing its actual work. A reviewer should separate process existence, dependency connection, application readiness and a successful Notes transaction. A restored previous configuration is a recovery outcome, not evidence that the new configuration deployed successfully.

Practical worksheet

Record the proposed listener binding, what will change, who approves it, which dependencies may be affected, how the change is tested, and how the previous configuration can be restored. For a first exercise, write no real secrets and make no operating-system service changes.

Review questions

  1. Why separate configuration from program binaries? The same tested program can be deployed with different controlled settings.
  2. Is a successful process start proof of service readiness? No.
  3. Should secrets be committed to Git? No.
  4. What should a failed change report? Failure plus any independently observed recovery, not false success.

Next: Chapter 83 — collecting an incident timeline without collecting unnecessary private information.

System Administration · Stage 6 · Chapter 83

Chapter 83 — Remote support, monitoring and incident evidence

Bits to Banking · System Administration From Zero · Stage 6 · Umicom Foundation
Prerequisite: Chapters 35, 47, 59 and 73–82.
Safety: Observe your own system or approved lab; never paste credentials, patient/customer data or full internal network inventories into public reports.

The support question is not simply “is it running?”

Imagine a fictional Umicom Notes service becomes unresponsive just as a trainee tries to open a saved document. A process may be alive, its TCP port may accept connections, and its log may contain no fatal error—yet the requested Notes operation can still fail because a storage dependency is unavailable. Reliable support therefore separates uptime, service readiness and business correctness.

A professional incident report records a timeline of observations, not a string of guesses. Include the time, machine or service label, source revision, check performed, observed result, expected result and relevant error code. Distinguish observed, inferred and not checked. If a remote operator cannot access a required log, record that limitation explicitly.

Terms

Word Meaning
Event log A stream of events recorded by an operating system or service.
Metric A measurement such as memory use, request count or queue depth.
Correlation ID Identifier used to connect records belonging to one operation.
Incident Unexpected event affecting a service's quality or availability.
Escalation Transferring a problem to someone with the right role, expertise or authority.
Redaction Removing sensitive information before sharing a record.

A metric such as high CPU is evidence of resource use, not automatic proof of the root cause. A log message may describe a symptom while the underlying failure lies elsewhere.

Windows PowerShell — capture your own process baseline

Step 1. Read the timestamp:

Get-Date -Format o

The ISO 8601 output includes a timezone offset, helping later readers compare records. Confirm the system clock is accurate before relying on event ordering.

Step 2. Read basic process observations:

Get-Process |
    Sort-Object -Property CPU -Descending |
    Select-Object -First 8 ProcessName, Id, CPU, WorkingSet64

This reports cumulative CPU time and memory-related metrics. High CPU in this table does not necessarily mean high current CPU utilisation; the sampling method matters.

Step 3. Inspect recent application-log entries only if your account is allowed:

Get-WinEvent -LogName Application -MaxEvents 8 |
    Select-Object TimeCreated, LevelDisplayName, ProviderName, Id

This does not expose every service error. Some systems restrict event-log access, and an empty list does not prove health. Do not export entire logs into a public issue.

Linux terminal — ordinary user observations

date --iso-8601=seconds
ps -eo pid,comm,%cpu,%mem --sort=-%cpu | head -n 9

For a user systemd session, where supported:

journalctl --user -n 12 --no-pager

Record journal unavailable if your environment has no user journal. Do not switch to root to obtain every system log for a class exercise.

Practical Umicom incident example

At 10:00 a trainee says “Notes will not open.” At 10:02 the operator observes a running process. At 10:03 a local TCP test succeeds. At 10:04 the Notes operation still fails. At 10:06 an approved storage-health check reports an unavailable dependency. The responsible team assesses whether to restore the previous configuration. A technician should not declare success at 10:03 merely because the network port works.

A clear support report might contain:

Time (local offset) Observation Evidence Remaining uncertainty
10:02+01:00 Process present PID and process name No business health confirmed
10:03+01:00 TCP accepted Loopback connection check Authentication/operation untested
10:04+01:00 Open Note failed Sanitised error code Exact storage cause uncertain
10:06+01:00 Storage unavailable Authorised readiness probe Remediation not approved

Do not add real customer records to such a table. Use pseudonymous service labels and technical identifiers approved for disclosure.

Guided exercise

Create an incident timeline for a fictional failed remote SSH access: DNS resolves, TCP connects, the SSH host key is unexpected, and the operator stops. Identify the correct outcome: connection blocked pending host verification. Record the warning, the target from the approved inventory, and the person responsible for verifying identity; do not attempt a second connection with validation disabled.

Common mistakes

Changing a firewall before examining listeners, rebooting a host to clear an unknown state, discarding logs before analysis and calling recovery “deployment success” all destroy useful distinctions. When changes are genuinely required, obtain approval, record the last known-good configuration and test the result independently.

Review questions

  1. Why use a timezone-aware timestamp? It helps compare events from different systems.
  2. Is high CPU proof of a coding defect? No; investigate workloads, sampling and dependencies.
  3. What makes an incident report useful? Reproducible observations, chronology, uncertainty, ownership and safe next actions.

Next: Chapter 84 — full capstone and professional support handover.

System Administration · Stage 6 · Chapter 84

Chapter 84 — Capstone: prepare a safe remote Umicom support review

Bits to Banking · System Administration From Zero · Stage 6 · Umicom Foundation
Prerequisite: Chapters 73–83 and Stage 5 private deployment.
Learning outcome: Explain and verify the readiness evidence required before a remote support session.
Safety: Offline simulation by default; no production account, firewall, SSH server, certificate or service is changed.

Your task

You are a junior administrator supporting a fictional Umicom Notes training service. Another person reports that it has stopped responding. Your supervisor asks you to prepare a short preflight review without connecting to production. You have an account label and a claimed host name, but no approved host-key fingerprint yet. A professional should recognise that some information is missing and refuse a remote session until those checks are completed.

This capstone combines remote identity, SSH keys, listener investigation, network boundaries, least privilege, configuration changes, backup/recovery and incident evidence. It also connects the classroom exercise to the new C23 remote-access-review laboratory, which consumes the previous deployment evidence model rather than building another production security engine.

Step 1 — write down the system boundary

Create a private training note containing the following fictional fields:

Field Example value How it is verified
Service notes-demo Approved application inventory
Remote host label notes.training.invalid Must be replaced with a real authorised target before access
Requester MakerA Authorised identity system
Independent reviewer CheckerB Separate accountable approval
Source revision Exact Git commit Read from the actual deployed artifact/manifest
Host key Not yet verified Obtain fingerprint from a separate trusted channel
Network scope Local or approved sources only Authorised firewall/routes review
Recovery plan Drafted, not executed Approved runbook and restore drill

The correct decision with the host key missing is BLOCKED. Do not fill in a value you have not checked.

Step 2 — confirm the local environment

Windows PowerShell:

$PSVersionTable.PSVersion
Get-Location
Get-Command ssh, git, cmake -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue |
    Select-Object Name, Source

Linux terminal:

uname -s
pwd
command -v ssh
command -v git
command -v cmake

Expected: Your actual tool inventory. If a command is missing, record its absence; do not silently install tools or claim you ran tests with them.

Step 3 — verify the previous native evidence laboratory

From your checked-out Umicom-Bits2Banking root on Windows PowerShell:

Set-Location "C:\umicom\Umicom-Bits2Banking"
$env:Path = "C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin;$env:Path"
cmake -S ".\labs\native\remote-access-review" `
    -B ".\output\learning-build\remote-access-review" `
    -G Ninja `
    -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER="C:\msys64\ucrt64\bin\gcc.exe" `
    -DBUILD_TESTING=ON
cmake --build ".\output\learning-build\remote-access-review" --parallel 2
ctest --test-dir ".\output\learning-build\remote-access-review" --no-tests=error --output-on-failure

The remote-access-review laboratory requires previous Updates 39–42. Do not run the commands if those files have not yet been merged. Each prior library remains the authoritative C23 implementation of its own educational contract.

On Linux:

cmake -S labs/native/remote-access-review -B output/learning-build/remote-access-review -G Ninja -DBUILD_TESTING=ON
cmake --build output/learning-build/remote-access-review --parallel 2
ctest --test-dir output/learning-build/remote-access-review --no-tests=error --output-on-failure

These commands may create files inside the private build directory; they do not configure a real operating-system service.

Step 4 — run relevant negative tests separately

Windows PowerShell:

ctest --test-dir ".\output\learning-build\remote-access-review" `
    -R "bits2banking\.remote-review\.(host-key|stale|rollback|atomic-output)$" `
    --no-tests=error --output-on-failure

Read the results for four different concerns: missing remote identity evidence, stale observations, unsuccessful deployment and preservation of output when data is invalid. A test passing means the simulation's policy behaved as expected. It does not establish that a real host is trustworthy.

Step 5 — decide whether to escalate or proceed

Imagine two situations:

  1. The service's host identity is unknown, but network access appears possible. Decision: Block and request verified host identity; do not try credentials.
  2. The last deployment failed, but the previous state was restored and independently checked. Decision: Report restoration, not successful delivery of the new release.

For either case, record what was done, what was not done, who owns the decision and which checks must happen next. Escalation is a professional action, not a personal failure.

Practical assessment — 10 points

Criterion Points
Identifies requester, reviewer, scope and authorised target 2
Distinguishes host-key identity from user authentication 2
Inspects environment without creating service changes 2
Runs native tests and records actual observed result 2
Reports BLOCKED versus RESTORED_ONLY without overstating evidence 2

Suggested passing standard: 8/10 with no critical safety error. Critical errors include ignoring a host-key warning, publishing a private key, changing a firewall without permission or falsely claiming production readiness.

Instructor notes and answer guide

The learner should demonstrate the ssh -G read-only configuration preview, understand why an SSH hostname is not automatically trusted, and be able to say “not tested” when no authorised server exists. The C23 lab is deliberately non-operational: no tool-generated decision is an access grant. Review the case notes for accurate uncertainty and sensitive-data redaction.

From beginner skills to Umicom architecture

A Framework application should not build its own shadow SSH or credential subsystem. Umicom Framework owns reusable C23/Assembly contracts for VCS, configuration, security, service lifecycle and build verification; Umicom OS composes approved system services; Umicom Kernel owns privileged hardware/kernel behaviour. Bits2Banking supplies isolated exercises and helps learners understand each boundary. When the native lab is ready for production consideration, first compare it with existing Framework capabilities, design the contract, and obtain project-owner approval before any cross-repository modification.

Next stage: Secure administration beyond remote login—permission reviews, secure recovery, infrastructure inventories, automation governance and real operational acceptance tests.

Update 43 · Stage 6 learning reference

Stage 6 glossary — remote administration from first principles

Host: Computer or virtual machine offering a service. Client: Program requesting the service. Endpoint: Address/protocol/port combination that receives network traffic. Loopback: Interface pointing to the same computer, such as IPv4 127.0.0.1. Listener: Process awaiting network connections. SSH: Encrypted protocol commonly used for remote administration and file transfer. Host key: Server-identity material checked by an SSH client. Public key: Key data that may be distributed to authorised access systems. Private key: Secret signing material that must not be published. Passphrase: Secret protecting stored private-key data. Known hosts: Client-side record of server identities observed and trusted. Authentication: Demonstration of identity credentials. Authorisation: Decision defining allowed activities. Least privilege: Restrict access to what a task requires. Service identity: Account or workload principal under which software runs.

Firewall: Policy mechanism controlling selected network flows. Inbound rule: Policy for arriving traffic. Outbound rule: Policy for departing traffic. Allowlist: Explicitly named permitted actors, paths, actions or addresses. DNS: Name-resolution infrastructure; it is not a source of user authentication. Route: Rule selecting the next hop toward an address. TCP: Ordered, reliable byte-stream protocol. TLS: Protocol providing authenticated encrypted transport when correctly verified. SAN: Subject Alternative Name; the names a certificate covers. Certificate authority: Trusted issuer within a particular validation context. Expiry: End of a certificate or approval validity window. SFTP: File-transfer protocol using SSH. SHA-256: Cryptographic digest for comparing observed file content, not proof of user authorisation.

Uptime: A process or service has remained available at a level being measured. Readiness: The service is prepared to perform a particular operation. Business correctness: The operation produced its intended controlled outcome. Incident timeline: Ordered and traceable observations about a problem. Correlation ID: Identifier linking logs and operations. Redaction: Removing sensitive data from a shared record. Rollback: Restore a previously accepted state after an unsuccessful change. RESTORED_ONLY: Classroom state indicating the previous release was restored, not that the new release passed. REVIEWABLE: Classroom state indicating all supplied fictional policy fields are present; no real approval has been granted.

Update 43 · Stage 6 learning reference

System Administration From Zero — Stage 6

Secure remote access, network services and support evidence

Bits to Banking · Umicom Foundation · Chapters 73–84 · October 2026

This stage builds on the existing 72-chapter course. It teaches how to reason safely about remote administration before trying to connect to another computer. It does not expect students to own a server, know Linux administration or have an SSH key. Most exercises inspect the current computer and write only in an expressly chosen private learning folder.

Suggested progression

Chapter Topic Practice outcome
73 Remote administration boundaries Name client, host, account, identity and authorisation.
74 TCP listeners and ports Explain loopback and identify a local listener.
75 SSH host identity Preview client configuration without connecting; refuse unknown host keys.
76 SSH key pairs Create an optional disposable key in a private practice directory.
77 Least-privilege service identities Distinguish human, service and support permissions.
78 Firewall policy Observe profile/rules without opening ports.
79 DNS, routes and TCP Diagnose failure by layer rather than guess.
80 TLS and HTTPS Explain hostname matching, certificate validity and trust.
81 Controlled file transfer Copy harmless data locally and compare SHA-256 hashes.
82 Service configuration Draft a private, non-executable configuration review.
83 Incident evidence Record a chronological, redacted support timeline.
84 Capstone Produce a safe preflight report and run the offline C23 lab.

What the learner needs

A normal Windows PowerShell 7 terminal or an ordinary Linux shell, a text editor, and enough rights to read information about their own computer. SSH, Git, CMake and GCC are optional in the early lessons. Students who reach the C23 capstone need Updates 39–42 already merged with their preserved native labs.

Never request or share real passwords, SSH private keys, account tokens, customer/patient files or full internal network inventories. The examples use notes.training.invalid, a reserved fictional hostname. A real connection requires independently supplied permission and verified host identity.

Practical goals

By the end, the student can differentiate transport reachability from authentication and business readiness; produce a non-sensitive evidence table; explain why an SSH host-key warning must not be ignored; and run deterministic C23 tests that deliberately reject missing observations. The lab's REVIEWABLE status is not a remote-access grant.

Continue with Chapter 73 and keep the Stage 6 workbook nearby.

Update 43 · Stage 6 learning reference

Stage 6 instructor guide — from local commands to responsible remote support

Course: System Administration From Zero · Stage 6 · Chapters 73–84
Teaching duration: Six to ten sessions of 30–60 minutes, adapted to age and prior experience.
Prerequisite: Students can type commands and tell the difference between reading and changing system state.

Teaching objectives

Learners should explain transport versus authentication versus authorisation; identify where a listener binds; distinguish SSH host and user keys; describe the risk of unverified host-key changes; recognise DNS/TCP/TLS/application failures; produce a short support timeline; and demonstrate a bounded C23 offline review with explicit failure cases.

Lesson order and checkpoints

Sessions 1–2: Chapters 73–75, no network connections required. Ask students to identify the local host, ssh client and listener on their own machine. Session 3: Chapter 76, optional disposable key creation—verify the training path is outside Git and do not collect the private key. Sessions 4–5: Chapters 77–80, permissions matrix, firewall read-only inspection, DNS route ladder and HTTPS hostname verification. Session 6: Chapters 81–82, local integrity-copy exercise and a non-executable configuration proposal. Sessions 7–8: Chapters 83–84, support timeline, negative CTest cases and capstone report.

Safety boundaries

Do not give students production remote server credentials, real patient/customer data or permission to change firewall rules. Hostnames ending in .invalid are illustrative and should not be used for live connection. A real instructor-provided VM, if used, must have clearly documented permission, student isolation, approved host-key fingerprint and an expiry/deprovisioning policy. No exercise requires Administrator/root by default.

The course's C23 tool merely evaluates caller-supplied fictional evidence. It never performs SSH, TLS, routing, deployment or human authorisation. Never treat REVIEWABLE as “safe to log in.”

Assessment rubric

Use the Stage 6 workbook. Score concepts, safe command execution, honest recording of unsupported environments, and evidence-based conclusions. Penalise unsafe shortcuts even if they produce the expected output. Younger learners may draw the trust model, describe command output verbally and complete a supervised local-only exercise; older learners can submit a concise, fully redacted support incident report.

Common misconceptions to correct

  • A running process proves business readiness: false.
  • A successful TCP connection proves server identity: false.
  • A public SSH key provides remote permission: false; the host owner must authorise it.
  • ssh-keyscan independently proves a host's key: false.
  • curl --insecure is an ordinary certificate fix: false.
  • An automatic green CTest count authorises a production change: false.
  • A failed upgrade whose previous state was restored is a successful upgrade: false.

Instructor evidence sheet

Record the actual teaching OS, shell, observed installed commands, number of tests run, sources used, student safety decisions and any blocked exercises. Keep private information out of public class reports. When a resource is unavailable, mark it not run rather than substitute an invented result.

Update 43 · Stage 6 learning reference

Stage 6 command reference — safe local checks and optional practice writes

Audience: First-time system administrators. Every command in this reference is interactive shell usage, never an implementation script. Check current directory and user authority before every write.

What you need PowerShell 7 (Windows) Linux Changes files?
Show your current folder Get-Location pwd No
Local computer name $env:COMPUTERNAME hostname No

SSH client version ssh -V ssh -V No

List local TCP listeners Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen ss -ltn No

Your login identity whoami whoami and id No
Firewall profile/manager Get-NetFirewallProfile command -v nft No

Review native C23 tests ctest --test-dir <build> --output-on-failure Same Tests write only where their own contracts allow

Do not use as routine fixes: ssh -o StrictHostKeyChecking=no, curl --insecure, firewall disablement, broad recursive permission changes, deletion of all known_hosts, git reset --hard, git clean -fd, git push --force, or unapproved service starts/stops. A failing or missing command is diagnostic evidence, not a request to escalate privileges.

If a step requires a specific server, replace placeholders only with approved training hostnames supplied with independent identity verification. Never paste private keys, tokens or sensitive network diagrams into public chats or repositories.

Update 43 · Stage 6 learning reference

Stage 6 workbook — safe remote administration and incident response

Umicom Foundation · System Administration From Zero · Chapters 73–84

This workbook is designed for students of any age. Each exercise begins with a question, asks for an observation, and ends with a short explanation. Never include real credentials or confidential information in a submitted answer. An unavailable tool or missing approved training host is a valid outcome; record it rather than simulate a success.

Exercise A — A remote connection has several gates

On paper, draw a local computer, network, remote host, SSH user, and policy reviewer. Label who checks host identity, who checks user authentication and who can authorise a task. Write one sentence explaining why a TCP connection does not give permission to change a server.

Suggested answer: TCP reachability only shows that a connection can be established; server identity, user identity and action permissions are separate controls.

Exercise B — Identify a local listener

Run one read-only listener command from Chapter 74. Record the selected local address and port, and whether the associated process name was available. Circle 127.0.0.1 for loopback, or another address if observed. Do not create a new public listener.

Suggested answer: A 127.0.0.1 listener receives local IPv4 connections only. A wildcard address is broader but not necessarily reachable from the internet.

Exercise C — SSH host-key change

Your training SSH client reports that a familiar host's key has changed. List your next three actions.

Suggested answer: Stop the login; retain a sanitised report of the warning and destination; verify the intended host and approved fingerprint through a different trusted channel. Never bypass host-key checking.

Exercise D — Public versus private keys

If you choose the Chapter 76 training key exercise, record the names of the two generated files and only the public key's fingerprint. Do not attach the private key to your coursework. Explain why a key pair does not provide a server account automatically.

Suggested answer: The remote system must separately authorise a specific public key for a permitted identity and scope.

Exercise E — Firewalls and DNS

Classify each fictional problem: (1) a DNS name does not resolve, (2) a port is not listening, (3) the TLS certificate's hostname differs, (4) a Notes action returns an application error. For each, identify the stage where you should collect evidence and one unsafe shortcut to avoid.

Suggested answer: DNS, listener/TCP, TLS identity and application respectively. Avoid disabling security checks, arbitrary port exposure and changes without evidence.

Exercise F — Hash a local practice copy

Follow Chapter 81 using a harmless training text document. Compare both SHA-256 values. State whether the file bytes match and whether that proves you were authorised to upload them to any remote host.

Suggested answer: Matching digests support content equality, not permission to transfer data.

Exercise G — C23 review negative cases

After building the remote-access-review lab with previous Updates 39–42 present, run the host-key, rollback, stale and atomic-output named tests. Record the actual result, not the published reference test count. Explain why REVIEWABLE is not a real SSH access grant.

Final assessment (20 marks)

Task Marks Evidence
Remote trust-boundary diagram 3 Correct separation of identity and authorisation
Local listener observation 3 Accurate address/port, no changes
SSH-host warning response 3 Stops and verifies independently
Least-privilege matrix 3 Human/service/support permissions differ
Layered DNS/TCP/TLS diagnosis 3 No security-bypass shortcuts
C23 negative-test evidence 3 Actual test names and outputs
Redacted incident handover 2 Known, unknown, next action and owner

A pass requires no critical safety breach. Never publish a private key, bypass host-key validation, force a firewall change, invent a test result or claim production authorisation based on fictional C23 flags. A student who reports an accurate “not tested” meets the evidence requirement better than one who invents success.

Stage 6 conclusion — safe remote support

You have completed the introductory 84-chapter System Administration course. Your next learning project is to review an authorised training VM with independent host identity verification and to record what remains unverified. No lesson grants permission to connect to a production system.
